Review Title: Perfect Movie! I gave 9 because of potential wasted. It could be revolutionary in superhero movies. Joaquin is outstanding.
Review:
Yes, Todd Phillips said that this Joker has nothing to do with the Joker from Batman.
This is just a delusion from mentally ill person in Arkham State Hospital. Everything started when psychotherapist said Arthur that they won't meet again, and when Arthur stated that he won't be able to get the medication.
When Arthur stopped taking medications, everything started. From murders, Sophia, Murrey, Thomas Wayne, everything went to hell after that. At the end of the movie, psychotherapist is smiling at him. If he did everything he did, she won't be smiling.I expected character development close to Walter White. Mentally ill loser (Walter was physically ill) starting to snap because of injustice and torture. When he is Arthur Fleck, he looks normal from the outside, but he isn't from the inside. When he is under make up, he gets self-confidence, because he is someone else at that moment. After years of self pity and injustice, a moment happens when he feels someone's fear of him. And more he brings his own justice, he gets more confidence. And as movie goes, he became lost in his own view of justice. He started from someone like Walter White and became Heisenberg. More he feels it, more he likes it. He became what he is, because he believe justice is what he think he is, not what society tell him.Joker could be the hero of the poor, Robin Hood who steal happiness from rich people, not only money. Batman is rich, he is the opposite to Joker. That's way Joker has so many people with him. It could become a movement, like Anonymous in modern times.I always hated superhero movies, because it never had depth in villains minds. Why do they do what they do?! Give them a reason. People did terrible things in the past because of political or religion view of life, twisted view of justice. Give him a reason to believe he is right. It could be revolutionary in super hero movies. Create villains that people could understand they nature.

Review Title: First Impressions: One to Think About
Review: "Knock knock..."Joker is about Arthur Fleck, he's a disturbed and formerly hospitalized clown in Gotham City who lives with his sick mother he takes care of. He also has aspirations of being a stand up comic and is a big fan of the Murray Franklin Show, Gotham's big TV late night talk show and after a video of Arthur's bizarre stand up act gets shown on the show... he's invited to be appear on the show for an interview.So I JUST saw this movie....And... it's all still flushing around in my head so I'm having a hard time writing a proper review for it. I keep starting to write and then I start over and so on... so I wouldn't call this a review, more "first impressions".Because there's a lot to get into with this movie and there's things to discuss.I got home from Avengers: Endgame and knew exactly what I thought about it.Joker... I don't know, I need some time and maybe even to see it again. Maybe in IMAX which I can't BELIEVE Warner Bros put the time and effort into making an IMAX version of THIS movie...But... I liked it... might have even loved it.... but it's not perfect. It's not the R-rated Joker movie of my dreams.... which would kinda just be The Dark Knight but with blood. Like I already GOT my perfect Batman AND Joker movie in 2008 so anything after that is a nice bonus.There's nothing in it I disliked but... it never hit heights I would have hit if I was given the keys to the Gotham City kingdom. For one thing, it's a shockingly small movie, hence my slack-jawed reaction to finding out that right now people are watching this in IMAX.It's a psychological thriller, it's not a horror movie or a crime drama. It's a drama about an insane person.The movie it reminded me of the most wasn't even the Scorsese movies Todd Phillips says he was inspired by but One Hour Photo. This is a 2 hour movie where the only guy we're with is a complete psychopath.There's no hero in this movie. There's no relief, there's nobody trying to stop the Joker. So the worse he gets, the more tense the movie gets because we know there's no Batman or Commissioner Gordon coming to the rescue here. So this makes for a pretty unpleasant movie.Joaquin Phoenix gives an Oscar-worthy performance as Joker and he might even win for this movie. Is he better than Heath Ledger? No.... but it's SUCH a different version of the character it's not even comparable.... which brings me to maybe my main complaint with this movie....I think.... this movie would be a LOT better.... if it were not called Joker. I think knowing it's The Joker I had so many expectations of where this movie would take this character and that kinda hurt my first viewing.Maybe on a rewatch that'll go away completely but I kept thinking this movie would play better if you didn't know you were watching a movie about the Batman villain The Joker until the final act. Because I certainly kept expecting a lot more... Joker-y type stuff in this movie and it really doesn't tap into the Joker I'm familiar with.This isn't a criminal mastermind mixed with a serial killer with a permanent smile, it's not Nicholson's Joker or Ledger's Joker.... it's a whole new thing.It really is more of a Joker origin story than a Joker movie. Like this entire movie almost feels like the first act of a proper Joker solo movie. I REALLY hope they make a sequel because as much as I enjoyed elements of it I wanted way more.Lack of Batman is not the issue here at all, by the way. Joaquin Phoenix does more than enough to carry the movie on his own but.... at the end of the day I wanted more of a horror movie, more of a crime movie.What we GOT was very good..... but I can't help but think it could have been better.This is not a proper concise review, I might be able to have one in the near future. Because like I said there's loads to get into.But I'll say I liked what I saw... but I need more time to process it.I'm definitely VERY curious to hear what others think of Joker.

Review Title: Joaquin Phoenix sure to get Best Actor Oscar nomination for this
Review: "Joker" (2019 release; 122 min.) brings the origin story of Joker. As the movie opens, we are in Gotham City in the early 80s (late in the movie we see that "Zorro the Gay Blade" is playing in theaters). A guy named Arthur is working various gigs as a clown (driving foot traffic for stores, visiting children at the hospital). One day he is savagely beaten by a group of young thugs. Arthur is shaking up badly. Meanwhile he pursues his dream of becoming a stand-up comedian, but things aren't going very well with that either... At this point we are 15 min. into the movie but to tell you more of the plot would spoil your viewing experience, you'll just have to see for yourself how it all plays out.Couple of comments: this is the latest movie from director Todd Phillips, best known for "The Hangover" franchise. Here he goes a very different direction, bringing us the origin story of the famed Joker character in the DC Comics universe. Joker has been portrayed many times before (including Jack Nicholson and Heath Ledger), but it typically came across like an over-the-top, caricature-like performance. Not so with Joaquin Phoenix. Here we truly get to understand the person that became Joker. Joaquin Phoenix is utterly brilliant, and I have zero doubt that he will pick up a Best Actor Oscar nomination (and many other accolades) for this. The script brilliantly reflects the chaos that existed in New York/Gotham in the late 70s/early 80s (garbage strike, super rats, etc.). Please note that this film is MILES away from your typical "super hero" movie a la Avengers. For one, almost no CGI to speak of. Instead this is a dark, brooding and intense psychological thriller and character study. It is for me one of the best surprises of the year, period."Joker" has been playing in theaters for weeks now, and I finally went to see it this weekend. The Sunday matinee screening where I saw this at in a large theater was very well attended, and that tells you about the staying power of this film. If you like your comic super hero movies dark and intense, I'd readily suggest you check this out, be it in the theater, on VOD, or eventually on DVD/Blu-ray, and draw your own conclusion.

Review Title: A character study of a broken man who finally decides to embrace his insanity, that just so happens to be based on a popular comic book character.
Review:
'Joker' is not a comic book movie about the origin of a supervillain. Instead, it is a character study of a broken man who finally decides to embrace his insanity, that just so happens to be produced by a recognisable brand. And oh man, how I wish more mainstream films were like this.Joaquin Phoenix delivers a career-defining powerhouse performance as the lead that also arguably redefines the Joker. Whereas the character has previously been portrayed as a criminal mastermind that poses an unstoppable foil to Batman, or in Jared Leto's case, just a joke, Phoenix achieves something I previously thought unfathomable; he makes the character sympathetic.
This Joker, or more precisely, Arthur Fleck, is just an ordinary individual you could easily encounter in the street, who's constantly laughing from the pain of his mere existence. This guy can't catch a break, as he is continuously pushed around and mentally tormented by the world around him, and I could not help but feel pity and remorse for the guy. Even the most subtle nuances Phoenix imposes, such as his changing tone of voice or the way he walks makes his portrayal feel all the more real. When Fleck finally snaps back at the world, I didn't necessarily barrack for him, as his actions are violent and gruesome. However, I was deeply fascinated by how Fleck finally accepts himself as a sociopathic maniac and seeks his own personal justice through the persona of the Joker.
The rest of the supporting cast does a serviceable job, especially Robert De Niro, who hasn't given a performance this lively in years. But Phoenix is the main attraction, and rightfully so. To make the comparison to Heath Ledger's Joker and argue who's better would be pointless. This is a very different portrayal, and I believe the best of both worlds should be embraced.Apart from my ravings about Phoenix, I was very impressed with Todd Phillips' direction, especially considering his previous filmography comprises of sex comedies. Without going too far into spoiler territory, I found the way Phillips chose to tell this story pleasantly surprising. It takes a similar route to something like 'Fight Club' or 'American Psycho', wherein you're unsure whether all the events unfolding on-screen are actually happening in reality or merely the character's imagination. I believe it could be an entirely plausible origin for the Joker in the comics.
Under Phillips' guidance, the majority of the stylistic features are efficiently executed. The muted colour palette and handheld cinematography compliment the film's gritty, realistic tone very well. Hildur Guðnadóttir's score, which is mainly comprised of cellos and other stringed instruments, is hauntingly beautiful. It subtly underscores the Joker's deeper delving into crime and insanity until it crescendos into an anxiety-inducing orchestra when full-on chaos unfolds.My only issue with the film is despite its aims to be a standalone character study, it still dares to shoehorn in tributes and references to the comics. This is only done to a minor extent but it just felt jarring because it did not contribute to the story being told whatsoever.Although I had optimistic hopes for this film, I was still blown away by it. Overall, it was just nice to see a comic book movie that isn't part of a greater cinematic universe that has to set up multiple sequels. Despite all the controversy and criticism swirling around the film's release, I have no doubt over time it will be considered one of the great films of this decade. It is not the perfect comic book movie, but it is rather, the most personal comic book movie I've ever seen.

Review Title: Dark, Disturbing, Gritty, Adult, and Completely the Antithesis of Disney's Marvel
Review: After I watched Joker, I needed some time to really digest it. Joker is like no other comic book/superhero movie that has ever existed. It truly transcends the genre and almost breaks it entirely. It is the kind of movie I have been wanting to see take place in the Batman universe since the Nolan films: dark, disturbing, gritty, adult, and completely the antithesis of Marvel and all it's Disney friendly content.Joaquin Phoenix is amazing in this movie. My wife asked me if he was better than Heath Ledger and Jack Nicholson as Joker. My first reaction was that he was not, but it is because he is playing a character for the entirety of the movie that is still in the process of becoming Joker. Phoenix has created a an original character that takes very little from previous Joker portrayals. It is so different from Heath and Jack that comparisons seem unfair and unnecessary.The movie looks fantastic and beautifully shot. You can really tell the Scorsese influence, but I am 100% of the opinion that this is not a copy of Taxi Driver or King of Comedy, heavily influenced, yes, but most certainly something new. Todd Phillips deserves credit for making a movie that does not seek to please the comic book/superhero audience and instead gives them something challenging like nothing that has come before in this genre.I do have some small criticisms in terms of the plot, but they do not plague the film enough to knock it down. I recommend this highly. (A-)

Review Title: DO WE GET THE LAST LAUGH...?
Review: Todd Phillips (Old School/The Hangover trilogy, scary to refer to them that way) foray into the comic book world comes in the form of this origin story. Following roughly along the lines of the graphic novella The Killing Joke (w/sprinkles of The Dark Knight Returns), this dark tale focuses on Arthur Fleck's (Joaquin Phoenix) struggles w/his own brand of madness, working a sorry job as a clown, caring for his home-bound mom who once worked for the Wayne estate (played by Six Feet Under's Frances Conroy who was also in DC's ill-fated Catwoman w/Halle Berry) & pining his hopes on becoming a successful comedian so much so that he'll get an opportunity to appear on his favorite late night talk show (whose host is played by Robert DeNiro) but the world he inhabits (reminiscent of the Big Apple's grungy grime of the 70's) infects his very soul where even his laughter seems to be killing him (posited as an extension of his Tourette's syndrome). When things start to spiral (a vicious attack by some youths as he tries to recover property they've stolen from him) & the eventual release comes when he stands up to 3 Wall Street types on a subway car, Fleck ditches his meds & finds new purpose to his being as he rises to meet his fate. Heavily influenced by 2 pillars of Scorsese filmdom (Taxi Driver & The King of Comedy), not to mention the stunt casting of DeNiro (star of both those masterpieces) provides a template for this narrative which feels like a strong performance shoehorned into a very familiar & predictable story-line but other than some lapses in faith in the audience attention span, the film works in spite of itself.

Review Title: A brilliant masterpiece, but I understand why it's difficult to watch.
Review: My second review in IMDB. I went to watch this film for a second time and I'm considering a third. I have never, and I mean, NEVER, wanted to go back and watch a movie again and again. As other commenters - I admit that I also understand why the movie causes division. I understand the political views, I understand that many shooting victim relatives are worried this could somehow spark an individual with the desire to shoot, to really do it, I understand the movie TALKS openly about mental illness. I am so sorry to all victims. But you should understand that this movie is not MEANT to empathize Arthur through allowing yourself to justify his actions. He is a broken man, he was abused to the point he lost his way. People get all kinds of bullying and a lot of people survive though it, yet a lot of them don't. They either end it or they turn into the darker side - a coping mechanisms, sick mechanism. But this IS the human. It is complex, it is an endless encyclopedia and I think it is of a great importance to show this. Maybe the word you're searching for is heartbreaking. We see a man who could have survived through the bullying, but instead he gave himself to the demons, because of constant social suppression merged with the mental illness he already had. It is how it is. Should we ignore it? Should we slam it just because it's political, or because it's showing guns, or because it touches the topic of mental illness, or anything else that sparks controversy? No... Yes, these topics are complex, it's not news, it is the hardest things to talk about, but I think it's bold and brave to make this film and I appreciate the whole cast and crew for making it. This film shows all of it, all raw from the human soul. And what makes it good is, as our screenwriting lecturer in our film course explains, we show a complex character, which does bad things, but we understand why he/she does them. We are not MEANT to sympathise, empathize, but UNDERSTAND why they did what they did.I am sorry for those who find it dark or too involved in these topics. But I think it's extremely important for this movie to be here, to teach about things they don't tell us in school, but also to provoke yourself, to see what you should never turn into. This movie is NOT urging people to become criminals. No, no, no, no, no. It's supposed to make you sick, it's supposed to make you want to leave the room, because you don't want to ever end up in this situation. Because we understand how horrible all of this is. Unfortunately, not all people will understand this movie. And this is where all the negativity comes from. As I said, I understand the so many relatives, friends, acquaintances of people who have died in similar scenarios, I understand why they are worried. We don't know who is watching this movie, we don't know what is going through their head. And unfortunately, it may cause a spark in them. But if this movie is not out, we never see it. We never understand. We never are aware, we don't have the proper knowledge of it. Because me knowing more about mental illness teaches me how to protect, how to react, how to preserve. It teaches me to treat people right, to be there for them, to NEVER do them wrong. And trust me, one person is not a lot, but it is something and it could save a soul.It is a difficult film, but it was shown flawlessly.

Below is the transcript from my video review on my YouTube channel, Slice of Pai. Please subscribe, would mean the world to me and I'm trying to change it :)The Joker. I'm not joking when I say this could be the first time that two different actors could win an Oscar for playing the same character.Now the Joker is one of the most iconic villains of all time, but do not walk into this expecting it to be a typical comicbook movie with blockbuster action.First and foremost it is a character study of the Joker, of one man's descent into madness, but the terrifying part was just how real it all felt. Arthur Fleck, A Fleck, Affleck? is a really sympathetic character at the beginning of the movie and you really feel for him when you see how mistreated he gets just for being different and misunderstood. Things just keep going from bad to worse for him over the course of the movie until he finally snaps when he gets pushed to the edge.And when he hit Rock Bottom, he rose from the ashes like a Joaquin Phoenix.
Because at the end of the day, this is his movie and he carried it with ease. He has clearly been psychologically scarred, his laugh is something like a tic from a neurological condition and he does have something of an Oedipal complex as well. You can see the Joker's physical and mental transformation when he embraces his madness in all its perverse glory.Speaking of physical transformations, his method acting reminded me of Christian Bale's. His emaciated physique was a bit like the Machinest, and parts of the movie also reminded me of American Psycho and had me questioning what was real and what wasn't.As the whole movie is shot from Joker's perspective, it brings some very interesting twists to the Joker and Batman lore. I'll delve into that more in a spoiler section at the end of this video.The film is also a character study of society as a whole, and although it is set in the fictional city of Gotham in 1982, it's still social commentary for today. Too many people tear down others to feel good about themselves, too many people want to see other people fail, too many people have no empathy. The movie shows the dangers of nihilism that is caused by all of the above, and it shines a light on the importance of mental health treatment.The film also brings credence to the expression "Don't meet your heroes", as the public personas so many celebrities have of wanting to help people are really just facades, which is something I've noticed as well.The film was excellently directed by Todd Phillipps and although it was a slow burn, that simmering really gave Joker so much nuance and complexity. The colour palette was very gritty and Gotham-esque and gave the movie a depressed ambience to reflect Arthur's.Overall I'd give joker 4.5/5 Pais, but I'm bumping it up to 5 for Joaqin Phoenix's Oscar Worthy performance.Have you seen Joker yet? GRADE: B+THIS FILM IS HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.IN BRIEF: A terrific performance by Joaquin Phoenix makes this psychological thriller all the more memorable.JIM'S REVIEW: Going into Todd Phillip's Joker, I expected an origin tale about a super villain with standard comic book action, well choreographed stunt work, and enough CGI and explosions to cause any fanboy to fall into a stupor. I was greatly surprised and totally wrong!Instead, the film is a thoughtful examination of mental illness and also a thoroughly riveting psychological study of this iconic madman. The screenplay, by the director and Scott Silver, follows the mythology of DC Universe and its characters faithfully, with some added asides to their plot that seem more like a classy Martin Scorsese film than the typical comic book action fantasy genre. (This approach might disappoint the movie's younger target audience, but it had the opposite effect on this reviewer.)The movie aims to be much more in its depiction of a damaged man wanting to change the damaged world. This villain's method to his madness remains unhinged and savage, a product as cold and deliberate as the unforgiving society in which he exists. We go through each twist and turn on his journey toward insanity.Joker is the making of a murderer on a grand scale. Visually, Mr. Phillips skillfully delivers a film that is stunning to behold, from Lawrence Sher's stark use of chiaroscuro cinematography with vivid color and dramatic lighting to 's 60's meets 80's retro production design of a decaying Gotham. Add to that, the concise editing by Jeff Groth and Hildur Guðnadóttir's atonal music score that sets the ominous tone for the action on display.As the story unfolds, the film goes out of its way to make the title character, Arthur Fleck (aka Joker), all too sympathetic to moviegoers. This loser has been so abused by society and is literally beaten down by everyone in his orbit. The odds are against him. He just can't win. One can only pity this man. Yet, do these acts of violence justify his harmful actions? The film wants us to believe so. In fact, the movie downplays the Joker's murderous spree to any victim other than those who are cruel or mean-spirited. This is revenge fantasy, plain and simple. The filmmakers seem to say that the bad deserve his wrath.As Arthur plunges further into the madness that is known as Joker, the killings too becomes gorier and justify vigilantism and violence. This is a major misstep in storytelling, and a tad dishonest in its plot structure, as are some of his delusions which are not being clearly established as real or imaginary scenes. The blur between illusion and reality remains a enigma. Still the film continually intrigues with its edgy style, top-notch production values, and an astonishing performance by Joaquin Phoenix that demands to be seen.One would hope that Mr. Phoenix's performance merits Oscar consideration. The actor creates a character that is so operatic and over-the-top which adds to the enjoyment of this drama. His Joker has all of the signature moves that are even more troubling and pronounced than in previous interpretations. He gives his character so much complexity and angst with a hint of desperation. His high pitched laughter, graceful posturing, and exaggerated movement help to create a mesmerizing presence. His painted clown mask is wore well in order to hide all of the torment bubbling up inside. It is a revelation, an acting tour-de-force that will be long remembered.Providing strong support are Robert DeNiro channeling his The King of Comedy heydays as talk show host Murray Franklin, Glenn Fleshler as Arthur's belligerent co-worker, Brett Cullen as corrupt millionaire Thomas Wayne, and Frances Conroy as Arthur's sickly mother.Joker is not your ordinary comic book story of a megalomaniac and his conquest for fame. It is a complex and disturbing character study with an extraordinary star turn at its dark and heartless core.

Review: Don't trust good reviews. I'm not impressed. Bad reviews are coming out. Like a critic said: this film doesn't have much to say and says it loudly. The Gotham, Arkham world isn't fresh; same old recycled stuff; seen the TV series Gotham? It's like a bigger budget version of Gotham, focusing on Joker, compacted into a movie. The film's cinematic and atmospheric. But I preferred Joker's back story in Batman (1989). This film's too realistic: I don't want a superhero movie (or in this case a super villain movie) set in such a realistic world. Put simply: a guy named Arthur (Joaquin Phoenix) has problems; he lives with his mom; he works as a clown; he's fired and gradually becomes Joker, leading a social movement of disgruntled mob-mentality citizens dressed as clowns seeking to overthrow Gotham's elite. In the end there's a riot; the mob-mentality disgruntled citizens of Gotham are dressed as clowns. Wow. As if a TV show would invite a loser like Arthur to be a guest; TV host Murray Franklin (Robert De Niro) makes fun of Joker who, at this point's a loser named Arthur trying comedy at a stand up club; a videotaped clip's played and ridiculed on the Murray Franklin TV show: it was that bad. Then Arthur's invited to be a guest on the show: guys like Arthur aren't invited to be guests on David Letterman style TV shows; celebrities are, not mentally ill guys like Arthur. The film's all atmosphere and impact. But it lacks substance. I would've liked this as a Batman movie; the epic scale would make for an awesome Batman v Joker film. Joker isn't interesting enough to justify an entire movie spent on him. I remember reading a review of Solo: A Star Wars Story (2018) which pointed out that Han Solo's back story isn't interesting. Same here. And it's not like we haven't seen Joker before; Batman (1989) managed to do Joker's story, without it taking up the whole movie. 5/10.

Review Title: Joker is a profound character study, which intends to touch deep wounds of society that fit into the intrinsic political and behavioral issues of humanity
Review:
There are few films that can be considered a masterpiece of seventh art, which have a set of characteristics and qualities that take them to other levels. This new rereading of one of the most complex and controversial characters in cinema enters this gallery for being able to innovate in language and content. The fact that the Joker is a character from DC Comics' comics is a mere detail that, were it not for the character's characteristic clothes and makeup. It is a profound character study, which intends to touch deep wounds of society that fit into the intrinsic political and behavioral issues of humanity.
One of the first big surprises when we first heard about the film was the director. Until then known for good comedies, especially for the 'Drink, Don't Marry' franchise, Todd Phillips is responsible for the script alongside Scott Silver (The Winner, Decisive Hours) and the duo decided to take that deep dive into the psyche of one of greatest villains in history, presenting us with their lives, fears, afflictions and, especially, their motivations. Much more than being a film of the origin of a villain, the work aims to show a human being and his rise as a symbol in a decadent society. Knowing that the entire film would be sustained from the protagonist's performance, Phillips knew that for that he would need an actor who could embody this whole developmental arc and wrote the character with Joaquin Phoenix in mind to play it. After an initial refusal and much insistence, the actor was convinced by Phillips to bring the iconic character back to life through a new perspective on his origins.
In Joker, Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix) works as a clown for a talent agency and, every week, he needs to go to a social worker, due to his known mental problems. After being fired, Fleck reacts badly to the mockery of three men on the subway and kills them. The murders start a popular movement against the elite of Gotham City, of which Thomas Wayne (Brett Cullen) is its greatest representative.
To speak of 'Joker' is to speak of exquisite direction and impressive performance. Phillips and Silver's script is a millimeter drama that gradually builds the character in the public eye, making us understand his motivations. Joaquin Phoenix, who is known for the immersion he performs for his characters, is in virtually every scene in the film and dominates the screen impressively. The construction of the actor had to lose about 23 kilos for the character, in order to pass all the physical fragility, in addition to the mental character of the character. Phoenix also studied different personality disorders and practiced the characteristic Joker laugh over and over until he reached the desired result.
The first half hour of the film shows Arthur Fleck as a person with mental disorders, who suffers from anxiety, and is forced to go to a social worker due to his problems. Due to these disturbances, he laughs wildly not compatible with the feeling. The curious thing is how, throughout the film, the variation of laughter is used for the most diverse situations. To make matters worse, Arthur still loses his job unfairly, which further shakes him. Many consider him strange, which does not let him have real friends. Fleck is portrayed as invisible in society. People do not stop in the street to watch his antics, some attack him out of pure malice. Phoenix, at the beginning of the film, walks slowly, hunched over, practically dragging himself to reinforce the feeling of defeat before life. The only one who supports and gives him affection is his sick mother, whom Arthur takes care of with all the affection. His mother always told him that he was born to bring joy and laughter to the world, and that is exactly what he also believed in all his life.
From the murder of three men who provoked and assaulted him on the subway, we can see the turn in Arthur's life. By committing the act in a brutal way and not feeling remorse, he starts to gain confidence, his posture is erect, he takes on the face of the clown to commit other murders as his thirst for revenge against those who hurt him somehow, even against the closest people. Little by little, facts about Arthur's childhood are revealed, how he was adopted and suffered various types of physical and psychological violence from his mother's boyfriends, who did not protect him from his stepfather's aggression. Arthur is frighteningly transforming himself from a person no one noticed, to become a symbol of an uprising against Gotham's richest and most powerful. As the character himself quotes at one point, his life went from total tragedy to absolute comedy.
Phillips sets his film at a time, the turn of the 1970s to the 1980s, and builds on the cinema of that time. The film empathizes with the character of Arthur Flecker, and makes us sensitive to his plight. But the ailments suffered by the character do not ultimately refer to the social order, but to the family environment (especially from the moment when the madness of the mother and the abuse of the stepfather are revealed). Production designer Mark Friedberg and art director Laura Ballinger do not set the film in an imaginary city with imprecise temporality. On the contrary, the Gotham City that we see on the screen is evidently New York in the early 1980s. The choice is not accidental: it is the historic moment of the rise of neoliberalism. Moment of state bankruptcy and cut in public services - such as the psychiatric care service that Flecker benefited from - and the political projection of figures from the business world - such as Thomas Wayne, who proposes to save the city by running for mayor. The result is a dirty, brave and transgressive film, as consistent with the essence of its title character as with the idea of a chaotic, decadent and without any rules Gotham City.
The script has several inspirations, such as the classic 'The King of Comedy' and 'Taxi Driver' (by Martin Scorsese). Arthur Fleck and Travis Bickle (Robert De Niro in the Scorsese film) are men who are mistreated by the environment and socially marginalized. However, the arc of the comics 'A Piada Mortal', which is the biggest source of references of all in this feature. This mix of references has one objective: to criticize society. The film is an increasingly visceral and profound journey in a universe where madness meets cruelty. It is not a narrative about a failure with a gun, seeking violence to find its place in the world. The escalation of violence is not shown by the lack of empathy or the failure of its protagonist. In fact, it's just the opposite, with Joker making the viewer feel disgusted enough to not have the slightest empathy for the character. A joker is not someone to be inspired or glorified, on the contrary, the character is the refuse of a society that destroys everything and everyone. This interpretation is also the opposite of what was led by Heath Ledger in another brilliant interpretation of the villain. It is much, much worse, capable of causing disturbance. If the Ledger Joker was an anarchist, the Phoenix Joker is disturbed, traumatized and ill.
Todd Phillips also manipulates the narrative in such a way that the wildness of the Joker, or rather, of Arthur Fleck, is not only justified but, at first, almost forgivable. From a thorough character study, we followed from Arthur's still innocence to becoming a tougher and more confident man, in all the stages of a transformation resulting much more from society's vices than from his failures. Todd Phillips' direction is precise. He knows how to portray the decadent and violent Gotham City in a raw and visceral way. Phillips uses several plans from the bottom up to emphasize the superiority of the slight Joker to those who see him, as well as using and abusing close-ups and every minute bodily movement of Phoenix's interpretation. Also interesting is the staircase symbol used in the director's script, which idealizes the staircases as dramatic figures of rise and fall: if at a moment Arthur commits his first murders and, shortly after, he runs away climbing one of these stairs, it is in his discovery - in his self-disclosure - like who he is (or who he was transformed in) that he finally descends triumphantly. Coupled with the dark photography by Lawrence Sher, the precise editing by Jeff Groth and especially the soundtrack by the Icelandic Hildur Guðnadóttir, which creates an impressively disturbing melancholy atmosphere, the construction of this Gotham City and these characters that inhabit it is even more believable and real.
Without any previous reference, it is an original story that reinvents basic characteristics of the character, without ever actually modifying him or citing any of his predecessors. At the same time, it appropriates the collective memory in relation to the previous versions, not exactly in the sense of comparing them, but of knowing in advance what the character is sick and violent. The film deals with the lack of love, childhood trauma and lack of compassion in the world. Joker is a raw and visceral demonstration of the perverse, which shows a man with psychological problems, with a ruined family life and who is despised and ignored by co-workers and society in general.
The biggest problem presented by him is not the idea of a maniac being praised for his violent acts, but the fact that we are part of a society so sick and sunk in mud that the maniac ends up being glorified precisely for being who he is. When, close to the end, the Joker finally finds himself idolized by a crowd, there is an awareness of an artist there who has finally found his place in the world. And an artist who receives recognition is hardly deviated to another path. A mesmerizing work that uses violence to show the scorn of the current world. The feature comes to impact and make the audience reflect on society and on their own attitudes towards others.

I was born in a small town and grew up reading Indrajal Comics. My superheroes were more or less unidimensional like Phantom, Mandrake, Flash Gordon. The first introduction to Marvel was in the early 90s through Spiderman. My introduction to DC and Marvel was made much later in my life and took me a few years to realize the layers of a character like Joker. What I like most about the film is that you need not be an expert in DC Comics to feel the film. Joker has gone way beyond DC and the film is a perfect metamorphosis of a character from the comic book to a larger than life antihero.
Joaquin Phoenix has played a mentally disturbed man even in the past (To Die For). The character he played in Gladiator was also not of a stable man. I was extremely disturbed by Phoenix's depiction of the fictionalized version of Roman Emperor Commodus in Gladiator. But if that was disturbing, what he did as Joker is phenomenally disturbing, utterly unnerving and needless to say a brilliant performance. I think the history of cinema will remember Joaquin for playing Joker. As a performance, this is truly masterclass.
There are few films which remain with you for a while. There are few films that are difficult to forget and there are few films which you want to forget but difficult to get rid of. Joker is such a film. Todd Phillips has made a masterpiece.

Review Title: A New Take on the Joker
Review: Being used to disappointment by Hollywood, I'm always a bit wary of over-hyped movies. Especially when the hype precedes a major release. But the Joker delivers on all expectations and then some.Joker is an interesting character study into the descent of madness -- always a fun topic. Yet, the film goes beyond its protagonist and examines the forces that allow such evils to exist. Make no mistake, this film is dark, nihilistic, and gritty.There is also something authentic about superhero movies without actual superheroes. Joker's lack of superpowers lets the viewer put themselves in the protagonist's shoes. I also appreciate films that allow its audience to emphasize its villain. The fact that this character transformation can (and has) happen in our real-world adds another layer to the dark nature of the film.If the themes don't make the film dark enough, the cinematography and violence will. The entire film is run through a dark green filter that creates a dreadful mood throughout. Violence is R-rated and leaves little to the imagination. A much-appreciated move considering the overabundance of PG-13 movies out there.Soundtrack is beautiful and is artful. It's obvious that careful thought was placed for each scene for music and composition. The darkest scenes of utmost despair paired with soundtrack dissonance is stunning.Yet, the film seems somewhat incompatible with the DC version of the Batman universe. With the disconnect between this film and DC, it makes the film no better than Taxi Driver with clown make-up. But the ambiguity that comes with an unreliable narrator leaves lots of room for imagination. Not a lot of points to be taken off there.4.5/5. Beautiful, artistic, and dark. Easily Joaquin Phoenix's magnum opus so far.

Review Title: Got it: evil people have backstories and issues.
Review: Joker offers a detailed portrait of a sick person's backstory. In this way, it offers a leftist interpretation of "what went wrong". We have seen this before, and I suppose that Christopher Nolan's efforts on the joker (with Heath Ledger in Dark Knight) pointed the way, but here the emphasis is only on the backstory, with no big screen action to entertain along the way, and the same, simple message repeated over and over again.The performance by Joaquin Phoenix is very convincing and indeed worthy of the praise lavished upon it, but I believe that the metascore on this creation reflects the fact that this is not a film to be watched over and over again, to mine for more insights. There is only one insight here: that people are born into contexts and molded by the forces around them. This is a message which we often ignore in denouncing violent criminals, but here it is recited over and over again in a sort of incantation, with the aim, perhaps, of suggesting that society should focus more on "therapy" and "rehabilitation" than on punishment for criminals.I found Joker worth watching once, but I will not watch it again, despite agreeing that the lead did a splendid job of acting in this role.

Review Title: A little original, a little derivative, a lot disturbing, and TOTALLY well done
Review: One could argue this film is original (because it finds new perspectives on the most familiar of characters and stories) or one could argue this movie is derivative (because it basically just mashed up a Batman villain and Taxi Driver). Personally, I think most art mixes up familiar elements to make something new, from DJs to filmmakers. And the new thing that Phillips creates here is incredibly well done and evocative. It is not easy to make something that is so familiar and so new all at once. It is not easy to make a film that both comments on mental illness in society and re-tells Batman's origins for the umpteenth time. Not that long ago Logan reminded audiences that comics could still make great art when freed from the burdens of franchise/universe building...but I'm still glad that Joker reminded us again.

Review Title: Best Joker's body language thus far.
Review: Uniqueness of this production, when compared with Batman comic books, games and other movies, is undeniable. Joker's identity and his plans are very much the opposite of a mystery in here. This shift in perspective may just be what "Joker" needed to be the best movie based on a character from DC.For some reason, Joker is always taken very seriously by actors playing his role. Jack Nicolson's and Heath Ledger's Jokers were definitely phenomenal yet mostly acted by voice and facial expressions. It's fair to say that Joaquin Phoenix raised the bar by an order of magnitude. In his version of the Joker, voice acting and facial expressions are just minor parts of a bigger picture. His Joker moves like Joker. His Joker laughs and dances like Joker. It's very apparent how his Joker thinks, and he thinks like the Joker. He just feels like him. The level of immersion is unprecedented.Artistically, "Joker" is just beautiful. Music is perfect, Gotham feels enchanting but depressing, character costumes are very appealing. Whole experience is hypnotic, almost like in a comic book.Besides a true Joker and good Gotham, the movie contains some less important themes which aren't bad but may be distracting. It felt like they put two rather irrelevant scenes featuring young Bruce Wayne just for the sake of using the franchise. I also think that yet another version of Batman origins scene is the last thing a DC fan would like to see. All easily forgivable as everyone leaves their yaw on cinema floor anyway.

Wasn't really excited about seeing this movie, really ambivalent about Joaquin Phoenix actually, but my son wanted to go. Suffice it to say, I'm no longer ambivalent about Joaquin Phoenix! He is phenomenal as Arthur/Joker, without being cartoonish, over-the-top, or in-your-face crazy. His is a very very dark, but realistic, portrayal of years and years and years of insults, abuse, being dismissed as a nobody, to finally being essentially invisible, a non-entity, worthless, while slowly and painfully breaking down and apart from the inside out, until his transformation into the Joker. Phoenix made me feel sorry for Arthur; I cared about him, and could easily follow and understand how he could become Joker....I think that's a HUGE difference from all the other 1 dimensional versions of Joker. The violence is not scary or off-putting at all; rather, what horrified me the most is not only the breaking down of a human spirit so radically and completely, over a long course of time, by anyone and almost everyone that crossed paths with him, but also the realization that it is happening every single day outside of the movie theater, to real people. And no one did a thing to help him. Phoenix makes this comic book character so human, you are compelled to feel his pain and despair, and you can't NOT feel compassion for him! Definitely worth seeing!

Review Title: Worth every one of those 10 stars

The acting is just superb, the story excellent, the musical score was quite haunting and the directing was exquisite - quite simply 10 out of 10.How could so many people not enjoy it? The only explanation I can come up with it that perhaps they went to the cinema expecting a Batman movie, or hoping that it would be a CGI-packed action movie like the typical DC comic movie. If that's what you were expecting then I can understand the disappointment but to give it just 1 star because you felt stupid or foolish is really unfair.This is an incredibly compelling origin story with some sensational acting that deserves every Oscar it wins (which I am sure it will) but to those of you expecting a standard Batman or Ironman flick or if you're hoping for Wonder Woman to jump out from behind a car then you will be disappointed. Review Title: Joaquin takes us to a twisted, dark fantasyland
Review: It's hard to think of a film released in the past year that has been more polarizing than Todd Phillips' 'Joker.' Some loved it, others didn't. But most appreciated the beauty of the dark exposé on a symptom of society's ignorance of the mentally ill.'Joker' is nothing without its anti-hero lead, Joaquin Phoenix, who does what any true actor must do to get into the mindset of a poor, lost soul like Arthur Fleck. It's not just a physical transformation - which was impressive in and of itself given the actor's vulnerable, emaciated state - but it's an emotional downward spiral into oblivion that cannot be done without someone who has real acting chops. It's really no surprise this portrayal earned Phoenix a "best actor" nod. He brings Fleck's inner demons out onto the table, devolving into the monster he becomes as each minute passes before our very eyes.Aside from the acting prowess on display, 'Joker' showcases how a DC property can come to life on screen without allowing the good guys to win. The film cuts against the grain - everything we thought we knew about a "superhero" movie comes off the rails. It makes you think, too - who is worth rooting for in a situation like this? The grittiness makes everything that much more real, albeit not in a positive way.True, many feel conflicted about 'Joker.' On one hand, there is a "sick to my stomach" feeling that's hard to shake, which we get based on the natural good that's deep within all of us. But on the other hand, the film can be considered a modern-day cinematic character masterpiece, and that's likely the kind of legacy the film will have.

The cinematography is great, with exceptional sound design to accompany it. The acting is solid throughout and you may become convinced that Joaquin just isn't okay.The message of this film can be interpreted in many ways. One make an argument that 2019 is an awful time for this film to come out. But one can also say that the message is important to hear and consider. It's not political but societal, and no matter what your interpretation is, it revolves around the idea that we need to take care of each other as humans.Ultimately, this is a great story that's presented just as well. It's not necessarily gripping, and you probably won't get too emotionally invested. It's not going to tug at your heart strings either. You will, however, become empathetic to Arthur Fleck and his world, as he sees it, as he experiences it. And while you may not agree with his methods, you will agree that, in his world, something had to be done.

When I left the movie theater in 2008 after watching the "Dark Knight," I asked myself "can comic book movies be like this?" Jump to 2019, after leaving the theater from the screening of "Joker," I asked myself again "can comic book movies be like this?" Joker is Todd Phillips' magnum opus that is groundbreaking in its approach to the medium of comic book movies, and is a realistically unsettling look at how society can affect a person to become a heinous criminal. Joaquin Phoenix gives a tour de force performance - every tick, giggle, and movement seemed calculated while he was playing Arthur Fleck and when he inevitably turns into the Joker. In the movie Fleck is introduced as having a condition that makes him laugh uncontrollably, and sometimes when he laughed too hard, Phoenix would grab his chest in pain. As a viewer you can empathize with this individual who is marginalized by society, but at the same Phoenix's multi-layered performance hinted at a darker mind full of malice. Joker is definitely a villain, but Phoenix's performance made him a layered villain.I know this movie will do well simply because of America's fascination of true crime documentaries and shows. After leaving the theater, my friend who is also a true crime enthusiast let me know that if she hears, reads, or watches something about a shooter/killer in the news or show, she tries to dig deeper into that person's life, social media, etc. to look for clues as to why that person became such a horrible person. This movie really plays to the audience that loves true crime the most, as Phillips documents one person's turn from regular (but troubled) hard working man, to mass serial killer. It isn't a movie for everybody, but if you understand this movie is from the perspective of the villain, and it is a tragic tale of one man's inevitable fall into madness, then this movie becomes so much more.

Review Title: Astonishingly great; the solo film that the Joker needed
Review: In this brilliant version of the Joker's origins, we follow Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix) a man who struggles with societal 'norms'. Very early on, we see he has an inner conflict. Something dark and disturbing is inside this human being and the way it manifests itself is yet to be seen. He lives with his mother who he takes care of and watches his favourite show hosted by the popular Murray Franklin (Robert De Niro). He's an aspiring comedian; someone who wants to be recognised for doing something great and just to be accepted. He is hideously treated by people outside the comfort of his home, all fuelling his turmoil and boiling anger inside. Arthur Fleck is about to discover his alter ego... I loved this film. Not only is it a great DC movie, it's a compelling character study of someone disregarded by society to the point of insanity. I can't wait to watch it again and Phoenix is just phenomenal in the role; the way he contorts his body into the Clown Prince Of Crime himself and the physical build up to that is essential viewing along with the scarring psychological aspect. There are naturally going to be comparisons made to previous incarnations of the Joker, but they are all very different and Phoenix does something completely different with the character that we really have not seen before. Director Todd Phillips (The Hangover, War Dogs) who also co-wrote the screenplay with Scott Silver (8 Mile, The Fighter) has really shown the incredible potential of his cinematic vision. The way the camera moves, the ways the performances are captured, the in depth eye for detail, the pitch black humour spectacularly projected (especially in the scene of Joker's first bombastic killing; a disturbing scene but with a sharp comic edge). The psychological trauma of the Joker has not been captured this well on screen before in my opinion and it's a deeply engaging, beautifully shot and thought provoking masterpiece

Review Title: Social commentary smiling in your face
Review:
"Joker" is a 2019 drama directed by Todd Phillips starring Joaquin Phoenix and Robert DeNiro. When it was announced that the director of the "Hangover" trilogy would do a standalone movie for Batman's arch nemesis, many people expected it to be a total disaster, but when the first pictures were released around a year ago my doubts made way for extreme curiosity. Even more, when the first trailer arrived. After this I declared it a potential masterpiece. In those few minutes of footage it gave me goosebumps, mostly because it reminded me of "Taxi Driver" and even "Requiem For A Dream". As a die hard Heath Ledger fan, I was genuinely interested to see how Phoenix would portray the clown prince of Gotham. Now I finally got the chance to experience it - and it was worth the wait. From start to finish the film throws the audience into the depressing alleys of Gotham city and conveys the sad and oppressive atmosphere nonstop. As I expected, Joaquin Phoenix once again shows that he's one of the most versatile actors of his generation and delivers a powerhouse performance that still impresses me hours after the credits rolled. He gave his portrayal something no one has done before, he made him human and inhuman at the same time, an anti-hero the audience hates to identify with. The way he laughs, how he moves and dances and even his outer appearance gave this version something unique and outstanding. He treated Ledgers legacy well, least to say. It's reported that people walked out of the screening stating that it's to violent, but I think the people just felt uncomfortable, because they felt ashamed that what they saw is exactly how our modern society works. That's one of the most important aspects of the whole film: The social criticism hits you right in the face and makes you reconsider your own values and social behaviour. Of course it had gritty violence as well, but the way it was selectively used made it so unsettling. The plot is rich in detail and an absolutely well paced decline of the sanity of a social outcast. It even features instances of an unreliable narrator that fits perfectly with the overall storytelling. Several scenes gave me goosebumps and the feeling that they someday will be as iconic as the best "Taxi Driver" moments and I genuinely loved it. The final act was even the best of the whole film, it's dark and packing and I liked how it occasionally connected the independent story to the comic book source as well.
All in all, this film is a modern masterpiece that leaves you speechless multiple times and despite it's comic book origin manages to be something original. It is an outstanding character study about a social outcast that hits us at the correct spots: The way we treat people with mental illness and people that we consider as worthless. That's what this movie shows us, if we want it or not. That's what makes it so incredibly magnificent. It will haunt you, but justified. If Joaquin Phoenix won't get the Oscar as the best actor, many people will riot on the streets like Joker's henchmen. That's for sure.

Review Title: Phenomenal Comic Book Movie and origin story
Review: The 2010s have been a decade of comic book films, cinemas are overstuffed with bland superhero movies with headache inducing sequences that would serve better as video game cutscenes. "Joker" starring Joaquin Pheonix, is about the most infamous villain in Gotham City. The aesthetic of this Gotham appears as essentially a run down version of New York City, similar to how the city was in the 1970s. I love this aesthetic and always enjoyed films from the 70s that were filmed in NYC. Anyway, "Joker" tells a fantastic origin story for a mysterious character. We all know "Joker" is a chaotic lunatic, but generally his backstoy is not told, and usually is vague. Whether this births a new cinematic universe or not, this is a breath of fresh air for comic book movies, and is a great counter to what Disney has been releasing. The performances are top notch, Phoenix is a great Joker and De Niro is fantastic as always. I dont want to say much about this movie, everyone has seen the memes, but the film is great as well, and if you haven't seen it, you should. Its thoroughly entertaining throughout and mostly unpredictable. The direction is pretty good, some shots are very memorable and beautiful. There is also an incredibly relevant message about mental illness. I wouldn't call it a masterpiece of cinema, but as far as comic book movies go, its certainly the best one released this last decade.

Had it not been connected - albeit in an indirect way - to the Batman franchise, and instead marketed as a character study of a man struggling to shake off his childhood demons (Joachim Phoenix in You were never really here, for example) it would've been seen by a few and yet greatly admired by the critics. As it is, I see that it's got a great score on IMDb from the viewers, but less so from the critics. How can the critics be sniffy about this film? Apologies if this sounds pretentious but For me, it was a fantastic introduction to the masses of the delights of bleak drama at its best. Call a film Joker and set as a prequel to the Batman films and you're guaranteed box office success. I for one am very pleased that a film of such undoubted quality will be seen and enjoyed by so many people. And Joachim Phoenix? Review Title: He is the Joker Gotham deserves.
Review: I will start this off by saying this movie is actually pretty good. When a film is surrounded by as much controversy as this one, it really has to be a good enough movie for the controversy and the chaos to be worthy, and it is definitely worth it.Joker is such a legendary villain that not unlike his nemesis is more than a man, he is a symbol, he is an agent of chaos; this particular interpretation has created chaos on and off-screen as people have fought to boycott it and to defend it depending on their political spectrum, this is what Joker would want.The film does give us the origins of a man who ends up becoming a Joker, but will he be the one who becomes Batman's nemesis? At the end of the day it does not matter at all if he is or not, as the Joker figure is established as a symbol of pure anarchy, a symbol of a cultural war between the have too much and the have-nots, like Ra's Al Ghul said in another franchise "Create enough hunger, and everyone becomes a criminal." This movie is not the first to establish this concept, the TV series GOTHAM establishes quite well that Joker is not a man but symbol, perhaps as big as Batman as not everyone can believe in good when the world's greatest city is divided by extreme wealth and extreme poverty, it is a time bomb waiting for the right person to detonate it.Enters Arthur Fleck, one of cinema's most miserable individuals, a man whose life is a continuous hellhole, and who is played masterfully by Joaquin Phoenix. The thespian gives Fleck a humanity that very few villains can afford to acquire, a humanity that is more than an origin story, a story that is a comedy, a story of the man who laughs.The movie is slow paced, but I think that being truthful it deserves a 9 out of 10.Joker has been one of my favorite characters for as long as I can remember, and I can gladly welcome Joaquin Phoenix into the pantheon of amazing performances that together create the multiple choices' origin that Joker so desires.

My problem however, is the story: there is, at least in my opinion, no shock, no turning point, no surprise. It feels like watching a documentary. You aren't supposed to develop sympathy for Arthur, nor cheer for him, you are just meant to understand him. But to understand the fact that unchecked poverty and chained misfortune can drive a person into madness, I don't have to watch a movie.There are quite a few scenes which are rather open to interpretation, including the ending, but whatever interpretation you prefer, at best, Arthur is slightly "more in the right", but it changes nothing to the finale and that one is kind of unambiguous. You are bearing witness to a logical string of events which result in a foreseeable outcome. By the end of the movie, I don't really know what makes Arthus special in the world he's in. Maybe that's the point, that he's not, and it's fine, as he is not like the other Jokers. It still makes me wonder: what was the "point" of it all? It'd be a bit of an unfair understatement to call the whole thing trivial, but there seems to be no moral, no back and forth, no question at the end. It's just a plain road of a simple-minded man to hell.I'd still suggest it to specific people, but I don't think 10/10 is justified.

Review Title: Phoenix is masterful and lifts this film up.
Review:
The acting in this film is top notch and superb. Phoenix is amazing as Arthur / Joker.
Now the film for me is a mixed bag, if my score was on the film only, it would only get a four or five star rating but because it is based on everything to do with the movie, my rating is higher.
The film itself, well the first half is amazing and you see Arthur going through bouts of happiness and madness / grief in the world he lives in but alas this is where the film itself runs out of steam. By the end, the riot scenes, etc got me not so much as bored but I thought if the director had thinned out movie and made it a raw movie, then the whole movie would have been amazing.
All the cast do a fantastic job, of course Phoenix really carried this film on his performance and I doubt we will ever see a performance like this again for a long time.
Was he better than Ledger, one hundred per cent he was.
Apart from the dip in the film as I explained earlier, this movie is a superhero film but a combination of Taxi Driver and The King Of Comedy. If you have never seen those films, go out and watch them and you will see what I mean.

First things first, I am not a phycologist. But, I like so many in the aftermath of seeing this movie found myself discussing the threads of human nature first, the sinews of the film second.Every scene, every frame of this reminded me of a Gregory Crewdson photograph, every object picked with purpose, every room structured to affect emotion. I found it spectacular, ruthless, unforgiving and painful it might not even have been a movie it might have been interpretive dance. But constantly you can't help but ponder on the very nature of being human and how far could you be pushed; how far could you fall.Personally, I don't see this as the glorification of violence as some others might. I grant you it does traverse a very thin line at points, and this is massive credit to Joaquin Phoenix' portrayal of Arthur. I think maybe the reason so many people are finding it uncomfortable is that it actually cuts to close the bone, it unwaveringly shines a spotlight on how we are capable of mob mentality and how quickly and how far, when things go wrong, we as 'decent' human beings could go.I don't see the character of Arthur as simply he thrives on the violent acts, he doesn't, he thrives on finally being excepted and finding a place to belong. This Arthur within this DC Universe is a fragile one, at a crossroads within himself. This film documents what it takes to push him to become the Joker. The backdrop of social upheaval is the fuel needed to take him that extra distance and finally be accepted for who he has become.This is also about Gotham, a fictional place, conjured in the times around post World War economic boom in America, and based on a New York style with Chicago mobster mentality, all elements that play into the fat-cat nature of Gotham, the rich get richer the poor stay poor. Sadly, an idiom that we struggle with back in the real world. The really incredible thing this film does, is we know this character, we know how it ends up, he's Batman's nemesis, he's a fictional bad-guy, yet Todd Phillips and team show us a version of this character and his story such as it is, that we didn't know possible, where we are gestured to sympathise and understand how he became a 'monster'. In real human terms.Joker is an incredible piece of cinema and I think my opinion of it is open to change as I ponder the nature of being human more.

I was really excited to see this, but coming out, I felt rather disappointed. I mean, yeah, it gave us what it promised, Joker's backstory and how he descended into madness and became the Joker, but it was just... I don't know, I didn't care for how they handled it. I mean, I knew there would be some tragedy and I expected it, but I felt like they pushed that angle too much. I guess I was sort of looking for a descent into madness similar to how Jack Torrence in The Shining went crazy (minus the ghosts and supernatural) as opposed to what they did. And I'm not really sure I can even consider this a DC movie, since it had next to nothing to do with it. They could literally change the name of the Wayne family and change the name of the city from Gotham to something else, and it would have been a completely original, stand-alone, non-DC movie, that's how little involvement in it there was.But now for the big thing. Joaquin Phoenix's take on the Joker. Don't get me wrong, he did a fabulous acting job and was great for the role he was given, but that's just it, for the role he was given and the direction they took the Joker's character. But this just didn't feel like the Joker. It's like they just took some random character with a mental illness, slapped some clown makeup on him and called him the Joker. For sake of argument, lets just say they took the good Terminator from T2 and dressed him in a bat-suit then called him Batman, but he still acted like the Terminator. That's not Batman. Same here. Ok, maybe that was a bad analogy, but you know what I'm saying. This wasn't Joker. The character was far too anger, sad, pitiful, and fragile throughout the entire movie, even when he made his final "transformation" into Joker, it just wasn't him. Now, I know that there's never been one true, clear-cut origin for the Joker, which is part of his appeal, and those that do have one are always different, but this, I just can't see this being who was Joker beforehand or how he became Joker along the way. Parts of it, yes, but as a whole, no. One of Joker's biggest/greatest aspects is that we're all just one bad day away from completely snapping, and that life is just one big joke, so you should laugh at it. But this is just some sad, angry guy with a mental illness who has tragedy after tragedy fall upon him until he finally gives up and decides to go out with a bang while trying to take down the oppressive upper-class. That is not Joker. Again, I think Joaquin Phoenix did great for the part he was given, but like I said, I was expecting more of a Jack Torrence going crazy kind of origin as opposed to what they gave us.
Overall a great movie with an amazing direction but what really need to be mentioned is the brilliant performance by Joaquin Phoenix

I wanted to like this movie so much but from the trailer alone I knew I would have some issues with this and I was right.This is not a review, its a rant as I can't do a spoiler review before the blu-ray release. Right off the bat let me tell you that its a fantastic movie in almost every way. It is beautifully shot, has a good soundtrack, it is well paced and brilliantly acted. Joaquin Phoenix gives his best performance yet and I would love to see him get an Oscar for this. The supporting cast is also pretty great and as I said I have absolutely no complaints regarding its technical features. I could've easily seen myself giving this a 8.5/10 or maybe even a 9/10But I can't and won't. You see my main issue with this movie is with the Title of the film. Had the movie been called "ARTHUR" and it had no connections to the Batman mythos I could've and would've given it a 9/10.When a movie is titled "JOKER" there are certain things I would expect being a comic nerd and Joker being my favourite character of all time. Sadly this movie failed in every aspect of that, literally every possible way. The movie fails miserably every time it tries to shoehorn itself into the Batman canon. Now it might not be anything serious for most as they don't really care about the comics and considering the unanimous positive reviews everywhere I would say that number is a lot.But to me it is. Joker doesn't have a Pseudobulbar Affect or PBA, he doesn't laugh just because its a condition. He laughs because he finds it amusing. Stop trying to establish a relation between Bruce and Joker, it doesn't work very well. The very idea of a Joker origin movie is a contradictory one, even THE KILLING JOKE by Alan Moore was a mixed bag for awhile even though it is regarded as one of the best comics ever.Also I wont spoil but what the hell was the cinema hall scene? Are you trying to alter and take a piss on the most iconic origin story in all of comics? That's a big red flag, atleast for me. I seriously mean it when I say it was the most infuriating scene I've seen in any comic book movie ever. That scene alone forced me to deduct another point from the already below average score I'm sadly going to have to give it.The direction is pretty questionable too. Its almost as if the director had no faith in his work and decided to vehemently and forcefully tie the story to the Batman canon so people would see the movie. And that is what exactly killed the movie for me. It would've been a fantastic take on a character similar to Joker that deals with Mental health issues, personality deterrents and societal abrasion. Instead what we got was a half baked comic book movie with a confused direction and its feet in both boats.This movie had so much going on and should've been a surefire hit. The amazing technical aspects and a mindblowing performance gets washed away by its need to mindlessly shove itself into the Batman mythos to stay relevant. It was simultaneously one of the best movies I have watched this year and the most infuriating movie I have seen the same. I'm honestly saddened to my core for not being able to give this a good rating as it really is a good movie aside from the Batman bits.

Review Title: Joker: Visually Striking Horror Film Treads Familiar Ground
Review: 2.5 out of 5 stars (decent)Joker may well be the most controversial film of the year. From the moment its first trailer dropped, peoples' reactions have varied across the board, some calling the film a masterpiece and others deeming it a dangerous film in our society. Personally, I think Joker is like a stand-up comic who steals a better artists' jokes: They know the basic setup of the gag, but falter when delivering the punch line.Arthur Fleck (a committed Joaquin Phoenix) is a mentally-ill man with a job as a sign twirler who lives with his mother (Frances Conroy) and idolizes TV talk-show host Murray (An energetic Robert De Niro). Arthur's life goes down the toilet after a series of bad days lead to him murdering his attackers whilst wearing clown makeup. Now with a taste for violence and the attention of Gotham City gained, Arthur will rise to become one of its most dangerous criminals, The Joker. Oh yeah, Zazie Beetz plays a cute girl across the hall who could have been cut out with nothing lost.Joker is written and directed by Todd Phillips (The Hangover trilogy), and he unfortunately borrows from the work of Martin Scorsese (who also produced this) without the depth or nuance that made Scorsese films great. Joker is kept afloat by committed performances, hypnotic camerawork and a creepy score, but it has nothing new or interesting to say about its title character.Joker is a movie made by someone who wanted to honor his favorite director instead of making something new. Strong performances, a memorable score, and a horrifying ending keep it afloat, but this Joker can't get the last laugh. See it if you were interested beforehand, skip it if you weren't.Rated R for Strong Bloody Violence, Disturbing Behavior, Language, and Brief Sexual Images

Review Title: A stunning artistic achievement - DC at its peak
Review:
JOKER (2019) directed by Todd Phillips and starring Joaquin Pheonix in the role of a lifetime as the titular character, is a film that explores the complexity, stigma and volatility of severe mental illness. Set in the fictional DC metropolis, Gotham City, Joker paints a nasty portrait of a damaged city, struggling with rising crime, disillusionment and 'super rats'.Arthur Fleck is barely existing as a clown for hire, living with his elderly mother in their tiny apartment; their only relief from the tragedy of their lives is watching America's favourite late-night host, Murray Franklin (Robert DeNiro) on their old television. Arthur has delusions of grandeur, imagining himself as a successful stand-up comedian, which is ironic based on his 'condition' that elicits unprovoked and uncontrollable laughter in stressful situations. A journal contains all his dark thoughts and is littered with disturbing images and expressions of suicidal ideation.The film depicts Arthur's descent into psychopathy, through revelations and events that call into the question the reality he was brought up with. The film may be deeply disturbing for some, particularly the scenes of graphic violence, that play out with the same level of overt intensity and clarity as the rest of the film - nothing is held back. In fact, the audience is left in a confusing state between horror and humour, since many of these disturbing scenes include brilliant moments of levity.That's right, it's not all psychological horror, there are moments of humour that is the result of Pheonix's mannerisms and his diabolical laugh. It's a physical performance, while director Todd Phillips maintains a consistently gloomy colour palette that is broken only by the clown paint and the clown masks that show up at various points in the film.Speaking of Pheonix, he is incredible, fully inhabiting this character and creating a genuine debate as to which Joker performance was better: him or Heath Ledger. Although such a discussion is unnecessary since they are both transcendent in their own way.JOKER is a truly incredible artistic statement that will be remembered, revered and talked about as much as the last great DC film, The Dark Knight (2008). While I am hesitant to pump out a review immediately after seeing it once, there is no doubt I will watch it again and again and wait impatiently for the next one.Highly, highly recommended

Review Title: Go watch the Movie for an Unbridled Performance from Phoenix. And for the Filmmakers who had the Determination with go through with a Disturbingly Brilliant Ventures.
Review:
Never Did I thought there would be a redefining role for this character after Ledger. Phoenix puts his heart and soul into the psyche of a man who has little to lose, who's constantly at odds with what the society considers Norm.He tries to life by its rules, only to constantly find his back to the wall. Abused, Put down, Shaken up, Underappreciated.
It is only when he sheds his tattered concepts of morality, does the world start making sense to him. and his ascension spells chaos to the world.Joaquin Phoenix is notorious telling us stories not only through dialogue but also his Body language. And here we see, how as the strings holding him tied are cut one after the other, the timid, unsure and pitiable Arthur transforms into this confident reality he built for himself. Into what he sees as his destiny.There is no doubt that the movie is a vehicle for the character study of Arthur Fleck's descent into Madness. or as he sees it, his 'enlightenment'. the world, the characters, the narrative, even the colors and environment are set in a way to accentuate it.Make no mistake, This is not a Marvel brand of 'family Friendly' entertainment. Definitely not one you take the kids to. The actions and themes explored are chilling in how close they are to reality. They are scenes you cannot/should not be seeing, but will regardless. And it does an excellent job of making you squirm in your seats. As it should.The story towards the end overstays its welcome a bit. Without spoiling much, there were some parts where i thought 'this is when & how the story should wrap' but it kept pulling on. And at least one scene related to Bruce's origin seemed more like shoehorn. All in all, go and watch for Phoenix's Spellbinding performance and story with a heart of Dark Depravity.
