Review Title: Great, but man this is a tough one to pin down...
Review: Maybe because it is so tough, that is what I'm feeling the need to write about it for. I don't typically write reviews for movies, on here or anyplace else. First off... Everything about the movie was great. The acting, writing, casting, directing, cinematography...etc. I truly only have one issue with the movie in general. I am a huge fan of the comic book movie genre, particularly DC, and even more specifically Batman and his world. My issue is that it doesn't feel very much like a "Joker" movie. And I would assume that the actors and those involved in making it were probably not trying to make it like any other Joker movie that's ever existed. I applaud them for that and appreciate it for its artistic value alone. If they would have taken out any recognizable character names or the word "Joker" from the movie, I probably could've gone into it not knowing anything, and walked out not realizing that it was a Joker movie at all. I mean the makeup and the clown aspect would've hinted at those things, but in the context it could have simply been a man who had that type of job who just couldn't take anymore crap from the world.It's been done many times before, from the darkness and griminess in "Taxi Driver", to the emotional repression and complacency of the middle class commuter in "Falling Down", all the way to the hilarity of "Me, Myself and Irene". Even though it's been done before, this particular film did have a lot to bring to the table, if not only through the extreme talents of those involved in the project. There were things we hadn't seen before or that weren't shown to us in a certain way. For example, the mental health crisis aspect of the story, both for him and his mother.The main thing is... I never really saw "The Joker" when I saw Fleck. His character doesn't seem like a formidable arch-villain for arguably the world's most beloved and bad ass superhero/comic book vigilante...the Batman. I don't even think this Joker could get on base, much less bring it all the way home. Arthur Fleck isn't terrifying or very unpredictable. I could see his character arc and predict his actions very early on in the story. Most importantly he is not a sociopath, and I think he lacks the charisma to become The Joker that we all know and love... at least a recognizable representation of the character. No version of Joker from one movie could be switched out with one from another, they all work very well in their own particular world and compliment the Batman of that world. Who even knows what the Batman of this world would be like, or how he and Phoenix's Joker would play off of each other. It's hitting me as I'm writing this, that we have never had a Joker in a movie, where we hadn't already had a very particular and familiar version of Batman that fit into that world. By the way, the same goes for each inundation of Batman...it would never work switching Batman from one world to another either. Part of me doesn't want my Joker to have a backstory, especially one that I know anything about it. He is much more interesting when you think his acts are not justified and you don't sympathize with him in any way. The Joker is supposed to be an enigmatic criminal mastermind, and part of the character's appeal is that we have no idea what has made him that way... nor how we could get him to stop. The Joker is simply the conductor of a symphony of chaos... much like Heath Ledger's version. He's an over-the-top flashy intimidating thug/crime boss like Jared Leto. Hell...Jack Nicholson's threw a parade through the streets of Gotham, for no other reason than to kill everyone with a gas that makes you die with a permanent smile on your face. Why? Because he thought it would be fun and it would incite Batman to come out and play with him. I just can't see Arthur Fleck ever becoming or doing any of those things, or being a formidable opponent for Batman. I think Batman would just kick his door in and beat him senseless while he cowered in the corner pissing himself...then he'd be locked up.Other than that, I thought that the movie was wonderful! It was extremely well acted, well directed, and well produced. I just didn't walk out of the theater with this warm fuzzy feeling in my heart saying, "Damn I love me some Joker."I hope some of the other real fans out there understand what I'm saying and would agree with me.

Review Title: Solid 4 // The only superhero movie I've enjoyed in a decade
Review: As an ardent decrier of all things superhero, this movie won me over. It manages to avoid almost all of the things that usually turn me off about the genre - the formulaic, committee-think constructions, the overwhelming test-screened safeness, the crowd appeasement, the vanilla-flavored tone. Instead, Joker establishes an absorbing atmosphere, one that was surprisingly nihilistic, grimy, and even genuinely unsettling. This is probably the closest a superhero franchise movie is ever going to come to an art-house style character study and it's pulled off quite convincingly. It isn't exactly subtle, and there are some hamfisted moments (the totally unnecessary flashbacks regarding the love interest jump to mind), but as a portrayal of a deeply disturbed individual cast off and exploited, the movie was able to generate real empathy and disgust. Much of the success is, of course, owed to the excellence of Joaquin Phoenix's performance which elevates the material. I was pleasantly surprised by how compromised and pitiful his character was written to be. Rather than rise up by some grand anarchist scheme, his notoriety happens almost entirely incidentally while his own actions are fueled by apolitical and often delusional motivations. The entire third act of the film could be viewed as a wish-fulfillment psychosis as the underbelly of the city rises fantastically around him, offering him the stage he's always dreamed of commanding. While likely either a flashback or a flashforward, the final scene also seems to subtly reinforce this suggestion of psychosis and adds a nice sprinkle of ambiguity. Even if you're a superhero skeptic, give this one a shot.Solid 4/5

Review Title: To call this a 'Psychological Thriller' is an insult
Review: To claim that this film is anything other than a masterpiece is a claim that is tainted by a contradictory outlook on how mental illness should be portrayed/addressed by the media.You will ALWAYS have people who dislike films like this; to make a film this potent and powerful is to make a film that is going to be extremely controversial, and I'm sure that is exactly what the writers and directors foresaw in the making of this film.That being said, you can FEEL their vision with every single frame of this absolute masterpiece, and Phoenix not only gives the best performance of his life, but also takes the character of the Joker to a place we have never seen him before, and he takes society with him.The question of Phoenix vs Ledger will be no doubt raging within the coming months and years after this film's release. The fact is that the question is void because of the fact that they portray COMPLETELY different aspects of the Joker's persona, and both portray is masterfully. However, Phoenix's portrayal goes much deeper than Ledger's at least on an emotional level, which is all I shall say in that regard.The visceral assault of emotions I experienced during this film was unlike anything I've ever felt or experienced in my life. To portray such a traditionally psychotic character in such an emotional, and even sympathetic way, depending on your outlook, is an unbelievable feat.Everyone is entitled to their own opinion, and of course that is okay; people and critics are going to dislike this film, that is their opinion. But to deny that this film is anything other than a masterpiece would sadly be false, and I absolutely applaud everyone involved in this absolute work of art.

Joker is an excellent insight (albeit exaggerated) of society's view of mental health.
Arthur has serious mental health issues, caused or at least exacerbated, by childhood trauma and his relationship with his mother. Society isn't able to support Arthur adequately and his delusions and mental health are spiralling out of control. The movie allows us to have pity with Arthur, where it's clear that the 'system' has failed him.
Throughout the movie society ridicules him, work mates, members of the public, the general population (via Murray's TV show). His interaction with the lady and child on the bus is a startling revelation as to how, even though the member of the public is made aware of his condition, still shows no empathy or understanding and merely shuns him.Under no circumstances can we ever condone the violence, but the question Arthur poses to Murray towards the end of the movie should be a stark warning.
Ultimately, the way we treat our vulnerable members of society, our tolerance, understanding, empathy and support will determine who how society will develop. And we may well get what we deserve.This is exceptional movie and will become a classic (although won't be on each Xmas 😄)

The Joker does none of this.

When I first learned of an "origin story" for the Joker, I was at most worried because what makes the Joker an endearing comic book super-villain is his lack of a backstory. It added to the mystique of the character. That, and it wasn't too long after the DCEU had shown off their Joker in Jared Leto.But, the film was actually surprising. This was probably one of my favorite films of this year, even though most of the hype overplayed it. Here, we have Arthur Fleck who was born on the poor streets of Gotham where he takes care of his mother and works as a clown performer, a thankless job. A majority of the film devotes much of its time to seeing the Joker's daily life. Because of his mental illness, he is mistreated by the populace and always looked down upon. Eventually, he would devolve into the Joker, becoming the most dangerous criminal that Gotham City would ever know.There's no use comparing Joaquin Phoenix's Joker with that of the late Heath Ledger's or even Jack Nicholson's takes on the Clown Prince of Crime as they are all different interpretations. Here, Joaquin Phoenix did a great job at playing a broken man who was continually beaten down by society until he lashed out at his mistreatment. I feel what makes movies like Joker, A Clockwork Orange, and American Psycho insightful to many is the fact that at heart, some would want to be free to do what they want regardless of the consequences. I don't mean as in going out and robbing banks or anything horrifically evil, but these films serve as forms of escapism.We would want to take sweet vengeance on those that mistreat us or to prove the naysayers wrong, but because of our convictions, we instead resolve this by watching escapist films much like Joker. I wouldn't have thought that perhaps outside of The Killing Joke that a film could make the Joker seem tragic. Phoenix does a good job at portraying the torn down, down on his luck and trying to make ends meet. It gets to the point where once he starts changing you can't help but feel for him. You have grown to love this man for the first acts of the film, that seeing him take that big leap into villainy is heartbreaking. But at the same time, there is some instances where you feel that he is correct in his actions. He's that dynamic of a character, that once he starts on his journey of no return, you are conflicted by it. There is a point where you stop sympathizing with Arthur, but even then, it goes to show how complex of a character he is.Really, the only flaws I can think of is that the first two arcs are a little slow and less interesting. And Arthur laughing makes sense in the film as it is explained away as a result of the mental illness, but it can kind of get annoying at some points in the film. Aside from that, I can't really think much of any other flaws. An otherwise great film that was a pleasant surprise.

Review Title: Joker is a glorified journey into a man's descent into madness.
Review:
#Joker is an intense character study movie, not your typical comic book story movie at all (and hence, not for everyone and certainly not for teenagers). It's a deep, crude dive into a man's descent into madness and a lucid depiction of a sick mind. It's filled with gritty raw human emotion with no sublimation. It leaves you with a tormenting bitterness that might stay for a while!It draws widely from the source material in terms of small arcs, character details and lines, though the latter is a bit generalized. References to "The Killing Joke" are alluringly evident here and there. There is a handful of great lines that shine in the context of the portrayed suffering. It's violent, dark and will keep you at the edge of your seat with all its painstalkingly disturbing unfoldings, but do not jump on the propaganda bandwagon on this. It's dark!! That's true, but certainly not darker than the source material.Cinematography and camera angles are a work of beauty. Music shares in the buildup of a certain aura. Screenplay and plot are orchestrated to serve the general scheme. Todd Philips's narrative unfolds after elaborate buildup. He follows in the steps of Scorsese an borrows his glasses sometimes to shine the spotlight on his creation/theories. He tries to sell outrage, societal oppression and politics and their cumulative effect on the chaos that ensues. Joaquin Phoenix is totally brilliant. He gracefully jumps from a state to another and drags you into opposing points on the spectrum of emotion in an effortless-seemingly act. There have been calls claiming his act is Oscar-worthy!Joker, as a character, is an oversimplification of an idea that fights to takeover as much as it can of our psychology. He's never the answer but often the question that nobody asks. An unstoppable force premise, flawed but existential.Joker, the movie, is a masterpiece in every aspect that's definitely not for everyone! It points out to a problem and a problematic solution in a world of widely-gapped societies and self-centered ideoligies that overcompensate with interest-driven orientation, vindictive projection and malice. It's an incarnation of the chaos that uproars inside us and the most vile and horrid outcomes that can unravel out of it.. with a bloody smile!!#TheJokerMovie 🤡

Review Title: The Clown Prince of Crime is born!
Review: Yesterday, I went to watch the Joker, and I have to say that the film was absolutely brilliant. It has genuinely put a positive smile on my face! Joaquin Phoenix's performance, the overall storyline, along with how the film was put together is completely worth watching.As the Joker is a standalone film from the current list of DC films, it was refreshing to see a bold, dark and gritty attempt to deeply witness Arthur transform into one of the world's most notorious comic book villain. I would like to go in depth about his transition, but it is something the viewers need to watch for themselves. For me, this is one of the reasons why I enjoyed this film - it is not just about the Joker being a psychopath, but it is about understanding Arthur's circumstances, as well as his perspective about life.In terms of Joaquin Phoenix's portrayal of the Joker, I really enjoyed his take on the character, and his version is currently my favourite. The insanity and brutal stance (attitude) of Joaquin Phoenix's Joker is just mind-blowing, and this film gives us an opportunity to see an untamed and extreme Joker in a live action film.This film does contain some shocking, violent, along with gruesome scenes, and this is to be expected with a character like the Joker. He is not the clown you invite to your child's birthday party for an amusing experience. Looking back at the film, certain scenes were not even that horrific, and critics and individuals are unnecessarily attacking this film. There are other films and TV shows that are much more aggressive than the Joker.If you are yet to watch the film, go and see it without overthinking it. The hype that was within the trailers, expands throughout the film. It is that good. The Joker is a one of a kind film, and Todd Phillips has shown us what is possible for mature, in depth and dark comic book films.

Review Title: A Welcome Aboard movie for newbie cinephiles
Review:
On top of everything that is going on and actually went on, the hype, the negative critics, the awards and the nominations, I have to state firmly that Joker is a solid, good movie, good enough to drive one into the deeper world of more eye-opening, profounding cinema than their usual favorite superhero flicks. This rather untraditional out-of-comic-book adaptation captures the theme of 'society to insanity' at a reasonably compelling level while delivering it in a dirty-beautiful 80s New Yorky Gotham, all displayed on screen with state-of-the-art color grading. But did it move me the way Psycho or One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest did? Needless to say, 3 different movies can't be compared for the most part but considering all 3 have that same 'insanity' atmosphere going on, Joker didn't push me to that very end of my seat.However, unlike most of what people who didn't enjoy Joker had to say about their taste in violence or acting, my judgement comes from quite an opposite direction. While most of them think Joker is too violent, I think Joker is not violent enough. While also some of them said Joaquin's performance was sub par after seeing the movie, I say he did great, way too good to be exact.The reason I have behind this thought came around after I have not only seen the movie, but also taken a look at the original script and some behind the scene stuff. What I found out was, Joker is supposed to be way more down-deep crazy and gory. Arthur, in the screenplay, was going to rip his mouth off with a piece of glass to enlarge his smile and to become the full embodiment of the Joker, right in the middle of this chaotic riot on the burning street of Gotham. I wondered how impactful and stunning was it going to be if the actual ending was just that. But it didn't make it to the final work, and so were many too-cool-for-school words and plays in the script shared the same fate. At that moment, I realized the studio still wanted to please the crowd, even when the R-rated tag can't be avoided. And to do that, they intentionally missed many opportunity to turn this thing in to an absolute dark masterpiece. Now if I watch Joker again, I will see the scars from that destructive action in every frame, which is not quite what I think is enjoyable.If that visible hole from the film was still one way or another can be neglected, then Joaquin's performance definitely cannot. He did such a great job, it was perfect. However, that is exactly why I felt less of Arthur Fleck the character and more of Joaquin Phoenix the actor, which is to me, defeats the purpose of acting in cinema.
The weight losing, the psychotic behavior studying, he did a lot of work, which is a thing all the Awards love: an accomplished & wealthy actor willing to shed tears, blood and sweat doing hard physical labor for the sake of art.In contrary to that, my concept of what is great acting differs. Great acting is supposed to be effortless. When the acting reach its highest level, the actor is the character and vice versa, so when he or she acts, it's not really acting, it's just showing, living, being their usual self. One of the nicer examples of great effortless acting would be Faye Wong in Chungking Express. It's Faye's first role in her career, but she made it look like she already did a thousand films more or less. The character she played, also named Faye, is technically herself in a different world. When you watch Chungking Express, no way would you be able to see Faye the actress-pop superstar. You can only see Faye the character, and that's it.Now back to Joker, I can't say I saw the same thing. I could feel Joaquin's admirable effort, I saw that he's trying to get in character, and that's the problem: I am not supposed to see or feel any of that. To me, Joker is a step down from Her with Joaquin, if you just forget about the awards and really consider the magic acting brings to cinema beyond corrupted competition.

Joker is a good movie but it could have been great. The positives are too visible and obvious that I have to focus on the negatives. One of the fundamental problems I have is that this film doesn't really know what it is and what it ultimately wants to say.Is it a probe inside a shattered mind?For that the film is too incoherent. What is the true nature of Arthur's psychosis? It seems he just suffers from too big of a number of unrelated conditions that come and go with no real explanation or reason. On one hand he experiences great trouble with even the most basic tasks and social interactions. On other hand he is capable of planning, eluding the authorities and see himself with objective eyes which all seem much too normal for his character, I think. In the later parts of the film he even seems to be enjoying his state of mind and yet describe himself from an outsiders point of view. Isn't that strange for a man who, in his own words, didn't even know if he existed? There were parts that felt real about him but overall Joker seems like an incredibly mentally challenged character written by someone who has no real experience within the field. The result seems to be a bit shalow view of an incredibly complicated mind.Is it a social critique?What seems to be too coincidental about Arthur is his ability to apparently stay out of trouble for most of his life yet his first burst of violence in this film seems almost unprovoked and without any deep merit. The film acts as if the state of society and Gotham City is a factor but Arthur himself states few times he doesn't really care. He just wants to be seen. And that I understand as from the movie's point of view the clash of rich and poor in Gotham is just a thing that doesn't really have any concrete reason or development until the first subway incident. It is just a climate Arthur lives in but isn't really influenced by. The film acts as if there was only one person to blame and doesn't really care about anyone else which seems very superficial and prevents viewer from creating any real relation to the cause.Is it a comic book movie?Joker tries so much not to be a superhero movie that it strips us from anything extraordinary, different or grotesque. Gotham seems just like New York, lacking any charm or special features. Apart from Arthur there are no really interesting characters in this movie. They all seem too flat and no one has any real space to show anything. Sure, I understand the film wants to underline how all people are the same, apathetic, grey.. But the result seems to have almost opposite effect and Arthur feels somehow more invisible in the company of others. There are scenes to evoque some kind of connection to the Batman universe but overall fall almost forced and have no real meaning in this story.Whose point of view are we observing?The biggest problem for me is the way the film is shot. The camera is too objective, uninvolved, cool and all attempts to delve viewer into the dark chaos of Arthur's mind fall a little flat. Yet there are times when the camera tricks us and we find out that we weren't presented with reality. But to make us feel we see the world through Arthur's eyes it doesn't suffice at all. Yes, we feel for him and maybe even understand but what we don't really feel is his depression as the movie appears to be scared to keep us in his mind for too long and therefore fails to create any kind of subjective ambience. Protecting us from the anxiety and depression makes Joker, to much regret, too mainstream of a movie without no real artistic components.I would love to see more nuance, more personality. I feel Todd Phillips' effort to keep the film as minimalistic as possible but he tends to take out the parts that we need and add things we really don't. The screenplay lacks more imagination and originality and when you try and imagine this movie without the main character and the devastating, physically painful, all-in performance by Joaquin Phoenix, there isn't much left. And that simply will not do.

Review: I do not like super hero movies. Fortunately, this is not one. This is an incredibly disturbing character study of a man who happens to appear in comic books and other movies. This man is different than all of those other men. This man has nothing to do with those other men. It is not necessary to compare Arthur Fleck to the Joker of the Dark Knight. This is not about that joker. Arthur Fleck does not become that Joker.This is the story of a mentally ill man who becomes an accidental icon. It is not a negative statement against mental illness. It is a look at one mentally ill man. It is not in any way saying that all mentally ill people become homocidal maniacs. Arthur Fleck just happens to become one.Joaquin Phoenix gives an excellent interpretation of a very creative script. He is not trying to play "the Joker". He is trying to tell the truth of one mans life, and he succeeds. It is very disturbing to watch. It's more disturbing to sit with the thoughts you will have about yourself and about society while Arthur's story unfolds. I was also disturbed by the audience around me, and also by myself, laughing at dark moments in this mans life. This movie holds a mirror to society and it's hard to ignore the image you see reflected before your eyes. Go see it, it's worth it.

Review: This was a fascinating watch and is a movie I'll need to see a second time before it leaves cinemas. What might have unsettled me most on this viewing was the guy sitting next to me, because of course these are always sitting right next to me, who was laughing at everything the Joker did. Everyone else was as shocked, engrossed and completely silent as me. You could hear a pin drop, and once a phone, but that man was pretty much laughing throughout. At all of the deaths and at every smile or gesture of the Joker. I really don't understand that one bit. That this did not take me out of the film is probably the biggest praise I can give Joker. Obviously, Joaquin Phoenix nailed it and is the film's biggest plus. A fully believable portrayal of a complex figure that does not stand for anything and has no clue what it wants, but only knows he can't keep taking it any more. I don't think the film makes him out to be a normally awesome dude who just had some bad experiences in life and now is shooting people, and so should you. No, I think it just shows this man and asks us what to make of him. How come no one was taking him seriously till it was too late? What can we do to prevent people capable of acts like these, from executing them? And many more questions. It's a puzzling story in various ways and a movie where I can fully understand the people who dislike it. It makes you feel absolutely horrible for a while. At least that's the effect it has on me right now, but I do think that makes total sense. It is a snapshot of our current time, as well as any other time really, but is relevant nonetheless. It shows for example, masses on the streets hopelessly worshipping someone although they have no idea, nor care, what this person actually thinks or stands for, or if it does. Ultimately the movie seems to be about utter chaos and that, needless to say, always resonates. This film is a lot to process and these are just some feelings and thoughts I have about it at this time. I'll maybe leave a more detailed review at a later date once I've seen it again. By the way, yes the movie is not exactly brilliant or all that new but it does what it does effectively and is extremely stirring, at times difficult to watch, and that is most likely how a story like this should be told. Shoutout to the great cinematography, editing and especially to the score. Hildur Guðnadóttir is an incredible talent. Annoyingly Todd Phillips is a quite the idiot, yes, but many morons have made good films. That has always been the case, it is just more apparent nowadays. So I don't know what to tell you. It is what it is. Somehow this is a great film against the many odds.

Review Title: The film shines a mirror on society, and society does not like what it sees.
Review: There is so much that can be said about this spectacular film. Those who call it boring or dismiss it for being too violent are doing their best to quantify a piece of art they are not able to completely understand. Ennui only comes through disinterest and emotional/intellectual distance. The subtleties of Phoenix's performance to some, are undercut by his denial that he did not have to give himself to the role as much as previous Jokers have had to. People want a story of struggle and pain ending with high accomplishment. But the actor achieves this with skill and mastery of his craft. I'd watch the film again and again just to enjoy how Phoenix deftly makes be believe and empathise with a sociopath, a victim of circumstance in this interpretation.Brilliant cinematography and self-conscious homages to classic Scorsese masterpieces are testament to the wider scope Joker seeks to reach. The public seem so worried about how this film could incite violence and negative behaviour. My appreciation for the artistic calibre of this film resides it its ability to incite such controversy and opinion. Instead of shouting at the screen ask yourself why you feel the way you do and question your own tendencies rather than seek to project your insecurities on the world. What a film!

Review Title: Perhaps one of the greatest films but also one of the most depressing
Review: There are obviously and quite deliberately so many parallels between The Joker and the world that we live in today. For this reason the movie is at times incredibly painful to watch and will gave you silently and automatically comparing so many scenes to modern-day planet earth.The rich get richer and even the poor have no time to care about each other. Money talks and as always the rules don't apply to those who have power, or who can at least buy their way out of trouble. Life is all about "who you know" rather than "what difference can you make?"The Joker is more-or-less a wake-up call for planet earth.As for the movie and Mr. Phoenix's performance. As many others have said, it's faultless and time that we stopped comparing performances actor-to-actor. Ledger's portrayal was fantastic and Leto's could have been better sure. Though at the end of the day these are just different portrayals of a different role.Without judging people who disagree with me and generalizing them, I'm just going to say that if you didn't like the movie, it most likely succeeded in delivering its message. If you did like the movie? It still most likely succeeded in delivering its message.I hope we don't find ourselves in such a similar Black Mirror-esque situation in the future as a species.

Review Title: Complicated, DEEP, different, unusual and thought provoking!
Review: Let me start by saying that when I left the cinema, I felt that I liked the movie a lot, and at the same time I felt disgusted by it. Maybe it's the portrayal of a broken man that has been put over the edge and gets really violent and crazy that left me feel that way.This movie offers a LOT of things to think about about our society, about our life in general and the way we treat the weak among us. I think this movie TRULY depicts how a psychopath is formed and the consequences this brings.The Joker is not "likeable" character but in many cases I think the public can explain his actions as being reasonable and logic.The movie is very, very, very deep and it's not just for entertainment purposes. I advise the public watching it have the mindset that they will be watching something truly different and not think of it as the latest Hollywood flick, because it is not.The movie is so deep I believe you have to watch it 2-3 times to grasp it.The acting is not great - it's UNBELIEVABLE! Joaquin MUST win Oscar with this. Movies like this are very rare and far in between. I hope more people can understand it because this is a complicated movie and I fear the broad audience won't grasp it's meaning.

Review Title: This is the kind of movies I want to see...
Review: It's undoubtedly a transgressive, relevant and ambitious film that opens a door for comic characters to begin to star in films that are not necessarily action, and that deal with more complex and adult themes that the sober fight between good and evil. For an audience and a society that are no longer so clear about the line between what is right and wrong, and who are so willing to side with the villain, this is a cathartic, hard and difficult film, even because of the tension, the embarrassment of others and the sorrow that its protagonist causes.'Joker' does not aspire to please everyone, but aims to address social issues and invite reflection. Faced with a Marvel that clings to its family entertainment formula, as infallible as it is safe, DC has accepted that it cannot do the same and has set out to address the most forgotten audience in theaters, the adult.

When DC took a risk on Todd Phillip's R-rated Joker, I don't think they actually knew what they were doing, because if they did, it would have been a much tamer version of what we got. This movie is an unflinching look at the rise and rise of Gotham's psychopathic clown prince of crime, and man does it not flinch. It (narrowly) takes the title from The Dark Knight as the best comic book-based movie ever made.
Incredible movie, unbelievable acting, a masterpiece!

It wasn't a fun movie, it wasn't an atmospheric one. There was no likeable personality, no wow-moment, no food for thought. Below average in every sense. Overall, just a very bad piece of movie, and I absolutely regret the time spent.

Review Title: Good movie, but not a good message.
Review: I went to this movie despite the outcry on social media. I heard the stories about the feelings inspired by the movie. Nonetheless I wanted to see it for myself. After seeing it, I can tell you one thing - this one was different.I knew it was different when I walked into the theater and two police officers were stationed at the front doors. It was different when there really wasn't much laughter during the movie - even at the parts that were deliberately meant to be funny. When the movie was over people weren't laughing on the way out or talking about how great the special effects were. Very few people were talking about the acting, the plot, or any other things people normally talk about after seeing a movie. Why? Quite simply, it was "too real" for what people expected from a movie based on a comic book.From the events of the movie to the lines that were said; every step of the way was unapologetic and brutal. Growing up over the years with movies and video games of our day; I am admittedly desensitized to a lot of the violence in movies. I usually have no problem with separating what I know is not real and "just part of a movie". That was definitely harder to do in this movie. The violence was a little too realistic, and I think that was intentional. The writers and directors knew exactly where "the line" was that nobody is supposed to cross, and they crossed it anyway. Ironically I don't think they did it just for the sake of being edgy or just trying to get a rise out of people. I think they did it because they wanted to make it irrevocably clear that all of the terrible things in the movie are real. Not in the sense that something like that could happen... I mean that it many places around the world, some of those events *have* happened, and continue to happen every day.To acknowledge something like that does not give you a sense of happiness or make you feel good about the state of our world that we live in. For most of our lives we do our absolute best to avoid thinking about the worst parts of our world. Many choose to believe it doesn't even exist. This movie went out of their way to clearly point out that evil exists in this world. It showed the progression of it and how evil leads to more evil. Most people did not walk out of that movie feeling good about life. It was a very depressing movie to watch. Honestly I do not think I could recommend anyone to watch this movie, because I would not intentionally want to put anyone through that experience. Granted, it may not have "hit home" for everyone as it did with me. The plot, the acting, the cinematography, etc. - all top notch. However, I'm not a fan of the message this movie represents. From start to finish, it is nothing but dark and negative. I get the point, but I don't feel like it was "fun" by any stretch of the imagination.For me this movie instilled in me a feeling very similar to how I felt after I first watched Childish Gambino's music video for "This is America". It painstakingly points right at the darkest parts of humanity, and does its best to hold your attention so you can't look away. However, unlike "This is America", there was no ironic lightheartedness in The Joker to take a little of the sting out of the hits. I see now why people disliked the Joker movie, because you know before it even starts that it is not going to end well. Even when the Joker "wins", everyone loses - including himself. There was a defining moment where the writers and the directors pointed out specifically what message they were trying to get across to the viewers... I won't go into any specific "spoilers". However, I can at least say that it was the tipping point that led to the climax of the movie. The Joker finally got to "say his piece" to the public audience. He had finally been pushed beyond the breaking point, and all hell broke loose.While I feel like I get what they were trying to do with this movie, there is one very important aspect that I disagreed with. Through all of the brutal in-your-face darkness and violent acts in this movie; it consistently ends on a bad note. There is no redemption or a final "good" outcome at the end. Granted, there doesn't always need to be any redemption... Sometimes a movie about a villain is going to end badly because, well... It is about a villain. However, there are other ways they could have resolved it. The common them throughout the movie was that life is hell, and it isn't going to get any better.*While I can attest to the fact that evil and darkness exists in our world, that is not all there is.* Even when a majority of the people choose to ignore everything that is wrong in our world; there are still good people who choose to do something about it. There are charitable organizations, religious groups, and just straightforward good people who do their best to showcase the good parts of humanity. There are people who choose to help when they see people struggle. There are those that call their friends to check in when horrible things happen. There is no reason that a person cannot have a realistic view of the world around them, and still choose to make it better rather than worse.Even though I disagree with The Joker's overall message, I grudgingly have to agree with a lot of the points they made... Specifically, there is absolutely darkness in this world. We cannot choose to ignore it and hope it will go away on its own. Also, mental illness is *not* something that doctors made up one day to sell medication. It is absolutely real, and it is something that affects far more people than we realize. I can guarantee that everyone reading this post knows at least a few people who struggle with depression, or anxiety, or any one of the various mental illnesses out there. I can also guarantee that for every one person that you know that struggles with soul crushing depression or suicidal thoughts; there are probably ten more that do so without you knowing about it. I'm sure that every person reading this review knows a dozen people who struggle with depression or another serious mental illness. People call depression "The Silent Killer" because it can destroy the best of us without anyone even knowing it was happening. It is for that reason that I can appreciate what movies like "The Joker" are trying to do. They are making it harder to ignore the realities of this world and the mental illnesses that plague us. Hopefully, raising that awareness will lead to more support and better help for the people that desperately need it.If you or anyone that you know needs more help than someone just to talk to - there are absolutely resources out there.

And finally, the direction of Todd Phillips, along with his screenplay with Scott Silver, bring all of these elements together to portray a haunting tale of how a man with a fragile mindset can be turned into a monster by an unforgiving and corrupt society which won't be forgotten anytime soon.

Review Title: A Chilling Ballet of Mental Illness, That Dances Between Life's Tragedies
Review: The Joker is not a comic book movie, but rather a master class in character study. The film follows your lead Arthur Fleck or "The Joker". You're told the story through his eyes, and through this lens it is easy to find Arthur extremely sympathetic. Jaoquin Phoenix's portrayal, coupled with Todd Phillip's writing had made for a character who holds onto your attention the whole film. There wasn't a moment of the film I wasn't in awe, when the score would slowly creep in to give you chills over a scene that was previously completely silent, or still shots of hallways, and stair cases as Arthur is alone in frame, just to give you a gripping sense of loneliness throughout the film. Though the plot can be fairly predictable, it's how those moments play out that are surprising. You feel like you know something will happen one way and it does happen never in the way you feel it will though. The script can often times be dull for some, but to me I saw these moments as cold, hard bits that look into Arthur's psychy. Like a scene in which Arthur is in a comedy club and doesn't get what's funny and what's not so he just laughs, none of the jokes are really funny, but they're supposed to be things we know are supposed to be funny so we see that Arthur doesn't understand. There are other jokes that aren't laugh out loud hilarious, but are just funny enough to get you to think they are, and then immediately, a like of dialogue comes in to make you feel bad about laughing about that.The best things I can say about this film can't be said without spoiling it, all I can say is that it is a cold, gritty horror film about the horrors of the human psyche that'll leave you uncomfortable towards the end, with many questions about yourself left in your head after just one viewing.

My Verdict of JOKER 2019
Joker movie is a thunderous masterpiece! Can easily compete with the best comic book films of all time. The best movie of 2019 which belongs more in the Joaquin Phoenix Universe than the DC Universe. In the media, director Todd Phillips's Joker movie has been frenetically celebrated and a possible Oscars 2020 blessing (otherwise unthinkable for a comic-based film) is speculated violently. Let me say it loud and clear: there is not a word of it exaggerated Joker movie is an "origin story", which tells how poor Arthur, nicknamed Happy by his mother, will become one of the most famous enemies of Batman. However, here there is no question of the Dark Knight, the story unfolds when Bruce Wayne is still a child. Surprisingly, Joker movie is totally a drama. A hard drama, rough, bitter, in a sticky environment. An environment that does not help Arthur to adapt. Director/writer Todd Phillips & co writer Scott Silver take time to present the characters, places and situations. Joker movie is a work closer to auteur cinema. It's important to note that there's nothing wrong with this movie. Director Todd Phillips manages to infuse a very stylized colorful theme with the dark at the same time. It's bold, devastating & utterly beautiful. The some where staging tackles you from the first second, shaking you through for two hours and never letting go until the last second. Joker movie is a horror story, not the celebratory tale of an antihero. Joker is a game changer and plays in a league of his own. The great soundtrack consists mainly of classics of the swing era (Frank Sinatra at all) and is an integral part of the plot. The congenial score of Hildur Gudnadottir amplifies the power of the images many times, so that every scene penetrates deep into the bone marrow. Director Todd Phillips is a revelation at the helm and does the best directing job of his career with the twisted material, able to strike a tone that straddles stabs of bleak darkness, gasps of hope and pangs of inevitability. I doff my hat to you sir! DOP Lawrence Sher's no-frills work to emphasize twisted, dark city escapes, streets & nightmarish forms deserves a huge shout-out. With picture-perfect contrasts & color, sublime compositions, the rich and complex mise-en-scène succeeds in elevating the movie. But all of this impressive, stylish construction wouldn't have worked without Joaquin Phoenix. He inhabits his role with a commitment that's magnetic in its unpredictability. His unbelievable performance will leave the most lasting impression on the audience. Robert De Niro - one of his best roles for a long time! Zazie Beetz is remarkable. I left the cinema with lasting impressions & my mouth open. Beneath this gripping, bold, revisionist psychological thriller, Joker is the comic book villain we deserve right now. Joker movie is a masterpiece! Its understanding doesn't cross the line into sympathy, as we're left watching a man who becomes less & less human as his tragedy unfolds. We repeatedly see him burst into laughter, but can never rule out whether he's actually crying.
10/10

Review Title: Grim, artistic and deadly cautionary tale-Joker is good but not super
Review:
Released AFTER rave reviews, with much fanfare and a deceptive buildup (the trailers only showed Joker as a victim) Joker is many things. A good piece of art and storytelling, a depressing cautionary tale, a moral sewer that is also entertaining, a dark harbinger of things to come as more ... We also have a cynical directors effort where he stole several previous films ideas (Taxi Driver, Falling Down, others)....In Joker we witness the downward spiral of the highly symbolically named Arthur Fleck. An abused child who as an adult absurdly attempts to be a professional clown and stand up comic, despite the obvious fact that he is decidedly the opposite of funny. Gradually, Arthur's world unravels and he crosses the line into pure madness and mayhem. It is clear that the viewer is suppose to be sympathetic towards Arthur but the big question is, should we ? At what point should stop blaming society and give the individual responsibility for his actions ? Normal people should feel some sort of revulsion towards Arthur/Joker as the film progressed, but unfortunately many people uncritically root for him to the finish.
The ending is confusing. I think the director got cold feet and added the ambiguity in order to avoid an even rougher ending that was certain to inspire real life violence, which I would be surprised if it does not anyway. The director punted.
Joachuin Phoenix's performance/ interpretation of the anti-hero Joker is outstanding- this is actually the best part of the film. The main flaw in this tragedy is how the story near the end actually violated English literature 101 dictum of "show, don't tell" This is why I give it a 7.5
Joker's politics can be viewed from both a left and right perspective but what is almost never mentioned is how the movie indicts single motherhood for being the toxic societal ill that it is...Watch this movie and know that there untold thousands of real life Arthur Fleck's out there...you have been warned.

You like social commentaryStream of consciousness review:I cried several times during this movie. I cried for the brutality of humanity and the depth of suffering we can experience at the hands of one another. I cried for Arthur. I cried for myself because in him I could see a frightened child, one which I still have. I cried because it was all too real, too accurate, too brutal. The violence was not in any sort of murder; rather, the violence was a mental one.Joaquin brought to life the tenderness of the open wound that is the human condition. One could view the entire thing as "trying too hard" but I did not go in with a cynical mind. And I'm sure glad I didn't because if I were cynical about everything I would hate everything. The commentary of a generation, the suffering. Feeling out of place in a world that moves too fast. You stop and smell the roses, and someone, out of spite, cuts your roses up and poisons the well. This may seem an extreme assertion on the surface but take a moment to think about times you have exposed your heart of hearts, to have it degraded, or worse, dismissed.The human condition is something we should start taking seriously again, because we are losing our humanity. We are losing our soul. I found it fascinating, the "jokers" running around, and then for this piece to come out, to address the shredded chord, the perforated vein running through all these folks. It is a dangerous slope, and we joke and ridicule those who would have something to say about it, but I believe this is out of fear. I understand that fear.

Review Title: I've seen sociopathy up close, this is the real deal!
Review:
This movie made me create an account to review it.
I've watched it twice in the cinema in 12 hours.
Here's the thing, I studied sociopathy for a few months after seeing it up close in a close person. Joaquin Phoenix didn't just deliver what may be the best performance an actor ever gifted the world (perhaps tied with Branston Cranston's Walter White in Breaking Bad).

This movie will still be remembered a century from now.

I really really liked this movie. It's very well acted, paced, directed, composed, and is overall one of my favorite movies of the year. Joaquin Phoenix steals the show again with what I think is the best performance of the year. The pacing is slow but the movie still manages to keep you entertained and on edge. All the camera work and music and sound design and set design came together really well. The script and the dialogue was also pretty good though it's not what makes this movie so great. It's just a very well executed movie.But, it's not a perfect movie, and there are some noticeable problems. The biggest complaint I've seen with this movie is that it's very similar and takes a lot from Taxi Driver and other Martin Scorsese films. And though I also wanted a more originality in the writing, I think it still works really well for this movie and for the characters. One thing I also noticed was the sometimes in your face feel of the movie, I definitely thought movie a bit more subtlety in it's presentation. The thing is, I think all these problems stem form the fact that Todd Phillips is very inexperienced in making these types of movies. But for every moment that highlights that, theirs a moment that shows his and potential once he becomes more experienced.There's also some other things that I liked that I think make this a 9/10 rather than an 8/10, particularly how violent and disturbing it was willing to be. And overall it's just a really really good movie.

Review Title: Dark, deep study of a man battling mental illness

His performance harkens back to his role in the obscure indy film "Don't Worry, He Won't Get Far on Foot." His role in "The Joker" is a study in madness you won't soon forget.The first 90 minutes of the film is absolutely gripping. The final 30 minutes delves into a zombie apocalypse that distracts from the personal focus of the film. However, there is a school of thought that the entire closing sequence was merely a fantasy in the Joker's disturbed mind.Much of the violence is suggested in the film; this is not all about blood and gore, though it does contain graphic, shocking scenes. Movie fans of shoot-'em-up, CGI Superhero films will be caught off guard by this biopic-epic.Robert DeNiro's supporting role as a talk show host is refreshing and a welcome relief from his endless stream of buddy films that has made people forget that he was once in the conversation as the best actor of his generation.A must see for movie goers who desire some adult drama instead of viewing yet another regurgitated comic book flick.

The Joker has been a staple in the world of DC comics and movies since the 1940's when he first appeared in the debut issue of the original comic book, "Batman", released on April 25th, 1940 written by Bill Finger. Since then, the Joker has been one of the most recognizable, favorable, and beloved characters of the DC Universe. The new 2019 "Joker" film is no exception.In the past, the Joker has primarily been focused and prayed on as a villain in the comics and movies such as "Batman" (1989), "Batman; The Dark Night" (2008), "Batman; The Dark Night Returns" (2013), and "Suicide Squad" (2013). In the new movie, "Joker", however, the film takes a new perspective.In the newest film, "Joker", we see a different side of the Joker portrayed by Joaquin Phoenix. In the beginning of the movie, we are introduced to Arthur Fleck, who later is referred to as the Joker. Arthur is a failed street clown with a disorder that causes him to laugh at random, and often unfortunate times. Because of his disorder, he is often tormented on an off again by people all around him. In the beginning of the film, we watch Arthur struggle making a living as a surviving clown. Shortly after as Arthur is walking home, we see a group of presumably pre-teens chasing after Arthur, eventually finding and beating him violently. This scene in the movie is hard to watch but intriguing for the viewer, making them question "why?". Later, we learn more of Arthur's condition and how he often states he feels "invisible" to his therapist. Arthur eventually starts to use the clown makeup that he used for his job he was recently terminated from as a way to feel more apart of the world, or less invisible. As the story progresses, we the viewer slowly learn how the Joker became what we all know him to be, a villain.Despite this movie being one of my favorites from the year 2019, I do feel that some aspects of the movie could have been improved, just like any other movie. I personally feel that some of the citizens in the movie who played small parts, such as the man that Arthur worked with in the clown business towards the beginning of the film could have been stronger actors. I wish some of those smaller roles had better actors playing them to better shine light on the general glory of this movie, but overall, they weren't terrible.In my personal opinion, I absolutely loved this movie. Weeks after seeing this movie I was still raving about it. In my personal opinion, I don't know how anyone could not like, or at least in the slightest, appreciate this movie. One of my favorite characters in any movie or comic ever as a child was the Joker, despite him always being portrayed as an antagonist. I personally feel that Todd Phillips did an amazing job directing this movie. I feel that he projected a bright, new, and interesting perspective on the way the Joker is as a character. I always felt like I wanted to know more about the Joker's backstory, and with "Joker" I feel like I received just that.

Review Title: No matter what anyone says, this film is a true masterpiece!

Joaquin Phoenix shows every layer, every nuance of Arthur's character, we actually get a peek inside Arthur's mind, and that is all I had to say about this, the screenplay by Todd Phillips is awesome, and in particular, special appreciation, shoutout, mention to Lawrence Sherr as the cinematographer, his camera is awesome, one of the best camera work in recent cinema and the background score by Hildur Gudnadottir, man, her score is just spooky, it just amplifies the mood and tone of the movie by leaps and bounds and the production design by Mark Friedberg looks stunning as he makes Gotham a truly dark place that the movie requires, this movie is subject to perspective, if you look at this movie as a piece of artwork, you will love it, if you look at it as a form of message, it truly would disappoint you, though, the overall message of the movie is for society's good. Review Title: Too stunned, too disturbed, too excited, too moved, too overwhelmed, in every good way possible.
Review: On the contrary to some critics' concern that this movie promotes meaningless violence, Joker does not glorify violence; it instead beautifies insanity with bittersweet and painful sufferings all attached to it, overwhelming the audience with unresolved feelings they never knew existed inside their past dreams, disappointments, aspirations, despair, hope and hurt. Don't be mistaken: Joker does not sugarcoat it or even set aside pains that come from years of abandonment, abuse, mental illness, severe depressions and disorders, and most painfully, the exhausting cycle of daily life after another. Instead, it takes it all in, put into beautifully stark, if not disturbing, images, with captivating soundtrack and music that chills your back even hearing it again long after the movie has ended, like a dark whisper, a reminder that the line between tragedy and comedy is not a line at all-because life is both, never less. Joker does not justify violence, but it attempts to get the audience to see a man's transformation from already troublesome life into the end any shred of sanity he has maintained.

Review Title: Joker- Discomfitting right up until the last scene, but worth the watch
Review: Humanity is not known to be empathetic towards those who are percieved weak. Here, we have a Joker, who's weak.. stunningly so. Joaquin has conveyed just how terribly weak he is, in the most convincing manner. His hair, his gait, his mannerisms, his tics, his speech. And the reason why most would find this movie an uncomfortable watch is mainly because the movie really doesn't give any excuses. It basically puts up a mirror to how society can and often does behave.The class divide, the class envy, the apathy towards sorrow (however big or small), the absolute indignity of life and living- none of it has been exaggerated. That does make the movie a little hard to palate. But precisely why it should be watched.The movie was beautifully shot, the background score was absolutely fantastic. Those are the technical aspects that have to be appreciated.. acting wise, it was a stellar cast and everyone did justice but of course Joaquin completely outshines everyone by the way he's committed himself to this role.Go watch this movie, but fair warning it's not meant to be a super villain origin story and therefore doesn't have any of the gimmicks associated with these comic inspired movies. You are basically watching a mentally ill man who's unravelling and reveling in the chaos that ensues.

This film is the difference between reading a comic book and reading a graphic novel. Both have their merits, their distinctions and their own arguments over what constitutes what just as a movie versus a film. From the very beginning, you get a very nostalgic look to this film including the title. This is an artists film and not a superhero movie; but that would be apparent from the posters and trailers alone, right? Most going into this will get exactly what they want. Some may be enticed, by the promise that it is not what they would expect from such a film, they will not be lied to. Any lover of film will at least like this movie as long as they do not mind seeing a little violence and being made to feel a certain way. This film invokes thought and emotion almost entirely throughout and will almost certainly leave with the viewer in conversation or contemplation. All of the cast is phenomenal and the script leaves very little if anything to be desired. The cinematography does wonders for making the viewer feel exactly as I believe the director intended, and the score will still be resonating within me even into the following weeks. I have not been to the cinema much lately as I prefer to view from the comforts of my own home, but anyone who feels as thought they should see even one movie in theaters a year, I would recommend this one to them. The conversations afterward alone will make it worthwhile, even if it would be to say how much you disagree with everyone else.

Beyond that... i don't know... I think nobody can dive deeper... there is no further depth... that's my point of view anyway...

Review Title: Disturbing Film that Celebrates the Sociopath Villain
Review: I just saw "Joker" starring Joaquin Phoenix, as the titular character, directed by Todd Phillip, because of its Oscar nomination for Best Picture, and the great odds that Phoenix will win the Oscar for Best Actor for his performance.That being said, I had a lot of apprehension going into it. I had put off watching it for more than four months, as it released on October 4. The movie, as expected, was very dark and very violent. The gun violence in particular is a disturbingly prominent component of the movie.A central theme of the film was mental illness and society's ignorance and lack of concern for people with very real needs. The unfolding of the horror on screen highlights some of the complicated issues involved. There are certainly no easy answers or quick fixes.Another theme was pitting the rich against the poor. Arthur Fleck, aka Joker, is a struggling comedian, living in a rundown apartment with his aging mom. Thomas Wayne is a wealthy philanthropist, who speaks out against the murder of three Wall Street stockbrokers on the subway. The film revives the ongoing discussion of wealth inequality of the 1%, movements like Occupy Wall Street, and films like "V for Vendetta." Fleck, though an outcast, bullied his entire life, laughed at (not for the jokes), becomes a symbol for the poor and downtrodden to stand up against the oppression of the wealthy.The film portrays him both as heinous villain and unlikely hero. The ugly crimes he commits make you turn away, but also causes you to pause. Joker becomes the leader of a revolution, however, you can see that revolution through violence and hate leads to a dark, destructive path.The film also stars Robert DeNiro, Zazie Beetz and Frances Conroy, among others. It was nominated for 11 Oscars including: Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Costume Design, Best Makeup/Hairstyling, Best Original Score, Best Film Editing, Best Sound Mixing, and Best Sound Editing.How do I feel about the film? Joaquin Phoenix was an excellent sociopath.But I wouldn't watch it again.The movie depicts how scary anarchism could really become if people chose to rise up and follow someone like Joker. I think there are some terrifying parallels between someone like Hitler and Joker. People filled with hate, who experience a taste of power, and then decide to wield that power to carry out their own personal vengeance against the object of their ire. The fabric of society tears apart at the seams as hate overtakes all reason.

Joker (2019) delivers a masterclass of acting by Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur Fleck and tells a deep and meaningful narrative in relation to society today. When critics compare it to Heath Ledger, or downplay Joaquin Phoenix's character as an incel or angry white guy, they are sorely mistaken and most likely misunderstood the narrative of the film. Heath Ledger's Joker was a brilliant take on the character but you must understand that the 2019 Joker is introduced in a more psychologically engaging manner, where we are able to directly see Arthur's life before he became the joker. Whereas in the Dark Knight, the audience is only able to see the Joker post origin. If you think about it, the Dark Knight's joker has had many years to perfect his violent strategies, but Joaquin Phoenix's Joker is quite literally about the beginning of he Joker and what caused it.Put it simply, comparing the two Jokers would be unnecessary and irrelevant as they are focusing on the character in completely different parts of their lives.
No need to attack the film because it felt uncomfortable and real, this film was designed with that in mind and to make the audience think long and hard about the society they live in, including mental illness in contemporary society.

Christian Bale's performances in American Psycho, The Machinist and Harsh Times all have merit with regards to roles pertaining to the dark side of mental illness. Joker takes this genre to a new level. This psychological thriller is perhaps the most captivating movie you are likely to have seen. Superb.

Review Title: If Joaquin doesn't get the Oscar, I'm suing
Review: Among the most anticipated movies in 2019, two have clowns as main characters. One is the adaptation of a novel about the return of a monster clown. The other is of course the backstory to the birth of Batman's arch nemesis: The Joker.The latest cinematic iteration involving the Clown Prince of Crime easily gets 9/10 in my book. I was helplessly hooked from the start, even if it's dragging like an extended bad trip to a wrong rabbit hole. I have my resentment towards this movie, though. How would I not: I had to watch the movie twice in two days, just so that I could assure myself the movie is a mere product of art, not a real footage of one's miserable life that brings all my pities and makes it all so relatable.Joaquin Phoenix as Joker is flawless and perfect. The pain and angst presented through his lines, interjections, mimical expressions and physical movements are all so real. His portrayal of a character who constantly struggle with a "condition" amidst the depression and disillusionment in his entire life is of utmost brilliance. It's hard to imagine any other actors in the business currently who coukd take the role to such a devastating effect, not even the Oscar nominated Jared Leto :-DThis year's Joker is last year's Freddy Mercury. Both provide a great template for the lead actors to explore and exploit an already well known figure (a source of other actors' envy), though Joker is certainly more multi-dimensional as a character. Since Heath Ledger's portrayal, we are used to see a Joker who's not always tidy and well dressed.Joaquin Phoenix helped create a sequential environment where the titular character is finally at his most insane state of mind, unlike Heath Ledger who brought up a maniacal/chaotic personification from the outset. It effectively provides the real and sensible feelings as we can witness Arthur Fleck's transformation from a helpless loser into someone that resorts to chaos and violence to ease his pains. No previous movies with similarly dark and disturbing nuances, such as "Pi" or "Requiem for a Dream", or even any of David Lynch' offerings in his most depressed mode, had left me THAT bothered and yet impressed all the same."Joker" is not a mere character study: it's a psychological outreach programme served fresh from Hollywood's darkest alleys. If Joaquin doesn't get the Oscar, I'm suing the Academy.

Review Title: It's indeed a very good film, but not a masterpiece like some people think it is.
Review: Let me just say that I thought Joker was a really good, well made movie. Hell, I might go as far as to call it a great movie. But it's not a 10/10 masterpiece, like the majority of reviewers are saying it is. The Irishman and Avengers Endgame were much better in my opinion. That's not to say it wasn't good because I loved it, the cinematography and music was great. There was also Joaquin Phoenix's amazing performance, which was very mesmerizing and enjoyable to watch when he was on screen. But I think we all know that he is a great actor, he has movies like the Master, You Were Never Really Here, and The Immigrant under his belt. Honestly, I think critics got a bit too offended with the subject matter and the darker tone, how it was handled, but regardless of woke politics, a reviewer's thoughts on a film should be somewhat impartial and unbiased. I will say that the movie starts off a bit slow, however, it is a really rewarding buildup that makes it pay off at the end. The cons of this movie are few and far between, but this movie is definitely not perfect. The first thing are the plot holes, which I mostly brushed off, but it's still an easily perceptible flaw. Secondly, Arthur's character arc and origin story, while I liked the overall way it was executed, I did feel the ending felt a bit unsatisfying. Third, it isn't totally original, as it does unashamedly rip off Scorsese a little bit, as its familiar story borrows elements from the King of Comedy and Taxi Driver, I still thought it was a well-done tribute, and I felt that it ripped him off in a good way. Those are a few minor flaws though, otherwise I'd highly recommend it, I thought it was a very good movie, possibly even one of the best films that came out this year, but it's not better than films like The Dark Knight or Spider-Verse, let's not go THAT far. I still thought it was much more interesting and original than the vastly overrated Black Panther though, and I would love to see it again. I hope this review was helpful and I think if you like comic book movies or the Joker character, you should be able to enjoy the movie at least as much as I did. My Final Rating: 8.5/10

Review Title: Excellent, refreshing take on a classic Batman villain
Review: The film is filled with awkward, intense, cringeworthy moments where you don't know whether to laugh or be horrified - and I loved every second of it. Director Todd Phillips take on the Joker was as good as it was due to Jauquin Phoenix's incredible take on such a storied character. To me, this movie was a much more modern and "real" take on how Aurther Fleck became the joker. Make no mistake, this is not a polished DC style movie with CGI and crazy effects. This is a gritty, dark drama that explores a man who feels alone, as if society has forgotten about him all together. His response is something the viewer can understand and even empathize with to some degree. The focus on mental health brings a move like this home and makes it feel far more down to earth than any other super hero movie. The different perspective on Thomas Wayne, Alfred, and other key characters in the Batman story provide an interesting counter point to the perfect benevolent super hero's were used to seeing.I can't seem to understand the negative reviews for this movie as this was easily one of the better movies I've seen this year.

Review Title: A Unforgettable, Profound, Deeply Moving Masterpiece
Review: This movie was simply beautiful, a masterpiece for all time. I think the reason why so many of us feel pity and - yes - sympathy for Arthur is because to one extent or another we have all experienced tragic moments and sorrow like he has, but we were able to pull out of our dark moments. Unfortunately, he never did.It is a truly realistic portrayal of how a cruel society can send essentially good person into the darkest depths of madness. The movie will not once let your mind drift into distraction as it is mesmerizing and fascinating from the very beginning to the very last moment. Despite the violence, you cannot help but feel for Arthur Fleck - Joaquin Phoenix's character - and may actually root for him, cheering him on in the hope that somehow everything will eventually lead to some form of happy ending for him. You'll have to see the movie to find out if it does.As for the movie reviews, some have been entirely unfair and biased for some strange reason I cannot fathom. One critic from a well known New York publication (btw, I'm from NY, too) criticized it for not being "fun," which makes it absolutely clear that guy has no idea what this movie is about and should probably dedicate himself to something else. If someone is out to see a "fun" movie, this masterpiece is not for you. As someone said in another review below, other movies are like going to eat a hamburger; this is more like a $1,000 steak. Fortunately, the success of movies by and large do not depend on film critics but rather on the general public and what we think about them.Regarding the references to Heath Ledger, with all due respect, it's like comparing apples and oranges. I saw his performance, and it was decent for entertainment purposes. But Joaquin Phoenix's performance is simply breathtaking and perhaps unlike anything ever seen before in movie history; Joaquin Phoenix descends into actual madness before our very eyes. He takes us an a journey through the human mind, with moments of light and moments of sad and disconcerting darkness, all while winning over the audience and getting it on his side. It's a depiction of life that we can all relate to in one way or another, which is why his performance is so unique.In terms of movie directing, Todd Phillips needs to be given credit, as he should be for offering us such a masterpiece. I'm sure it will mark and change his directing career.Finally, this is a movie I will see again, and again, and again to the end of my days. My former favorite movie of all time was Planet of the Apes (1968) because it had a deep message about the world and society, one I could relate to even though I was born years later. I think 'Joker' will replace it because it has touched me so deeply. I will simply say it had such an impact on me that I couldn't help but get emotional more than once.

Review Title: A realistic view into a villains uprising - finally !
Review: Before I touch upon the content of the movie , I have to say the vibe it creates is like a Taxi Driver of the modern age with super villain in the making overtones ; which is funny because Deniro is in the joker , I wonder if the director did this purposefully ?Anyways , this movie was an amalgamation of emotions stirred up for a person I didn't think I ever cared for , aside from being a badass in a previous portrayal by Heath. Let's put this to rest right now ; Joaquin's Joker was so real to the point that I connected on a more personal level (than previous jokers including heaths) and I can see authenticity in this joker being THE joker that eventually faces off with Bats - even in this "depressing" formative period of his .... despite being exposed to an action packed super intelligent Heath Joker years before this .The feeling of powerlessness and a world against you is really what gets you down through your first 40 minutes or so in the movie but it's not a depressingly down feeling it's more of a contemplatively-down feeling for Arthur's condition and his situation in life . Essentially , it's hard to NOT feel for Arthur as opposed to what previous movies would conjure up in us for the joker - which always painted him as a one sided villain as opposed to the complex more than human Joker we see in this film.Overall the scenes were shot so well I felt like I was watching an old movie, which also helped complete the feeling of taxi driver (also that revolver Joker gets seems like a snubbed version of it), but also gave the setting of the film a perfect alibi - this WAS INDEED the time before Batman ; and we can tell from the scenery , the outfits and the props ... very well done. I feel although there's no promise of a sequel , the director and cast HAS to deliver a sequel - as the roller coaster ride of this journey has just begun and they really pulled the tempo of the film off correctly as to really entice us to be hungry for more screen time of Arthur In his very earliest joker years .If I could , I would see this made into a tv series as it seems so realistic with the way it displayed this joker , and the action was spread out enough to create suspense and many other emotions . If this was done I would expect them to cast Joaquin , due to his great performance , or at least someone that can emulate his exact performance and demeanor - as this was a performance I didn't expect to "attract" me so much as it did .Great film , 10/10 for me - if it weren't for the critics mindlessly bashing this title I wouldn't have written this review , but I feel like this is something we need to speak up about because everyone seeing this film either really likes it or LOVES it - BESIDES the critics ... hmmm I wonder why ? Maybe it has something to do with the AGENDA of those that wish to push a specific NARRATIVE for their platform? Look that's fine and all but please be a bit more transparent with your bias if you choose to run a review website .Compare the critics to the user reviews , how many of each one and you will see who the liars are and who is telling the truth about the movie . Everythings an "opinion" they will say after slanging dirt in an untruthful review ... ok that's fine but don't go bashing something that was shot , edited , directed , and written WELL and try to pretend like it's just some unbiased opinion, we can see through that !I, like thousands of others , went into the film UNBIASED and loved it , do the same and you will too ; go in there thinking the movie will have your incel neighbor boy kill you , you will leave there confused just to go on your critic profile on meta critic and bash for no reason and that will guarantee you have a bad time under the guise of social semantics .

I don't think Joker succeeds in everything it tries to pull off. The start of the film makes it much more clear how messed up and sad Arthur's situation is, but the second half of the film seems to want you to root for Joker a bit more than I think is appropriate. Like the end of the film, where Joker triumphantly stands atop the wreckage of those who would imprison him, cheered on by the masses he unwittingly and uncaringly inspired, as he fully embraces the mad persona that is the pop culture staple we know as the Joker. The film seems to want you to think this is victory for Arthur and his followers, but isn't this really defeat? The society has failed him and everyone and broken a man, creating a monster that will haunt this city for years to come. I feel like a more sombre tone of music might have fitted better. (Also the cartoon chase at the end is silly)It has been noted how much the film draws inspiration from Taxi Driver and The King Of Comedy, but I feel like there was a good deal of American Psycho in there as well. The main characters are on opposite i8 of the socio-economic spectrum, but they struggle with many of the same psychological problems, especially the dissociation with reality. (Can we please have more movies that deal with mental illness that don't have imaginary people though)I liked the cinematography, the colour palette was distinct, notable, memorable and pleasing, while still fitting the dirty tone of the film. The music was pretty good too. Joaquin was really good, but what did you expect?I really liked the ambiguity of his origins and mental illness, but not so much the ambiguity of the events in the film. It makes it too easy to go "It was all a dream", which is one of my biggest pet peeves.
