It arrived, it delivered. That's what it comes down to. Joker lived up to the hype and then some. Originally, I was not sure how well a standalone Joker movie would play out, I thought it would be better of linking to a batman film e.g. Dark Knight but I was pleasantly mistaken. I have no doubt that Joker will be a contender for film of the year.The first thing that Joker does well is to pick the correct actor for the job. My god did Joaquin Phoenix give a phenomenal performance. I know that Joaquin only picks roles that he believes he can excel in and I would have never pictured him for this but easily one of the best performances he has done. You feel bad watching the character slowly snap, lose his mind and turn dark. You are rooting for him throughout and that can only be achieved through great acting. Joaquin is in for an Oscar for his role, could easily see him winning it but you never know, a nomination at least. Everyone else does a standup job as well especially Robert De Niro, if I didn't know him, I would have thought they got an actual TV show host on to perform his role. Stellar performances all round, bravo.The plot is original and well laid out. There is a good plot structure so some build-up to a great ending. You can tell that the writers focused on Arthur as a person rather than the Joker character, it could have been portrayed with nothing to do with the Joker. It was a nice touch that they didn't just lean on the big name, they instead delved deep into a psychotic person and added the Joker name as a topper. This created a nice blend of source material and new original ideas.Emotions will be pulled from you. As I mentioned earlier, you honestly feel for the guy, you get a barrage of different emotions throughout. One moment you think things are going well the next you feel worried and concerned. Not many movies are able to get this from you so well and so frequent.The only negative I had with Joker was the over-used Batman scene. It's such a small negative that I wasn't going to include it but I keep thinking it over and I didn't see the need. Would say spoilers ahead but it has no real link to the film and its been seen many times, you'll know it, trust me. So the classic scene where you see Thomas and Martha Wayne get shot down the alleyway, necklace snaps off as it always does and Bruce is left standing there. Good scene but this happens near the end of Joker and I feel like they could have done it better with just having the shot of Bruce being alone. You didn't need the full scene. It was an exact copy of all the other films that have portrayed this. Like I said it's a small nitpick but it just didn't fit right playing the full 5-minute scene.Joker, an amazing film that gives you true emotion, an original, decent plot and some of the best acting in the business. You will find very little fault here so watch Joker as soon as possible.9/10P.S - People saying they walked out the cinema because of how dark this is, yes it's dark but c'mon get a grip it ain't that bad.

Review Title: A Breath of Fresh Air From Your Usual Hollywood Film
Review: In my opinion, Joker did not quite live up to expectations. The amount of hype this movie received was insane, and it would have been quite hard for the film to be as good as I was hoping it would be. Despite my slight disappointment however, I still really enjoyed this movie.Arthur Fleck's character and his arc are both tragic and moving. Taking the concept of the Joker, a character who is commonly portrayed as a chaotic evil villain, and turning him into a sympathetic person was quite daring. One thing I especially liked was how Arthur's fall into villainy took it's time and was built up on a lifetime of cruelty and mistreatment, instead of a singular incident being the cause of his evil.Joker also did a good job in setting the grim mood of the film with it's depiction of Gotham City. The dull grey color palette and the ominous soundtrack at the start of the story really added to the overall affect. As the film progresses the weather becomes brighter and the soundtrack becomes more upbeat to indicate what Arthur Fleck is feeling. These little touches make the atmosphere more real and alive.It goes without saying that Joaquin Phoenix did a spectacular job. I had no doubt he would win that Oscar. While I did not enjoy his performance as much as Heath Ledger's Joker, Phoenix's Joker is completely unique and memorable. Doubtless this film wouldn't have been as enjoyable as it was without Phoenix. He is a spectacular actor and I look forward to watching some of the other films he's been in.The story is quite slow-paced, but I was never bored. Arthur's sympathetic character and the city he lives in were quite gripping and hooked me for most of the story. It was slowly building up to a climax, and when the third act did finally arrive I was not disappointed. The final thirty minutes of the movie were almost perfect.There are a couple of things that annoy me about this film, such as the unnecessary inclusion of Bruce Wayne and the extreme lack of subtlety. Bruce Wayne does not really have a place in this plot and his scenes were basically just fan service. I like the ironic twist that Joker ended up creating his own enemy, but it detracts from the main focus of Arthur's story.I also wish that the movie was a tad more subtle in it's message. Subtlety isn't necessary in good film making, but this movie forces the message down your throat, without leaving anything for your audience to figure out for themselves. These problems, in my opinion, hold it back from being a true masterpiece. Still, it is a great film and I look forward to watching it again.

Review Title: If DC can take a hint, Todd Phillips needs a script for 'Transmetropolitan' ASAP
Review: With all the goofy, CIA-Project-Mockingbird Media surrounding this, PR firms starting fights in the blogosphere, oligarchs in silicon valley (and so DOD) raking in the ad revenue- with all the hype- 'The Joker' is really just a cartoonish character study, and really more of an homage to a certain type of character- a meditation on absurdity and chaos, than it is some 'brilliant psychological' work. The hype surrounding it sort of shot themselves in the foot, considering the violence, agitation, and chaos was coming more from their assumptions, anodyne analyses of the film, than from the film itself. The American people, and others around the world, are just sick and tired of being dismissed, and any characters who can animate this in an accurate way are bound to get attention- they strike a chord, and they should. And for those of you who think this was some brilliant piece of psychology- see the films of Bergman, Cassavetes, Haneke, Dreyer- those are some of the true masters of psychology in film. Not to play down Todd Phillips effort here- he did as good a job as someone could probably do w this material, and it was cool that they had no problem admitting it's homage to films like Taxi Driver and Fight Club. The truth is, until Frank Miller came around, the Joker really wasn't this interesting- people kind of built him this way, especially after the death of Heath Ledger cemented the role's legacy. A much better, more controversial DC character- and better comic in my opinion- has yet to see the screen- Transmetropolitan. Today's environment, with the indictment of Assange, mysterious death and labyrinthine past of Jeffrey Epstein- as Whitney Webb has chronicled on Mintpress News- this cynical, yet noirish technocracy- that is the world of Transmetropolitan. And the hero, or anti-hero, Spider Jerusalem, is what this new Joker wishes he could be. DC- get the best script of Transmetropolitan to Todd Phillips, pronto! You've got territory here that Marvel is clearly scared to explore- the territory of the counterculture.

The Joker. Purchased those tickets expecting the return of Batman's most famous villain? Laughing whilst killing cops? Robbing banks? Burning down hospitals? Well prepare for quite a dissatisfying 120 minutes because this time, Joaquin Phoenix is not playing as the Joker we know, he's playing as someone much more than a maniac and representing something much more than lunacy.Joaquin Phoenix's superb acting and taunting yet victorious music by Hildur Gudnadottir go hand - in - hand and alas produces an almost disturbing and, at the same time, wonderful piece of art. But what enthralled me more is the film's embedded symbolism.Do try to decipher the meanings behind the film and not just merely watching it because by then, what is in our sight takes us away from what is not. How one decipher those meanings may differ, meanings are subjective, but do take notice on the common ground that we can all agree on. For the first time - or for the first time that we realise - the crazy mad clown killer represents the unfortunate, the underrepresented, the disabled, the labelled-as-unhinged...the people. Throughout the first half of the film, Joker is seen as an invalid that no one cares of. Then there is the Wayne who proclaims to be the cure for Gotham, the cure for the madness that people like him (the upper classes) have created, a satire to those who now rule, but never govern. Now watch as the clown that everyone laughs at becomes the person they have always needed, but never knew. In the end, the society's shadow rises as the symbol and the centre of a revolution, an upbringing of the left behind. For once, people realise that maybe they are no different from that clown, the clown that has had enough of the lies, ignorance, and the fake promises of the ruling classes that Wayne represents.One -- I hope -- can realise that this is no ordinary DC film, this is a story of a joke that is our society and a clown who has become weary of laughing.

Review Title: With style over typical substance, "Joker" delivers an unlaughable masterpiece of its own.
Review: "Joker," the tragic crime drama, loosely based on DC Comics' iconic villain & directed by Todd Phillips is a film of many layers but definitely not any sort of one typical comic book film. The impact and influence the film may as well leave behind is unimaginable & will definitely go down as one of the most iconic comic book films ever made.Now, before jumping onto anything, let me be clear - Joker's story is weak to certain extent but it's upto personal realisation if a "story" is really possible in real life. Yes, the Todd Phillips (and Scott Silver) made sure that the film stays as realistic as possible throughout & I believe, they've done an exceptional job. Each & every directors have their own unique style of filmmaking. Someone like James Cameron prefers a proper cinematic story, someone like Makoto Shinkai prefers metaphorical exploration and depiction to explain the context, someone like Christopher Nolan or Quentin Tarantino prefer nonlinear storymaking with additional dynamics through extraordinary usage of camera & music. Todd Phillips' Joker is completely different from anyone of them because right from the first minute, the film doesn't seem to develop a story but rather get driven by the characteristics-development of Arthur Fleck & the consequences he faces in daily life due to an unfortunate neurological condition, which makes him laugh at any given time without consent. And to think, that's where the "plot" begins interestingly!Nothing to take away from Joaquin Phoenix though as he undoubtedly was the best part of the film! The impeccable performance he delivered is definitely rare nowadays & it'd be unfair to not stand up and applause at the end. He made sure that the viewers actually start to feel his life of betrayal by the loved ones and ignorance by others as much as him, himself, while keeping the political tone of the film intact. Yes, undoubtedly Joker, the core character of the film, will go down as one of the most influencing, significant & impactful characters in film history. Dialogue writer, too, deserves a lot of credits. But at the end, it was upto Joaquin Phoenix only for portraying the highly complicated character. But other than that, the rest of cast had pretty much nothing to do (other than Thomas Wayne, who's the key of the film as well as Arthur's mother, whose own mother ended up being the biggest betrayal of all) & therefore, expecting some high level casting would've been unfair. Nevertheless, each & every minor characters didn't lack any kind of acting skills.But every significant incidents that occurred & the impactful and questionable consequences took place in return in the films, largely find their tones due to the background scoring by Hildur Guðnadóttir. Pretty much on a Hans Zimmer's level performance, Hildur manages to provide an identity to the film as much as the director, writer & of course cinematographer. Laurence Sher, the cinematographer, too has had an exceptional performance behind the camera as he managed to capture the essence of poverty of America and how neglectful we, at times, are. The technical department, without a second thought, deserves one third credits for the success of the film and to be honest, that's highly usually as most of the time, their efforts go unnoticed. But this time around, the case is impressively different.At the end, I'd say "Joker" is pretty much an unique and exceptional film & extremely rare of its kind. The title itself is a metaphor depicting the panglossian man whose optimism is being mocked and his core being shaken over & over again, rather than showcasing the glory of undoubtedly one of the most gruesome villains of all time as it's not one of your daily comic book films. It's not following any old storyline. It's not one pure psychological "thriller." It's not about just action, because the actions here are mostly not physical but mental. And it's definitely not about the iconic name of "Joker." It's about the negligence unfortunate people face, it's about events that can turn any person into criminals. It's about many things, which a film usually would fail to recognise or portray perfectly, unlike Joker & that's exactly why it's a must watch masterpiece. Todd Phillips & Joaquin Phoenix's true agathokakological representation of "Joker" sure is one that'll go down as one of the top (much deserving) contenders for Oscar 2020, one that'll highly influence you to not remain ignorant anymore and start to treat the unfortunate equally if not better, one that'll keep questioning you till the very end, one that'll test your own moral, one that'll shake your belief, one that'll introduce you to the actual dark world & most importantly, one that'll leave you spellbound to be answerable to yourself.

Review Title: Have people seen the film or just giving the trailer a 10?
Review: Look, in some aspects the film is a triumph. The way it has been shot is beautiful, the score is excellent, there is a true depression to the film that feels authentic and the performance from Phoenix is flawless.The main problem is that the Joker is supposed to be the archetype of a super villain, causing chaos where ever he goes, charming, intelligent and ultra violent. Phoenix's Joker is as far removed from this depiction as possible; a pathetic loser that only by luck it seems fulfils his destiny. Whilst I really enjoyed the premise of the film - a slow decent in to insanity, it would have been a lot more effective if the character was a little bit more sociopathic and a lot less self loathing.Another thing that really stood out for me was the lack of subtlety in the script, it seems as if the director has no trust the viewers intelligence, numerous times throughout the film you are basically force fed the narrative as if you could not figure it out for yourself.For all its attempts of being a psychological thriller, the Joker unfortunately misses the mark, which makes me just a little bit crazy.

The basic plot setup is the same, but the execution is so different so I wouldn't compare the two. All in all, I can't recommend this movie enough.10/10 would forget the snacks I brought with me again

Joker is a disturbing character. From the few I can remember about him, I was shocked by his cruelty. I was dreading to watch this movie because of that.But this film is different. This film presents the man before the criminal. Or more precisely, how the man became the criminal. We enter into the psychological complexity of someone who is rejected, mistreated by the society. There is no need to have former knowledge about Joker and the DC universe to understand this movie. It may be Joker as it may be any other men. It is probably a more realistic representation of the character, and that may be the most disturbing about it. But we don't leave the movie without having been moved deeply.How can a man become a murderer? That was the great question. Is it a result of his misfortune? Of his rejection or his feeling of rejection by the society? Is it for recognition? Or perhaps for a mixture of all these reasons, and others. The film aims to address all these interrogations, and do it quite well!It is engaging, from the beginning to the end. It doesn't let us getting bored for a minute. Joaquin Phoenix's performance is absolutely admirable! The music always appears at the appropriate moments to give us chills. The cello's sound, marking the emotions Arthur Fleck feels as the film goes on.

If what you want to see is the Joker doing his campy crimes, you wont see that.What you will see is a mentally damaged man doing the best he can. Trying to be happy, trying to make others happy, trying to do the right thing. Then watching as seemingly every one and every thing beats him down. He is forced to accept that he will never have a fighting chance at hope unless he accepts what he is, how he feels, and trusts that it is "right" in his own mind. Arthur Fleck was never supposed to be a villain, he was made to be a villian. And that's why I love this movie.Small addition to the compliments: the colors were very vivid when they needed to be among the dismal scenery. Joaquin's pain in the viewer was felt every time he represented it. The actors were all stunning (aside from young Bruce who could have been a mannequin for all I know) and the music was ON. POINT. I'm noticing a lot of Hollywood movies are like that recently and I'm LOVING it. And finally, for an origin, every single scene mattered. No wasted dialogue, no useless characters. I'm happy all over.

Review Title: It's a good movie, but it's not Joker
Review: It's about a mentally ill person pushed to breaking point and he snaps. The depictions of his world is haunting, beautiful yet soul-wrenching to watch. Great credit to directing, acting, cinematography, and overall production.But, is he the Joker? Sure, the film goes to great lengths to show he's mentally ill. Everything is explained, from his condition to his costume, to his iconic smile. Everyone who gets hurt deserves it. Everything has a reason.Really? This is the Joker? You feel sorry for him, not fear him. Where's that sense of anarchy? Where's that guy who just wants to watch the world burn? Where's that maniacal prankster?I get this is an origin story but there's no foreshadowing at all of the criminal mastermind he's supposed to become. There's not a hint of elaborate scheming, or manipulation or the slightest clue of mischief or glee in hurting people. I would imagine Joker is the child who delighted in painting his dog red and then framing his neighbour's kid and giggling at it.No, this version of Joker is just a sad man who needs a hug. He's totally no match when Batman comes.

Review Title: Joker is a masterpiece which a lot of people deserve to see
Review: Joker starts off as a slow movie following the character Arthur, who is a mentally ill man who faces many problems throughout his life, however this movie which was slow for about 15 minutes of the movie soon takes a turn and introduces a roller coaster of emotions, which can make the audience feel both uncomfortable and intrigued. This movie also makes the audience ponder on the joker's actions, should you sympathise with what he does, or should you feel horrified. Joker also introduces these emotions with Joaquin Phoenixes Oscar worthy performance. Acting as a clinically insane man broken down by society would be difficult to play, however I believe that Joaquin Phoenix did an incredible job playing the Joker and I don't think it could have been done any better, same said with the story. Now I'm not going to spoil the story but I do have to say the story is completely different and adds a whole lot of surprises compared to the trailers. But don't let this stop you from seeing the Joker. The story is better than the trailers as it is a lot more interesting and gripping. That being said Joker does have its small problem, the music and sound. Don't get me wrong the soundtrack is great, but the original composed soundtrack feels out of place at times and takes a little while for the audience to really understand the emotion that that sound gives, however this is only on a few scenes so it isn't that big of a problem. Joker is definitely a different take on the criminal mastermind that we are normally used to, and it's an extremely good version of the joker and one which may have an impact on different comic book characters in the superhero movie genre. Overall Joker is a 95% out of 100%, it is a masterpiece and the jokes are on you if you don't go out and watch this movie or watch it on its disc or digital release.

Review Title: A very moving, very bold and very important film.
Review: Excellent film. One of the best Batman films I have watched (if not *the* best): A well-written and entirely believable origin story. Phoenix's portrayal went above and beyond my expectations - I think this is the best performance I have ever seen from him. The comparisons I have seen between him and Ledger are unfair in my opinion: They both portrayed very different parts of the Joker's history, and they both did an incredible job.The compassion and empathy I had for Arthur moved me to tears. It was very emotional to watch, and probably would contain many triggers for people with past experiences of abuse. Without exploring his history in detail here, his background resonated with me. His family history and present situation, employment circumstances, bullying and ostracism (both the overt displays and more subtle, insidious ones), deterioration in stability, dissociation and delusion, fury and hopelessness, and even his laughter. I do not have the same condition, but I have a history of laughing or smiling inappropriately in extremely uncomfortable situations (I lost a friend over it a long time ago), when I found nothing funny about them. I felt immense guilt, shame and questioned my morality whenever this occurred.I understand that feeling empathy for someone who commits murder doesn't sit well with people. I do not condone the character's actions or intend to minimise the devastating impact these crimes leave behind. I simply deeply empathise with how Arthur felt in the build up to that (although I do feel that the sequence of events in the first 30-40 minutes were a little rushed - more development would have been better in my opinion). I desperately wanted to comfort and support Arthur, before he reached that point. It was captivating yet heartbreaking to witness him descend deeper and deeper into a pit of despair and madness that he couldn't crawl out of. Throughout the film, I wished that someone noticed the warning signs earlier and cared enough to do something.Having been a support worker for people who committed various, serious offences - and raised within a family that has a dark history of abuse, crime and violence - I understand the sequence of events that can potentially lead to these consequences, without excusing or justifying them. I can even see how my own decisions and outcomes could have been dramatically different and I'm very grateful that I was able to choose an alternative way of life. Common themes for many of those I supported - which were also present in the film - were a perpetual cycle of abuse passed from generation to generation, violence being normalised within social circles, poverty, isolation and inadequate intervention.I like how the film looked at mental health provisions, austerity and how the system fails people. It also addressed the detachment and disconnection between service providers and service users in a relatable way. I felt Arthur's alienation and frustration. It's painfully pertinent to our current circumstances here in the UK.Unlike other critics whose reviews I have read, I didn't feel Arthur was nothing more than a bitter, entitled white man with a gun (although there was certainly an element of that, deliberately I suspect - the film unravels like a social commentary). I understand their perspective, but this oversimplifies his character tremendously. Perhaps simplification makes people feel more comfortable when confronting such dark and multifaceted matters, and when faced with the flawed, raw humanness of those who hurt others.A very moving, very bold and very important film.

Review Title: Best movie of 2019? For me: YES!

First of all, let me start with this:Why anyone would give this movie (or as a matter of fact almost any movie) a 1 out of 10, I just cannot fathom.There are so many aspects of a movie (storyline, acting, directing, soundtrack, camera etc. you get the point) and there is hardly a movie out there that really sucks at all those aspects, that a 1 is almost never justified, but ESPECIALLY THIS movie could never be worth just a mere 1 out of ten, so why be such a hater to give it a 1?The soundtrack, the camerawork, the acting, OMG, for these alone you should give this movie at least a 6 out of then, since they are spot on...The acting of Joaquin and all of the supporting actors, well you couldn't really find any fault in those as well , so that would also be at least a 6/10...the only thing that remains is the script/story. You might not like the heavy subjects (Things like mental diseases/ physical afflictions/ bullying/ (glorification of) violence etc. or the dark setting (remember, this is Gotham, and although it looks like New York it isn't)If those subjects or the overall atmosphere of the movie is not your cup of tea, you might give it a lower rating because of that, but never a 1 out of 10...that is just spite and hate rating, nothing else...
Something similar applies to a rating of 10 out of then, usually this is used by fanboys blinded by their love for the movie, not being able to be critical or to see any fault, because enough movies, no matter how good they are, have faults to some degree, so even the best movies hardly deserve a 10 out of 10...(or the 10 is given by paid accounts just to pump the rating :D )...HOWEVER, JOKER REALLY deserves 10/10...Aside from being a very depressing/heavy subject movie, it is done to such perfection, I just could not find a fault in my first viewing (I will watch it again, come Blu-ray time)
Yes, Joaquin should get the Oscar for lead actor, the score is spot on, should also be nominated, the camera work as well! The director and the whole movies should also fall in the nominee categories come Oscar time 2020.......
I say, go see it while it still plays, go with an open mind and please don't blindly give it a 1/10 ( or 10/10), give it an honest rating based on the sum of its parts...

Review Title: A fresh change from the usual blockbusters
Review:
Joker:
A Different comic book movie for better or worse. Most of the time it doesn't feel like one at all. It has been hyped up after its release mostly by DC fans and teenagers as one of the greatest and deepest movies of all time which it certainly isn't. I just took it as an entertaining movie and it was. Joaquin Phoenix truly delivers a knockout performance and is certainly among his 5 greatest ever. His performance certainly felt a lot like in The Master and I think that is why he was cast.So its basically about a guy who is a victim of the society and is preyed on by people because of his mental disorders until he snaps and becomes JOKER. It was pretty entertaining in a dark way and I didn't really feel bored at any time. But I didn't find it as deep as others think. It basically tried to cram in many social issues like Treatment on mentally ill people by us and also class struggle. But the director doesn't really come to a solid opinion on any of these nor does he raise questions on a new fresh matter. The only thing we can learn is that every person has a breaking point so we must all be nice to each other. Come on is that all he had to say? It sounds cheesy right. And coming to the technical things the cinematography and the score were really magnificent, so while watching for the first time it really blows you away along with Phoenix's performance. The writing is good for the most part but some dialogues felt ham fisted. But the thing which I hated most was the world building. It was basically on the society being so harsh to Arthur(Joker) that he can't take it anymore but the characters were all one dimensional. They just beat Arthur up because they can? Everyone was a prick to Arthur. There wasn't even a single good guy in the entire movie. Yeah it was made in order for us to sympathize with Arthur but should we really sympathize with him that much? Things could have been told subtly. There was no need for so many in your face things which was basically Todd Phillips screaming "Society is Bad" again and again. And it doesn't really tell why Arthur wants to kill people. Does he enjoy it or just for the publicity(I may be wrong as I haven't seen it in months). And comparisons with taxi driver and king of comedy doesn't help it either. Both those were made so well as it took a particular facet of our behaviour and explored it deftly and brilliantly. The only thing Joker does that is remotely close to those movies is Joaquin's performance which still aren't as good as De Niro's.But there were things which I liked a lot too. The final 30 minutes or so looked good and was entertaining even though it didn't make a lot of sense. The music was good as well. Even Gary Glitters song felt good thematically as it is showing a disgraced character dancing to the song of a disgraced man. And also theories that Joker is basically him narrating the entire thing as his backstory redeems most of the flaws of the movie as he is just trying to make us feel sympathy towards him hence making everything up. But I don't like these kinds of movies because what point does it serve? That's why I didn't even like Usual Suspects that much even though it was well made.So Joker is certainly a must watch as it brings something new to the superhero genre and could inspire other studios to make similar kind of movies. And it certainly is entertaining also with a brilliant performance at its centre. I personally don't think it inspires violence but I certainly feel the critics who have said it does do have a point. A 7 from me.

Review Title: Excellent example of mental health portrayal in film!
Review: Aside from the storytelling of how the Joker came to be, this film beautifully captured the true essence of what it means to be living with a mental illness in a society that struggles to accept and understand it. The inaccuracies and exaggerations that come with the portrayal of mental illness in movies are all things we are prone to see and unfortunately fuel the stigma surrounding mental illness. It's refreshing to see a movie that tackles that stigma at its core by showing problems with society itself and how society treats individuals struggling with mental illness. It's very possible to merge entertainment with education and this movie exceeded that. While addressing issues like societal judgement and unhelpful medical staff, we were able to see it conveyed in a way that was also interesting and entertaining to see. The aspect that resonated with me the most was when Arthur called his therapist out for not listening and asking the same questions every week. Another aspect I found particularly interesting was how even though Arthur made efforts to get help and treatment, he wasn't given help when his therapist informed him that funding cuts were being made and he wouldn't be able to continue seeing her. Keeping the momentum of going to treatments and trying to get better is a long struggle that takes a lot of effort and work. Not being given the proper resources or support to keep that treatment can also be extremely detrimental and many are unfortunately put in this position. There are many individuals struggling with mental illness that do not have the resources to get help. I'm glad this point was reinforced in this film because there are individuals that want and seek help but simply do not have the resources to continue or find it. What made this movie unique was its ability to speak to a large audience, not only those struggling with mental illness but also those seeking to understand those that do. One of the ways Joaquin Phoenix prepared for his role was he studied up on how to portray Arthur's mental health struggles in the most accurate ways possible. One of the best ways we can tackle the stigma is to show more accurate portrayals and working alongside mental health professionals or psychologists so actors can portray those characters in the most accurate ways possible. While there are no justifications for Arthur's crimes, we did see how lack of empathy and support influenced the way he saw the world. The world can be a very cruel place, but the most important thing we can do is extend a helping hand to a stranger to spread a little joy in the world.

Review Title: Wanna know how I got these scars?
Review:
Joker is, technically, a very good film.Todd Phillips' direction is evocative and at times, simply beautiful. Every scene, creating a strong mood. Usually one of unease and tension. Top job.Joaquin Phoenix is, as he always is.....just brilliant. That man is a gifted actor indeed. In the moments when he is experiencing his maniacal rage, all he needs to convey this, is his eyes. You see every bit of rage and hatred in those eyes. They tell everything.
Not many actors are so completely riveting as to just capture you, hook line and sinker, just with their eyes. He's a powerhouse of the art of acting.As for comparing Heath Ledger's Joker to Joaquin's, one review I read on here said it was "unacceptable" to do so.
I will go one further and say, it is not even possible.
These two characters, these two Joker's, are so far removed from the other, that one could not even think them the same character at all. Not even if they were from parallel universes.
That's how different the two portrayals are.
Simple as that.As indicated by my username, I am a fan of Heath's Joker. In fact, I'm a big fan. The only tattoo I have (and will ever have, cos damn that hurt) is a portrait of Heath as Joker, with the WSS catchphrase underneath.
This does not mean, however, that I don't ever want to see the Joker on screens anymore because Heath has passed.
And it does not mean that I have ridiculously high standards for post-Heath portrayals of the Clown Price either.
I've been a Joker fan all my life, through many of his iterations. I grew up with Cesar Romero. I was a teenager when Jack dazzled us with Burton's re-invention.
I'm not so fussy who plays Joker, just as long as it is Joker.So this brings me to the only issue I had with this incarnation.
Todd and Joaquin's Joker, just didn't "feel" like Joker to me.
There was one scene, about half hour from the end, when I looked at Joaquin and thought, "Wow....there's Joker." but it was brief and his character then reverted back, after that one scene.
I think the main reason I never "saw Joker", was because Fleck was portrayed as rather imbecilic. Of below average intelligence. Joker is meant to be the Crown Prince of crime. A criminal mastermind.
Joaquin's Joker was more like a homicidal maniacal Forrest Gump.
Even his laugh, didn't hit home for me. Just a personal thing, I guess.
Don't get me wrong, as I've stated, Joaquin was brilliant and it was hard to take my eyes off his riveting performance, but for me personally, it wasn't really Joker.
It was as if Fleck was the guy the real Joker was going to be inspired by. Be mentored by, even perhaps.

The film creates as true scenario and throws a fictional character in it to create the ideal comic book film. Review Title: While not a bad movie, it was a little disappointing
Review:
After all the high praise this movie got, I went to the movies with high hopes. The movie wasn't in any way bad, but not great either. Let's talk about the good.
Joaquin phoenix did a great job with his performance. Without him the movie probably would have been pretty bad. The story itself and the idea behind it was pretty good too. The acting was good of everyone and the character development wasn't bad either.The problem with this movie is that, like most comic based movies, is aimed at an audience that, let's say, goes there without wanting to think about it much. There is little to no subtility. It isn't a dramatic movie in which things happen that build up little by little until it becomes too much. It aims to be, but does so by going so far over the top it loses most of it's believability. Horrible stuff happens. One after another. One thing would be almost enough to push someone over the edge, but because it may not be apparant enough, there have be like 10 horrible things to make it clear that's what going on. Certain small twists are in in this movie that made me think: Hm, not bad. Sadly... the directors felt the need to show a lot of scenes to... make it clear there was this small twist, which ruined the twist for me. This movie has a lot of moments where it could have been better. It could have made the movie great, even. But sadly it goes so over the top that the majority of things make you sigh and think... no one would ever behave like that.Again, by no means is this a bad movie. But it shows that even a great actor cannot make a movie great if it is so dumbed down even my 3 year old would understand it

Review Title: One of the most depressive title I'd ever seen! Please keep young or happy people away of this movie.
Review: I'm a big fan of superhero movies and I had to see this one. I went to the cinema at one of the late shows so I will begin telling that no matter the movie is very long and the show was very late ( I sleep early), you don't blink during the whole movie. And I mentioned this because the movie Is kind of slow paced but no matter that, everything looks so well placed that anything relating to filmmaking cannot be criticized in any level. The sound is good, the music is mostly sad but fits so well that in the end that doesn't bother you. The sound is terrific. In summary everything relating to technical and artistic filmmaking is superb. But a movie is not only that, it has a soul based on the plot and this one has very good history but one just so depressing that cannot recommend this movie if you're going to the movies to have a nice moment. Seeing a movie is about feelings about a history and I consider that the history is key in how you feel after the movie, but this one goes too beyond in that apart. Is simply too much depressive. Not even sadness as we are talking of a villain. People is talking about darkness. Is not anything like that. Is just depression in maximum level. The character could be any other character that you can imagine. Name anyone. This is not a comic book story but the psychological fall of a person. A fall into a criminal citing society excuses. Doesn't need to be named the Joker. Anyone could have been the lead character Name. This movie could be named after anyone you can imagine. Don't need to be a comic character. This is not about comics or superheroes. Is about how humans minds can be devastated by society. You'll see a radiography of the society but a one that will highlights the bad in a way that will hurt your happiness. In summary, I give this one a 10 for is cinematic merits ( will receive Oscars for sure) and a 6 for being such horribly example of human degradation. In the end this one is a solid 8 to me. Not because any flaw of the movie on its own production, neither artistically or technical, but for the tone so devastating and depressive of the movie. Please keep young or happy people away of this movie. They will leave the movie on such low key that they don't deserve to see or have such a horrible point of view of life. For that there is enough on TV news. This Is not a superhero movie. Nor a comicbook one. It is a psychological study on how people lost faith in theirselves, fitted into a commercial character that drag audience to the cinema.

Review Title: This is how you do a comic book movie
Review: Watch out Endgame, you've met your maker. This is an absolutely marvelous movie. I was honestly worried that people wouldn't appreciate this film considering what it is. The criteria of comic book films today are so action-oriented that it took the cinema by storm. Joker is simply a drama-thriller film. There are little to absolutely no action sequences throughout the film, yet it still does the comic book genre so much justice simply by telling an origin story. Joaquin Phoenix played Joker to a tee. His laugh was so genuine and believable that, instead of seeing him as a madman, you saw his pain and anguish. Joker's characterization is so good here that, regardless of his criminal acts, the film still pulls you to his side. It gives you a clear understanding that murderers aren't born that way or don't just become that way out of thin air. That's what I love so much about this film. Even though it's a comic book film, the story and morals tie into society of the real world, which is something that most comic films avoid. You're doing yourself a disservice if you haven't seen this film yet. Trust me, it's worth your money. I'll end this review with a music quote that relates heavily to the film..."Anybody is a killer, all you gotta do is push them to the limits." - J. Cole (A Tale of 2 Citiez)

Joker is unlike any previous DC film, with Todd Phillips forming a more political and psychological take on one of cinema's favourite villains. Joaquin Phoenix, who appeared in the Sisters Brother earlier this year, plays Arthur Fleck, a failed comedian working as a clown in Gotham City, where tensions increase day by day. Fleck wears two masks: one is his clown make-up, and one is his 'happy face', which, along with his uncontrollable manic laughter, hides the reality of his dark and deteriorating mental state. Phoenix proves the perfect choice of actor, and arguably suits this style of Joker better than any previous actors would have. This is because the Joker in this film is not so much a villain as he is a victim - very different (but not superior) to the character played by the late Heath Ledger. The way Joaquin is able to contort his face and body, as well as displaying multiple contrasting emotions at one, means his character is deeply complex and utterly disturbing. Not a huge fan of DC and action movies in general, I was originally apprehensive about seeing Joker, but it completely defied my expectations. Instead, the events are frighteningly believable, and the film is really a delve into mental illness, exposing faults in Americas' support systems for society's most vulnerable. However, for those expecting the usual explosive action of previous DC films, this one may prove a disappointment. For most though, it has been received as a cinematic work of art. Despite having been blown away by other films this year, this is definitely the best thing I've watched in a long time, and it will prove a shock if Joaquin Phoenix doesn't win the Oscar for best actor. It's something I'd recommend everyone watch as it's a very accurate depiction of mental illness, and though it left me feeling rather uncomfortable, its message is a powerful and important one, especially in our current time.

Joaquin's portrayel as a man with a deeply disturbing childhood days and constantly fighting turbulent weather leads to a build up that almost leads you to diagnose the disturbed mind with a magnifying glass. Unending backstabs and an unstable mind's weight lead a marginalised Arthur, aka joker to creep into the centre stage and become a dark symbol of a chaotic revolution. The sequencing of scenes are buttery, natural and episodes, where his condition makes him laugh in despair and agony magically do the job of passing the pain on to you, and to the person next to you as well. What struck me the most is the sincerity with which a comic character was portrayed without the Shakespearean sentences that often come with a character of this stature. Also, subtle moments like Bruce Wayne and the joker crossing paths are imaginations worth a million colours. Super heroes aside, here is a movie that meticulously digs deep to study the rise of a homegrown devil. Review Title: Fantastic Movie, but also Fantastically Overrated
Review: Anybody who claims this movie is a masterpiece is 'fake deep'. The movie virtually carries the same underlying theme as Taxi Driver, but does so on the coat-tails of a more culturally prevalent character.The plot itself may be slightly unoriginal; however, Phoenix's acting combined with the absolutely ominous sound editing make this movie haunting a memorable. I was skeptical prior to watching this movie, because I was so overwhelmingly impressed with Ledger's rendition; yet, Phoenix portrayed the character exactly how it needed to be portrayed given the story's circumstances. Ledger was responsible with creating a maniacally evil villain that evoked fear within the audience, while Phoenix was responsible for embodying an individual's descent into madness. What makes this performance so prolific is that Phoenix evokes empathy within the audience, when they should be nervous and absolutely mortified by his character's behaviors. Phoenix's portrayal of Arthur Fleck almost leaves the audience rooting for him in the end; thus, causing the audience to question its own morality, and to reflect upon just how chaotic and ruthless our society has become.The story is strong, the sound editing is outstanding, the cinematography is complimentary; however, this film would not be nearly as memorable without perfect interpretation of this character by Phoenix.

Joaquin Pheonix played the Joker in the way it should. Review Title: Joker - Anatomy of a chaotic mind
Review:
Every day we see acts of extreme violence but rarely we reflect on the origin of such acts and study the characters behind them. Joker is a spot on character study which focuses on Arthur's life and his transformation into Joker. Director Todd Philips takes the chaotic and unorganized mind of Joker and make the entire narration equally unorganized and unreliable.
Todd Phillips carefully walks the line between tragedy and comedy and impeccable acting of Joaquin Phoenix makes sure that each emotion is captured in a single scene. The transformation into Joker was very well acted through an improvised dance scene in the bathroom (and many after) which reflects freedom and confidence Arthur was feeling after the acts of killing the vicious Wall Street men. This shows how well soundtrack, acting and directing are integrated throughout the movie. Especial kudos to the cinematography which emphasizes the loneliness and darkness Arthur was feeling throughout the movie.
Arthur draws depression & loneliness of Travis Bickle from "Taxi Driver", anger & frustration of Howard Beale from "Network" (all the characters based on 1970s America). Movie truly reflects a sick society in which a broken and mentally ill character was abused in childhood and later was regularly marginalized by society because of his mental illness.
With so much bad happening around the world it is easy to get mad as hell. Media and people are still talking about negative effects acts of violence shown in the movie but I rarely find anyone talking about lack of attention towards mental illness across the world and how a weak mind if put into situations like these can turn out to be a menace to the society. Because of the sheer performance by Joaquin and a huge risk taken by Todd this movie deserves Oscar nomination at the least and a rating of 8/10.
This film pieces together everything you need to understand the joker and how he came to be.

Review Title: Should have been called "Arthur". This is not the intelligent Joker we have loved for over 70 years.
Review: When I first saw the trailer. I was confused. Is this the joker from DC or something else? Learning it was the DC joker. I was immediately disappointed that this wasn't going to be what I hoped. A serious comic book like movie about a joker similar to Heath Ledger's joker. Let me explain... and why this is important for the joker character, because what we saw. Was a character definitely not capable of becoming the joker.Joker was a decent movie but a bad joker movie. It was slow and boring most of the time for me. It felt like your average horror movie. Slow, jump scares, mystery reveals, final act. Joker was slow, violent moments, mystery reveals, final act. It felt so average to me. I was hoping the whole time the joker character would start doing something joker like. You know... something intelligent. I wasn't impressed at all throughout and was glad it was finally over. I watch a lot of violent movies/shows. So none of the violence surprised me at all nor bothered me. There's some funny moments and some romance, but it all felt so generic. Stuff you see in so many films and shows. I didn't find anything unique about this movie whatsoever. When it came to the mental illness aspect of the movie. It was meh. It wasn't an accurate representation of mental illness at all as some people have claimed, yikes. This part of the world as well his life in general did feel like it came from some off story DC comic book the masses never heard about. This entire movie felt like it was trying to be a real to life movie, but was over dramatized and unrealistic in many ways that I don't want to spoil for anyone actually reading this. Hopefully you'll see this movie differently after this review.The good things to say about this film is it's beautiful film work and editing. The camera work and color grade is what really helped the audience get sucked into this world, in my opinion. Not the actors nor the score. The score was very clean and worked great for what was presented to us. Joaquin Phoenix's performance was great, but not the best acting I've ever seen like so many reviews have said. Sigh... There's just so many great performances similar to his. If not better. A recent example off the top of my head would be Split starring James McAvoy. He did an excellent job as that character. The Joker story was meh, but the way they went about it was pretty good. Letting the audience ponder on what was real and what wasn't is something that will be argued until the film is forgotten 60 years from now. I do enjoy movies that screw with the audience like that. Like the ending of Inception.To the final part.. Arthur... he could never be the Joker. He's not smart enough to be the Joker. Think about all the jokers before him. All the insane calculated plans. All the times he gets away. Do you really think this Joker could be one of Batman's greatest enemies? Lol. No way in hell. He would get caught by batman within the week the moment he exposed himself to the Gotham people. Are you still wondering why I'd say that? Then your not a true Joker fan and just liked a movie called Joker. The Joker has always been this evil chaotic mastermind that Batman has rarely been able to catch and put away. Just watch/read every popular film/comic that the Joker is in before you disagree. Arthur's decisions throughout the movie were emotionally simple. Not calculated. He never thought twice about his actions. He just did them. He didn't plan a single thing in this movie except maybe the last act. Everything happening around him. Wasn't because he planned it. He just so happens to be in it.. At the right time. Everything fell in place for him. He didn't put things in place. Like all jokers before him have. Another thing is he's old. 45 years old. How many people do you know who can change that drastically at the age of 45. You are set in your ways for life once you reach a certain age and he is definitely past that. Tell me I'm wrong. Another thing is Bruce is still a kid in this movie. Joker would be in his 60's at least before Bruce becomes batman. How does that make any sense? A dull minded 63 year old man as batman's arch nemesis? Getting into fist fights with a nearly 30 year old batman? Lol. Please.To conclude, this isn't a bad movie. Just a really bad joker movie. I will never watch this movie again. It should have been called Arthur. With some more action and characterization in it. With an additional 30 minutes added to the film length. Those changes would have had me rating it much higher. I'm worried this films success will forever alter the joker. The intelligent, funny, psychotic joker us true fans know and love.

Review Title: I've never had a movie make me feel this way
Review: This is my first review and I apologize for its length. I will not reveal any spoilers and it is simply my opinion. I have broken it into two reviews, a quick review and an in-depth review for those who are interested.Quick Review: 8/10The performance by Joaquin Phoenix is something that will be talked about for some time and the movie itself will continue to spark debate. The cinematography is gritty and real and easily evokes Martin Scorsese's New York City of films. While the amount of violence is relatively tame compared to, say a Saw movie, it is very gritty and real, a la Taxi Driver. Superficially, the plot is quite simple: a man gets continually beat down by people and society until one day he hits back, but below that, it is a character study. Todd Phillips stepped out of his usual comfort zone of comedies and has given us a comic book drama. Some people believe that this movie should not have been made and it should be banned, but I disagree. Other than the obvious Freedom of Speech right, I actually applaud the filmmakers for making this movie, not because I agree with the message or because I loved the movie. I believe that it took strength to make this movie. It was obvious from early on in the filmmaking process that this movie would generate buzz and controversy (good or bad), and the filmmakers held their ground and made the movie they wanted. Let me also be clear that this movie is meant for mature audiences only. Don't let the fact that this is based on a comic book character mean that younger audience members should see it. This movie is R-rated for very good reason and parents and/or guardians should be cautioned when it comes to younger audiences.In-depth Review:I don't consider myself a connoisseur when it comes to movies, but I do hold myself above the average moviegoer. I am not a critic and I usually don't write reviews, however, this movie has left me with a feeling I've never experienced before. Let me first say that I am in awe of Joaquin Phoenix. I was very uncertain of how he could portray this character and if I even wanted to see a new Joker; I am of the opinion that Heath Ledger's portrayal of the iconic villain is the best among the movies, followed by Jack Nicholson's classic take. Phoenix is almost unrecognizable, both physically and in makeup, compared to his other famous roles like Gladiator, Her and Walk The Line to name a few.I came out of this movie with an unsettling feeling, something I've never had, not even from the scariest horror movies. Is Phoenix's transformation something to behold? Yes, without a doubt. I truly believe he is one of the greatest actors of our time and even courageous, this movie has been surrounded by controversy and whether you agree with this movie being made or not, it took courage from all who made this to stand by the finished product and see it through to the end.So why was I unsettled by this movie? Did I dislike it? Did I love it? Do I sympathize with the character? I did not dislike the movie, but I can't say I loved it either. When I talk about love for a movie, I mean it is a movie that I would see again and again and everything about it was beyond expectations. I can't say that I will see this movie again and again, in fact I don't really see the need to watch it another time. However, I am very glad I did see it my not seeing it again is not to say I didn't like it. I know there is much controversy about sympathizing with the Joker and that if you do, then you're not a good person, it's not right to be sympathetic to a maniacal killer like Joker. Let me first say that I sympathize with Arthur Fleck, not Joker. Arthur is not a bad guy, he is a man who has a traumatic history and is unable to get adequate help from a flawed system. That, coupled with his economic class and being surrounded by a society of unrest makes me sympathize for him. It is these circumstances that end up creating the villain of the title's namesake.Watching Arthur's descent is difficult and disheartening. It is not one instance that turns this man into the Joker, but the combination of them all. I know there are some who will take offense to what I'm about to say, but I can understand how Arthur becomes Joker. That being said, I understand that there are many people who have endured similar, if not more, circumstances and events, and have never gone on to harm or kill anyone, but this movie is not about those who haven't. Like I said previously, I don't sympathize with Joker, I sympathize with Arthur.Todd Phillips did an amazing job in bringing his vision of the origin of Joker to life. Phoenix embodies the character and gives a performance that will be talked about for years to come. Love it or hate it, this movie will be talked about for its content and it's parallels with our society today.If you are looking to find a movie about redemption and hope, you will not find it in Joker. If you are looking for a comic book movie, you will not find it in Joker. What you will find is a movie with excellent performances from the cast, beautiful and gritty cinematography, a bleak and, at times, unpleasant score that perfectly matches the tone of Gotham City.

These two are hard to compare, because the aim of Ledger's Joker is to break Batman, while this movie portraits a society that breaks a man into becoming the Joker.
Considering this, both actors gave an unique version and performed brilliantly.But I honestly can't see why people are so shocked because of this film. It isn't nearly as dramatic as THE DARK KNIGHT for example, most of the plot is very predictable. And the violence isn't nearly as horrific as claimed by many vewiers. I honestly expected much more. Whit this movie being a standalone, many opportunities where thrown away.
Maybe most people are too accustomised by the typical MARVEL kind of movie, that this one left them surprised and shocked.All in all it's an outstanding movie that doesn't get boring at any point, but many missed opportunities lead to a very predictable plot.
The pictures are breathtaking, the music fits perfectly and the acting is fantastic.But is it something completley new? No.
Does it take serious risks? Not enough.
Therefore, is it shocking? A little bit.
So, is it overrated? Absolutely.But as already said, today's bar hangs extremly low.
So is it refreshing? Definitely!

Within the opening scene I could see why Joaquin Phoenix won the Academy Award for Best Actor. He was brilliant. The whole film was brilliant. Also terrifying.Vigen Guroian writes: "Plato argued that conversion to that which is moral, that which is just, that which is right and good is like an awakening-like remembering something long forgotten. Good stories have a special capacity to bring back to life the starved or atrophied moral imagination, to bring back to mind what we once knew... Fairy tales are not scientific hypotheses, nor are they practical guides to living. They do something even better, however. They resonate with the deepest qualities of our humility. They enable us to envision a world in which there are norms and limits, a world in which freedom respects the moral law or pays an especially high price."I had someone who heard I'd watched "Joker" tell me there was "nothing redeeming" in the film. He said he didn't like "all these films making evil look glamorous." I disagree. In fact I don't think it made the Joker look anything but sad and broken and nothing you would want to ever be.The film humbled me. It did what Guroian says good "fairy tales" should do; it enabled me to envision the world Joker lived in as a world in which there were norms and limits, and his abuse of freedom and disrespect of that moral law showed him paying an especially high price indeed.It isn't a "Batman movie." In fact if you knew nothing of Batman or "the Joker" you could watch this and just think it was an excellent film about a guy going crazy. It's a very sad story and character.It reminded me of "Memento" in some ways. The fragility of our minds and lives and of what "reality" is. There were elements of "The Shining." A man who is obviously already disturbed being pushed over the edge.The writing and directing and musical score (which also won an Academy Award) were all on the level of a Coen Brother's film like "Fargo." In fact the sadness and relatable / unrelatability of Joker was much like Jerry Lundegaard from "Fargo." Except, where Jerry loses himself in crumbles, Joker "finds himself" in his "triumphs."It has some violent scenes; made more disturbing because of the gravity of the film and the character. The world it is set in is real. There are no CGI effects or over the top weirdness. That too adds to its weight and gravitas.I would say it is definitely worth watching and even if you don't like it the film is excellent.(Now if they would just do films for all the other Batman villains... at least Riddler.)

A movie must first of all be interesting: it must have, if not a coherent point of view, at least a worked-out, thought-provoking set of themes, some kind of imaginative contact with the world as we know it. "Joker," an empty, foggy exercise in second-hand style and second-rate philosophizing, has none of that. Besotted with the notion of its own audacity - as if willful unpleasantness were a form of artistic courage - the film turns out to be afraid of its own shadow, or at least of the faintest shadow of any actual relevance.

Review Title: The Joker was a wonderfully dark masterpiece
Review: This dark, slow burn origin story of the Batman villain, the Joker, left you feeling unsettled and thoughtful. This film depicts a dark side of society and how it corrodes a man's life and leads him down a path of insanity and deviance. There is a theme of mental illness that outlines this movie, societies disregard for it creates a helpless feeling of a downward spiral. What little hope of happiness or at least contentment that you have for the main character is tragically crushed by the last half of the movie.The cinematography was beautiful with excellent use of color, making it aesthetically pleasing even though the subject matter puts a rock in your stomach. Joaquin Phoenix is hypnotizing to watch, he did an amazing job in this role that maybe even matches up to Heath Ledger's take on the Joker in The Dark Knight. The movie should be called "Arthur" and not Joker because Phoenix is only actually the infamous villain for the last ten minutes of the film, it is very much an origin story of his life leading up to the making of the villain. I was honored to witness Todd Philip's creation, however it is a very heavy film that I would not sit down to watch on a relaxing Sunday night.

'Joker' follows the story of Arthur Fleck, a troubled amateur comedian who is constantly beaten down by society, driving his transformation into the iconic comic book villain, Joker. With a great lead performance, good sense of atmosphere, an original score and pleasing visual style it is unfortunately let down by the script. Presenting underdeveloped themes, cheesy dialogue, cartoonish logic and poorly written characters. What is ultimately a slightly above average film has fuelled debate and division among film fans.'Joker' is a good movie. Kind of. It is entertaining on a first viewing but the more you think about the film, the less valuable it becomes, and the more issues start to arise. Joaquin Phoenix is without a doubt the film's greatest strength, he is one of the finest actors working today and while this is not his best performance it is still very good. After winning best actor at the Academy Awards it is likely that this will be the performance that most audience members come to know him for. Phoenix portrays the underlying sinister nature of Arthur as well as evoking pathos for his traumatic experience, making Arthur a character that is simultaneously pitied and feared. In addition to provoking emotion Phoenix brings gravitas to the roll, elevating what could have been comical dialogue in the hands of a lesser actor and giving it a sense of weight and believability.More stylish than most comic book adaptations, the film's design feels grimy and lived in, the period aesthetic bolstering the idea that Gotham city is run down, and the society locked in a negative cycle. The filth that festers and spreads through Arthur's world is captured for the screen with well composed cinematography. The colour, high contrast lighting, and effective use of shallow focus gives the frame a pleasing visual texture. The obvious attention to detail from DOP Lawrence Sher imbues the film with an artistic integrity often lost in a genre saturated by creatively stifled corporate products. The award-winning score from Hildur Guðnadóttir also deserves mention, with boldness and originality it is effective and emotive, carrying much of the film's tonal weight, picking up the slack where the writing falls short.The downfall of this film is the writing. The first half of the film is comically mean to the point of absurdity. Burdened by a very slow first act with little plot, the audience are subjected to a repetitive loop of Arthur being beaten down both figuratively and literally. It is effective in presenting Arthur as a victim of his circumstances however the excess of his suffering makes it unbelievable. Accompanied by the lack of narrative progression, it comes across as the writers stopping the story to over explain the idea that society made Arthur the way he is. The film is plagued with obvious writing lacking any complexity or subtly.The movie presents in a very self-serious manner but doesn't follow through with a clever plot or nuanced themes. There is plenty going on, but nothing is sufficiently developed. For instance, the social uprising that is sparked by the Joker is unearned. While there is clearly a class divide in Gotham there is a lack of build-up and no attempt from the screen writers to delve deeper into why the class divide exists, or what it is either side of the divide wants.But perhaps the plot doesn't need to be amazing, if it's a character study then the characterisation and character arc should be strong enough to carry the movie. Right? Writer/director Todd Phillips claims 'Joker' is a character study. However, it is difficult to write a compelling character study with a passive protagonist, one whose goals or actions are not the driving force of the plot. Arthur's lack of action comes as a result of his lack of clearly defined goals. Without a strong motivation he ends up reacting to the plot rather than driving it. This makes for a less compelling lead character and limits the opportunity for the writers to provide commentary on Arthur's intentions.So, where does the film sit morally? Arthur is clearly presented as a victim, and with practically all the other characters being exceedingly mean or evil, his violence seems to be justified. Presenting Arthur's violent outburst as his 'hero moment' and not providing an in-text counter voice of reason is somewhat morally irresponsible from the script and is further evidence of the lack of complexity. The film is angry at the world but not sure why it's angry or how to fix it. It is important to note that the film is not directly condoning violence, the performance from Phoenix and the score work in tandem to convey that these are the horrific acts of a delusional man. But, the openness of the film's message call into question what it was Todd Phillips was trying to say with this movie. The film becomes a kind of blank slate where audience members can project their own thesis statement about the broad issues the film identifies.For a more believable and morally complex world the film should offer a strong counter to Arthur. Yes, the film is from Arthur's subjective point of view but that shouldn't prevent the film from presenting an opposing view to his. While we as an audience will see the same things Arthur sees, how we see those things can still be different. A believable and complex world is not a necessity for good story telling, but if a film presents itself with the gritty self-importance that 'Joker' does then it should follow through with a more mature execution. While ultimately audience takeaway is more important than authorial intent there is still valid criticism in the film's execution of its goals.Why tell this story in a Joker origin movie? Obviously, the cynical reason is because comic book movies are some of the most successful and recognisable IP in Hollywood. The inclusion of comic book references such as the Wayne family feel forced and unnecessary having very little baring on the story and serving little purpose outside of the tenuous connection to the source material. There is nothing wrong with bending the source material to fit the story you want to tell but this film is trying so hard to be a 'real' movie that the comic book elements feel out of place and the film would have been stronger as an original concept. There is, however, a strong crutch provided by the source material that the film can sneakily lean on. We as an audience know that the Joker is supposed to be the bad guy and we know that Arthur is eventually going to snap and take that dive into comic book villainy. Phillips takes advantage of this giving the film a palpable, yet cheap, sense of anticipation.With all this in mind 'Joker' will for some people be well-crafted and entertaining, for others it will be thematically messy and problematic, and for some the film may be a deeply provocative character study that shines a light on class segregation and mental illness. Any of these reactions are justifiable when discussing the subjective nature of cinema. But, perhaps each of these different interpretations would benefit from a more critical analysis and a consideration of other perspectives, re-assessing the film's intent and success.

Review Title: A fine piece of cinema, but not a masterpiece
Review: So... I've finally seen it, in a near-empty movie theater. 🤡Let me first mention that the Joker is my favorite comic character, particularly since visionary comic creators like Alan Moore and Brian Bolland, and Grant Morrison and Dave McKean gave unprecedented depth and darkness to the character in the late 1980s. If you don't know The Killing Joke (1988) and/or Arkham Asylum: A Serious House on Serious Earth (1989), be sure to check them out. Together with Frank Miller's The Dark Knight Returns (1986), those game-changing comics paved the way to the first darker Batman films, created by Tim Burton.The darkness-with-a-wink of the Burton films was superseded by Christopher Nolan's more serious Batman trilogy in the late 2000s. Although I think the third part of that trilogy was weak and superfluous, the second part featured the late Heath Ledger as the bright, shining star of the show, single-handedly carrying the film to sublimeness. Because, let's be honest, Christian Bale's grunting Batman is a bit annoying compared to Ledger's fascinating Joker performance, lifting the Joker character to a new iconic level.Joaquin Phoenix had the very difficult task to match or even outshine Ledger's legendary Joker. Jared Leto's attempt failed miserably in The Suicide Squad (2016), at least that's what I've read everywhere, as the film doesn't attract me at all.What I really liked about the new Joker is the moody portrayal of the tragedy and isolation of mental illness, which was at times really emotional, mainly thanks to the intense, laudable performance of Joaquin Phoenix.I thought the metro shooting scene with the yuppies was powerful, inducing an emotional release after all the injustice, a feeling slightly reminiscent to the gratification of the classic revenge scene in Oliver Stone's Midnight Express (1978).Then there was the build-up to Joker's TV show appearance, which would be the climax after all the endured suffering and mockery. And to some disappointment the TV show climax turned out to be underwhelming. I expected more of it, such as a really gripping twist and/or an emotionally resonant speech to complete the built-up tragedy.The subsequent urban riot scenes and the ending also didn't really make an impact, although I liked the fact that Joker didn't purposely stir up the disgruntled people, but was turned into a figurehead by them. I also liked the homage to Ledger's poetic police car backseat scene.Joker is obviously a grim tribute to Scorsese's Taxi Driver (1976) and The King of Comedy (1982), not coincidentally both also starring Robert de Niro. There's also a strong hint of Death Wish (1974) in the plot development.All in all I think Joker is a fine piece of cinema, but not a masterpiece, as many others label it. Apart from the praiseworthy performance of Joaquin Phoenix, the plot is reasonably thin, with familiar elements: an introvert main character in a hostile, nihilistic society is pushed over the edge by caricatural bad people.Of course Joker is based on comic characters, but the film obviously tried hard to put the emphasis on realism, resulting in a slight identity crisis. It's not as credibly realistic as Taxi Driver, and not as comic-like as The Dark Knight.The bottom line: in my humble opinion, Heath Ledger is still the best Joker.

Review Title: A mirror that nobody wants to look at.
Review: I'll let other people focus on the incredible cinematography, nuanced acting, superb writing and detailed score. It's all amazing in my vastly unqualified opinion. What I'd like to offer my thoughts on is the underlying, cultural importance of this stunning, Kafkaesque caricature of life in an often solitary bubble that we somewhat ironically refer to as civilisation. It is the story of a man stripped to nothing but the subjective will to power without restriction, à la Nietzsche's 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra'. The introjected values that tether Arthur Fleck to society are diminished when they are not reflected in the behaviour of others that continuously overlook and mistreat him on account of his illness. He is relentlessly denied autonomy, agency, self-determination and subjectivity by a cold and abusive world until his climactic metamorphosis as this nightmarish, maniacal overman. I think the violence in the film speaks to a part of the viewer that we actively suppress because of our own introjected values and conditions. We leave the cinema and go about our day accepting that we've just witnessed an exciting, moving and deeply upsetting fiction. Yet in our dissonance between the aroused exhilaration and disgust, we are forced to acknowledge the very conditions that keep us in check within our role in society. It is a kind of thought experiment which ultimately highlights a very clear truth; society has a responsibility for it's own mental health, even more so to those that we have neglected and let down to the point that they break catastrophically. The upset and outrage inspired by the film is sort of the whole point. A film or videogame can't inspire violence in the meek, passive members of society who's sensibilities and expectations tell them that what they are seeing is horrific and unsettling. That's absurd. Equally, it can't inspire disturbing behaviour in those with the capacity to go out into the world and commit such acts. That darkness was already there, and it was foreshadowed by a lifetime of trauma and neglect. No, Joker doesn't beckon the bogeyman and instruct him to wreak havoc on the world. It simply holds a mirror up to society, showing us that the bogeyman is already here. We don't like what we see in our dire reflection because we were comfortable here in our faux, utopian soft play of ignorance and dismissiveness. It comes as no surprise that the establishment are already railing against this message, because they are the most comfortable of all. Let's not forget that we live in a world where pivotal books such Robert Cormier's The Chocolate War and Stephen Chbosky's The Perks of Being a Wallflower are still routinely removed from libraries. Yet, this bosom world in which we nestle is a fiction in itself. We value society because it offers protection, but what about the times when it fails? What about the neglected and the marginalised? Those that do commit radical acts of violence have ultimately been let down by the very social contract that promises to protect them, and it is on all of us to do something about it or accept our responsibility for the consequences. Joker is more than just a very important and timely admission of our shortcomings. It is a call to action; Not for revolution or civil unrest, but for compassion.

Review Title: Definitely a different kind of "comic book" based movie

The movie itself touches on a lot with regards to the origin of the joker, in particular his state of mind, which many DC fans know is not an easy thing to pin down. Without spoiling anything, much of this movie takes place in the viewers own mind. Leaving more questions by the end than you had going in, the movie manages to pull off showing us the Jokers history, while having us question if what we are seeing is in any way real, or if it depicts the character we think we all know. There are a few nods to the batman comics, but it isn't a batman movie in any way. Really, it isn't even a joker movie. It's a movie about a fractured mind in a fractured world, and it's self imposed confirmation, slowly becoming a character we both love and loath. Creepy, disturbing, intense. The Joker is a really intense, really well done artistic statement and I'm surprised that Warner Bros had the guts to put it out.
