The director, Todd Phillips, pulled no punches. The comparisons to Taxi Driver are justifiable but it's also very much it's own film. If anything, the DNA of Scorsese's style is a source of inspiration but Joker stands on it's own. I won't compare it to Heath Ledger's performance because the two films couldn't be more different. Joker is it's own thing and this is just another interpretation of the character. Being unburdened from the weight having to focus on Batman being present really allowed us to get deep with the character of the Joker in a way we haven't seen before outside of the comics. Yet this in no way was a comic book movie, it was probably the most serious film I've seen based on comic source material. It's comic book material elevated to art and I hope the movie and Joaquin both get recognition for what was accomplished. I'll say it again, it's an uncomfortable movie to watch but that's because it should be. It's one that really wants to provoke discussion with your peers and that's a refreshing change to the movies that have been coming out of Hollywood in recent memory.

Review Title: NOT a 10, at least not by any reasonable standard.
Review:
This is the first review I've ever left on IMDb. I've left ratings before but never reviews but I feel compelled to do so now. Joaquin Phoenix is one of the greatest actors of his generation and Joker expects his performance alone to carry the entire movie, which makes the plot and characters, including Phoenix's character, feel superficial and one-dimensional. The plot is extremely weak and the movie is entirely too long... the length added absolutely nothing to the story or to the characters. Joker is supposed to be intelligent, his motivation based on something deep and meaningful, at least in his mind, but the movie never examines this. Joker doesn't go any deeper than surface level, which reduces the Joker character to nothing more than a weak, pitiful, self-loathing idiot who, because of his own foolish decisions, eventually
becomes angry and bitter. This Joker is no different than your run-of-the-mill serial killer. He's not intelligent or resourceful, and he's certainly no criminal mastermind, as we know The Joker character to be. Those giving Joker a 10 must have watched a completely different movie. Phoenix's Joker could have been the best ever had the story been as great as his performance.

Review Title: Wow. Just wow. Such terrifying Art.
Review:
My friend Shelley saw this yesterday with her hubby, and her review was, "Wow". That's it, just "Wow". After just watching it myself, I understand the full breadth and depth of "Wow". IMDb gave it a 9.2. There was a cop positioned inside and outside the theater. Specifically because of this movie. I am not a fan of superhero movies. Ledger's Joker was the greatest villain of all time. And Joaquin Phoenix's interpretation takes Ledger's best moments in Dark Knight and runs them through the whole movie. This is maybe one of the most terrifying pieces of art I've ever seen, for one reason; it removes the barrier, the buffer of emotional safety created by garish, comical, superhero, antic, zingers that create our suspension of disbelief. It's gone. I watched two hours of a man's break from reality, one plausible, painful, crushing, brutal event at a time. Things that you and I experienced versions of one or two, or know someone who experienced them. If even a single one of the pins pulled in all the grenades that figuratively went off in this story had been put back in place, we would have no Joker. But they all got pulled...
There's an argument brewing in the back of my mind about "mental health and violence", "glorifying" or "shaming", and I wouldn't begrudge anyone their feelings about "Joker". But look around. You should be terrified.Again, imdb 9.2. Joaquin Phoenix better get some golden paperweights, as well as writing, and directing. Because - wow.

Firstly, for anyone expecting to go into this to see superhero antics will be let down. This isn't a film that's beholden strictly to the origins of its source material. The context of the Gotham universe it takes place in is simply a pretense to afford the witnessing of a man's descent into the depths of mental illness and insanity. This is a wholly distinct adaptation from all before it, it is very grounded in its fiction, and to humor the full realization of Joker's nemesis in this universe (even though a child Bruce Wayne appears) is completely unrealistic.This movie is nothing but a brilliantly, tightly focused character study of the consequences of mental illness and anguish left to run rampant. Phoenix's performance is remarkable in showing this, and I hope he gets the Oscar. It is a masterclass of acting and he is fully enveloped in this role, not only psychologically, but the physical lengths he's taken to compliment his conveyance of a man who is gradually spiraling into a hopeless pit of self-destruction, nihilism, and eventual violence. His body represents just as much a character as his behavior does, often contorted and always skeletal, showing his agony on the outside just as much as the obvious immense turmoil he's enduring on the inside. This is an extremely dark and somber film, brutally violent at times, and I can fully understand why it's one that's been mired in controversy. People claim it irresponsible and dangerous, but I think such a superficial dismissal is to miss the point. Joker isn't a validation of hate, disenfranchisement, incels, or mass shootings. It's a glimpse into the life and circumstances of a very mentally disturbed individual that can lead someone to such feelings that are conducive to the most horrific of outcomes.I suppose I love this movie so much because as someone who's battled mental illness all my life, I find it captures exceptionally well the overall feeling of sickness in the head that depression brings, and the dangerous spiral it can quickly bring. And while I can understand how others can view this film as minimizing, glorifying, and even romanticizing such a serious issue as mental illness due to it taking place in the context of a comic book universe and character traditionally known for being more of a mean spirited prankster, what many don't understand who aren't mentally ill is how this is how such illness in its most severe manifestation can skew perception. Joker takes place from the perspective of Arthur, and as he states at the end, his life "is a comedy". He's insane.I think it's great that a film finally comes along that confronts us with mental illness, which is what this film is about. Perhaps choosing Joker to do this was a miscalculation, but regardless, this is a film that's needed. What message does it send? What message does it need to, aside to demonstrate the evil, insidiousness, mental decrepitude that destroys and leads people into utter delusional madness?

Review Title: NOT EVEN CLOSE TO A MASTERPIECE!
Review: OMG... This movie was seriously BAD!As someone who watches a lot of movies, I could not understand why so many "reviewers" on here rated this movie so highly, many even calling it a "masterpiece".Am I glad I did not go see this in the movie theater, as I would have demanded a FULL refund!I got this on blue ray and was really looking forward to viewing it, cozying up on my couch with a large bowl of popcorn.I was expecting to see something in the likes of the genre breaking Dark Knight, Inception, or Batman vs Superman. Was I let down...Here's what's so BAD about Joker...1. The movie follows a sad clown with serious mental issues, who laughs uncontrollably at inappropriate times (due to a supposed condition). Said clown goes off meds & starts killing people at the slightest provocation. For no reason, whatsoever.The police have their suspicions but never bother to arrest the clown or even question him formally at the station.2. There is about as much suspense in this move as there is watching a traffic camera, and there is almost no action or tension, in any scene.No one goes after the sad clown, aka Joker, for murdering innocent people, there is no enemy/antagonist for the clown to go up against/fight with, but there is a (hardly believable) love interest that no one could fathom a sad and insanely weird clown of this magnitude getting an attravtive member of the opposite sex.3. And last but not least, the slogging music. The music (which takes over in EVERY scene) is just ridiculously overdone. If you closed your eyes while walking into a room where someone was watching Joker, you would swear a musical is playing on the TV.Additionally, the music in Joker makes you wonder exactly what kind of emotions the makers of this disaster of a film were trying to incite in viewers.I felt neither moved, sad, excited or any emotion whatsoever while watching. Not to mention the totally unrelatable central character (Joker) was the biggest reason I felt nothing.I could list MANY other things that are wrong with this movie, but will leave it at the above 3 as these are what lead this movie into disaster territory..To Sum It Up...Do your eyes and ears a favor and skip this one.If you want to see actual masterpieces and have a taste for cinema (that is seemingly starting to go extinct now days), watch or re-watch Batman Begins, The Dark Knight or V for Vendetta.2/10. 1 star for cinematography & 1 star for Jaquin Phoenix's acting.#thisisnotentertainment #unbelievablybad

The movie was culturally perceived to be the movie for 'incels' and 'mass-shooter' types. I had to go through a security screening to enter the theater when I went to watch it. Culturally the movie was perceived to be as having a strong political message that could lead to violence. The reality is, the movie is completely empty of any real message other than how hard it is for mentally disabled people to deal with the bureaucracy of their health care, and the isolation they feel in society. Unfortunately the movie tries to create a political setup between the poor and the rich where somehow the Joker ends up representing the struggles of the poor. But the world building and the character himself of the Joker are completely separated from this idea, so there never actually is a connection between the pseudo-politics of the film and the Joker - because the motivations of the Joker in this movie have NOTHING to do with the pseudo-political message that many people believe this movie has. I think this movie seems to strike a nerve with people that project themselves onto the film, reading too little into it, and add too much of themselves onto the film as if it were a repository for their angst. That is fine, and that is a perfectly fine way to enjoy the art of film. But objectively speaking, the film is pretty devoid of anything meaningful, every message you might think it has, due to its poor world-building, is obfuscated and muddled to the point of meaninglessness. I personally think this movie is against protesting, in fact, it paints class-struggle driven protesters as animalistic and unhinged - and at that, led by a character that has no respect for any real cause but his own personal quest for vengeance.

Review Title: Joker: Do we all have a Joker inside?
Review: I have tried to resist writing a review about Joker (2019), but this film covers so many exciting themes and its immediate relevancy of the depiction of our society today, that like the character Arthur Fleck I have succumbed to my dark inner side and given to temptation, so that I may share my thoughts on a fascinating and unusual film.For years we have been bombarded by some Hollywood studios, and comic book publishers turned movie studios namely Marvel and DC, with films that some viewers are turned off by and yet many other viewers love to watch, as evident in their box office success.One of cinema's greatest directors, Martin Scorsese, recently stated that Marvel movies - which have been the most financially successful at incorporating comic books into films - is "not cinema". He further elaborated:Honestly, the closest I can think of them, as well made as they are, with actors doing the best they can under the circumstances, is theme parks. It isn't the cinema of human beings trying to convey emotional, psychological experiences to another human being."Using the above description from Scorsese, we can examine how the new DC movie stacks up against criticism. Joker is the furthest a film can get from the Marvel template movies as one can get, and this is true for several reasons which we will discuss here.Joker is set in a more realistic and grainy world than the usual comic book films of the last ten to fifteen years. It is so gritty you can see the dirt under Arthur Fleck's fingernails. The movie feels like it was filmed during the late 70s or early 80s in New York, with special honour and respect shown to certain influential films of that time: Mean Streets (1971), Taxi Driver (1976), Raging Bull (1980), and King of Comedy (1983).The main character Arthur Fleck suffers multiple psychological and mental health issues, and uses medication to keep himself sane. He looks after his mother in a small apartment in a rundown block somewhere in Gotham City. He earns his living by playing a clown and soon enough loses that job, stops receiving mental health treatment and medication, and finds out a very dark and disturbing truth to his upbringing.Life seems to be going all horribly wrong for Arthur, and he begins to fall into a deep and dark state of mind, which either he gives into, or he has no power to prevent.The cinematography, set design, story and themes, script, direction and acting, clearly separate this comic book origin film from the many others that Scorsese has criticised. But does that make this version of the Joker or this comic book film better than the Marvel films? Venice International Film Festival jurors thought so, awarding it the best film of 2019, setting it up for potential success at the next Oscars.Some will no doubt compare this Joker with the Joker played by Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight (2008), but that is a mistake as they live in different movie worlds, and no comparison is required since both actors have provided powerful performances.What is evident from the themes of this film, are the problems that face the world in 2019; a sense of hopelessness, mental health problems, cut in social security and public healthcare, increase in loneliness amongst the masses, issues of domestic abuse, and a lack of faith and strong sense of loss in a world devoid of sacredness and anything divine.

"JOKER" Non-Spoiler Movie Review"Joker", starring Joaquin Phoenix is the story about Arthur Fleck, a common everyday citizen of Gotham who struggles day in and day out to get through a tumultuous life in a society that mistreats, ridicules, and misunderstands him partially due to their ignorance of a disorder he has that causes him to laugh hysterically and uncontrollably whenever he is anxious about something. Arthur lives with his mother, Penny Fleck who he is the caretaker of. He tries to make ends meet as a clown performer and aspires to be a famous comedian someday. But as he begins to experience more and more abuse, mistreatment, and closed doors of opportunity in his life, Arthur slowly starts to find himself loosing his sanity and is further traumatized by various people, particularly the wealthy and powerful. After he is involved in an incident that catches the attention of Thomas Wayne, Bruce Wayne's father vows to rid Gotham of all of its so-called "clowns" and save the city by running for Mayor. The incident itself and reaction by Bruce's father starts an uprising of protesters who begin to wear makeup and clown masks in support of Arthur. But after he is forced to stop taking his medications and ultimately reaches his point of no return, Arthur embraces his new personality and persona and subsequently becomes Joker.I saw this movie after hearing all of its hype and negative responses to it and after seeing it, I think it's a masterpiece of a film. From the opening scene until it's controversial ending, this movie captivated me to the core. It introduces Arthur as a good person at heart, yet who makes rash decisions and commits horrible acts in reaction to his warped state of mind. This film actually made me sympathize with Arthur's plight as it shows in vivid detail how he suffers with depression, psychological trauma, misplaced feelings, anger, and his visible display of physical pain due to his laughing disorder. It is truly a tragic story of a good hearted person who falls terribly from grace. I totally agree that Joaquin Phoenix deserves an Oscar for his performance as well as his supporting cast who are all deserving of awards and recognition of their moving performances. Joker is also a film that has certain moments in it that displays what could be seen as an artistic performance or poetry in motion. When it comes to the violence in the film, I didn't find it to be that difficult to watch partially because I've seen far more graphic scenes of violence, but I can see why it could be considered disturbingly violent because the violence looks so shockingly real and is shot without the interruption of camera cuts or distracting camera angles. As a whole, "Joker" is very well made film that should be seen with an open mind, not expecting it to be the typical "superhero/villain" movie. It is a dark, brooding, emotional, funny, thought provoking, disturbing, yet intriguingly powerful execution of filmmaking.

The film is an incredible character study in to the psyche and origins of one of comic books' greatest ever villains. The cinematography is absolutely stunning and the accompanying score and soundtrack absolutely perfect. I literally couldn't look away from the screen from beginning to end and Joaquin Phoenix is phenomenal in the role, and every bit of his performance is Oscar worthy as we watch mental health and unfortunate circumstances propel Arthur Fleck in to the downward spiral that makes him become The Joker. The script is full of powerful moments that director Todd Phillips brings to life perfectly. This is definitely Joker's movie but it also ties in to the Batman mythology perfectly. Robert De Niro and Frances Conroy also offer a great turn in supporting roles. Is the movie as hyper-violent has critics make out. No. Is it a gritty, realistic, and uncomfortable reflection of society? Absolutely.

Review Title: Top Class movie about a disturbed human being who becomes a Criminal Mastermind

At 77, he is so graceful and has a great screen presence.There is no CGI/special effects or any prolonged action sequences like we get to see in any DC or Marvel movie. Its not even a thriller. Its a brilliant character study. There is also some gruesome action scenes and some shocking twists.A must watch for every movie lover. Thankyou Todd Phillips, Joquin Phoenix & team for giving us the best origin story of the most loved and iconic onscreen villian.Audience was delighted and clapped at the end of the movie!

Review Title: Why JOKER missed the OSCARS. It's not a story , its a situation.
Review:
People always go after the hype a movie generates and all the big studios can do it very easily. I will only talk about its structure. Because that is where I can see a movie criticially. Being involved in action packed moives like James Bond series doesnt mean they all have stories in it. So if you want to see only the action, a movie creates, you have the liberty to do so.
Joaquin Phoenix, lives in a seedier, punishing version of Gotham City, where he feels persecuted by society at large. But why? If he's mentally ill, what choice did he have? So it's not his choice to adapt the course of his life rather its been dervied by his tic syndrome. So the film ends up as a revenge story where a person wants to get admired taking revenge against the society. So what's intersting in the character? why someone wants to be loved because he's handicapped? I don't want to see any character who actually has no choice of his own to go into the adventure of life. He's been derived by event after event where he only reacts and what he does, he kills anyone who humiliates him. This is not a story , this is a situation.
The film may be a reflection of sad version of our society but then why this character I should be watching, what's is his motivation? There is actually no. So it lacks structure as well. Does he have a desire? Yeah he has one that he wants to be an artist( comedian). The film should have evolved around his desire but it takes another course where the Joker becomes a more disturbed and lower-stakes version of the legendary DC Comics villain.
No doubt that its a piece of remarkable craftsmanship and impressive performances trying to catch the essence of Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy but it lacks the structure.
There is no relationship in his course of struggle through whom we can judge his flaws.In fact it's all his actions that shows him a villian rather than a protag. No physical antagonism evolved. yeah there had been one but no physical contact but only at one occasion when he's punched straight in his face by Thomas wayne.
Since the settings is Gotham as we can judge from the posters of that era when there had been rampant crime on the streets with murders and rapes on rise, we see that his mother had been an employee of her and had an illegal affair with him. So it seems he was his illegal child. This antagonism must have been dealt but infact it didn't.
Copying the style of martin Scorsese's body of work of 70's, and 80's American cinema in the vein of Taxi Driver, Todd thought to give himself a chance to be on the list of Martin's kind of elusive films ( though there are certin structure issues in Taxi Driver) but has miserably failed to shine.

Review Title: Joker is an in-depth analysis of one of the most popular villains of pop culture!
Review:
Well, firstly I want to admit I am a DC fan. Not a big one I suppose, 'cause I haven't read any of their comics. But I like their movies, mostly because they're dark and gritty. I actually had some issues with them when they tried to duplicate the success of MCU by making movies like Justice League and Shazam (I really enjoyed the movie, but that's like enjoying a Marvel movie, just fun but nothing intriguing). But right when I saw the first trailer of Joker I knew it that it's going to be just my type of a movie. And God damn it! It was a hell of a ride.
Firstly, it is not a superhero (or to say supervillain, as the Joker we used to know) movie, it's a completely character driven movie where Arthur Fleck's character has been examined and analysed in a very intriguing way. It's a slow burner. The starting is slow and after a half an hour you start to engage in the movie. It depicts how the mentally ill Arthur Fleck i.e Joaquin Phoenix's character becomes the Joker as we know from Heath Ledger's legendary portrayal of Joker.
In the beginning he is just a man, facing mental illness and hasn't got the sufficient funds for his proper treatment. He only talks to a psychiatrist where he talks honestly about his conditions, feelings and his dreams. He was an aspiring stand up comedian and usually dressed up as a clown, working for a company. The society never really empathize with him, and often calls him weird and humiliate him. Slowly when the story progresses you see how different circumstances makes subtle changes in him, one by one, and at the end we realize that he has become the Joker, leaving his identity completely behind. It's a brilliant psychological study of a character, perhaps easily one of the best of it's genre. And the fact that it has been delivered from a comic movie makes it even more fascinating!
There are two man who made this possible, and kudos to them. Firstly, Joaquin Phoenix. He is an astonishing performer. He played the iconic character effortlessly and surely he should book a spot in Oscar nominations by now. Secondly, the director, who makes the audience empathize and scare from the character at the same time. You root for Arthur Fleck, but you scare from the inner demon he is slowly unrolling that finally becomes Joker.
I rated the movie 8/10 here but if possible I'd have rate it 8.5/10. The only reason I am not rating it a 9 is because it could've had a better ending, and there are some questions that's left unanswered at the end.
The set up of Gotham and the comic book element of the movie are so smartly placed that you never feel like it's been happening in a fictional world. But everytime such an element comes into the screen, it can give a DC fan some real goosebumps! Overall, Joker is a must watch! Thank you WB for releasing it in India on October 2nd. You've made my Gandhi Jayanti awesome!

Almost perfection in every aspect of movie making, cinematography, soundtracks, story, acting and directing.Story & screenwriting:Not going with a comic book story aspect was bold by Todd, yes there is a couple of cameos from several comic books Joker story, but this new narrative for the character was amazing. It is hard to take the message in this film seriously when considering the context and who "Joker" is aimed at. What I'm trying to say is that "Joker" is a bit of a joke, it takes itself too seriously and unfortunately and I cannot help but laugh at the people who say it is a modern day masterpiece.The film opens with "Joker" acting bizarre and I cannot help but think that he's already lost the plot at this point: the opening scene. Yes you could argue that this is to indicate that he is an "outsider" not simply insane, however, after watching him brutally murder several men in the first half of the film I find this hard to believe. It appears that Joker is insane from the start so I then begin to ask myself what's the point of this film? The change we see in the main character is more of slight curve than a "character arc" and there is little/ no change in tone throughout."Joker" is incredibly unclear in its intentions and I frankly find it a struggle to get through, not because of the "edgy" violence but because the film is simply embarrassing compared to its many inspirations. If you take "King of Comedy" and take out all the good bits and replace these with scenes of violence, you will get something very similar to "joker". I was expecting something at least original from this film in spite of its incredible reviews but I suppose that was wishful thinking.I find psychological films simply fascinating because of their uniquely twisted characters, a great example of this is the great satirical character of Patrick Bateman from "American Psycho" who is portrayed in a very intriguing way that chills the viewer. "Joker" however, is a pretentious portrayal of a character with not much depth: he is just the joker. The same joker we saw in the dark knight, who's beauty lay in the ambiguity; we didn't need "Joker" to develop on this.

Review Title: When/where is this film worth watching?
Review: In this modern age of streaming and with a multitude of content available, taking the time and money to go to the cinema can seem like an unnecessary outing when so much else is readily available. If you're anything like me then your cinema trips nowadays, are limited to the big blockbusters (or kids films, for those that have) to make use of the big screen and sound, that you can't get in your own home.With that in mind my take on this retelling origin story of Batman's biggest nemesis is as follows:Firstly, it might be obvious from all the hype surrounding the film that this is not a comic book movie, those expecting that will be very disappointed. Instead Joker takes a look into the real life reasons why a normal man with mental health issues might become the bigger than life villain. Joaquin Phoenix Plays Arthur Fleck, a deeply troubled man trying make ends meet to support himself and his frail mother. Arthur has a condition that makes him laugh uncontrollably during times of distress and thus is and outcast of society. With this condition coupled with depression and a traumatic childhood, Arthur finds work in the only place he can as a clown for hire. The city of Gotham is in complete disarray, with it's people getting more and more violent towards its government and it's here where the two story lines intersect, giving a deep dark and sometimes very real account of wether it is nature or nurture that creates such people.It's certainly true that Joaquin Phoenix goes all in with the crazy, his performance is very 'I am Sam', if you get the Tropic Thunder reference. His body alone shows the dedication he's put into his performance, looking very malnourished and sickly. The plot itself stays grounded and doesn't take unimaginable leaps with it's audience.My issue is that this story and Phoenix's portrayal seem a bit reminiscent of other movies, there's a certain early Nicholas Cage quality about the more mad side of the character. It felt like the story was almost damaged by the expectation of 'The Joker' as a character or even it's comic book links. I left feeling that had it just been the same story and portrayal, but without it's links to Batman or the Joker it may have faired better.Answering my initial statement, it feels a lot of hard work and effort went into this movie and Phoenix is definitely engrossing to watch at times. JOKER is an absolute triumph of modern-day cinema. A depressing, exciting, horrifying, morbid, sad and multilayered masterpiece featuring one of the most riveting und heart-wrenching performances by an actor you're ever going to have the pleasure (and honour!) of witnessing on the big screen. Another (and perhaps the very best!) career-defining role by Joaquin Phoenix whose unquestionable talent is only rivaled by his 100% dedication to the craft of being one of the very best in what he does. And what he does in this film could only be described as a deep dive into the depths of one troubled soul and its tense relationship with a violent and uncaring world. Like Arthur's own reality. A reality that could chew and then spit you out like a tasteless fly. It clearly suggests to us that everyone's sanity has his/her limits, so when we pass beyond them and stop pretending that everything's " "eventually going to be alright", breaking the conventional artificial rules becomes the new norm. When everyone denies you love and legitimate care, you hit them back with as much hatred and anger as possible. If we are to live in a jungle, then one should start playing by its crude ancient rules. Or at least that's what the Joker wants us to think, because after all - he's telling us the story... from HIS perspective, right? But does that change the fact that his world, his dark and filthy Gotham City seems so awfully familiar???Todd Phillips' Arthur Fleck/Joker... You will like him. You will sympathize with him. You will cry for him. You will be scared of him. You will hate him. But most importantly - you will... understand him. And that may just as well be one of the most cathartic moments in your life as a moviegoer... and nevertheless as a member of a SOCIETY that unfortunately is still way too effective in creating monsters that no one can control. Monsters that we refuse to take the responsibility for and who may one day force us (in the worst case scenario) to pay the bitter price for our negligence.A DEFINITE MUST-SEE!!! This film is an event and Joaquin's performance is one for the ages. It will definitely go down in history as one worthy of being mentioned in the same sentence with the likes of Brando's Don Vito Corleone, Daniel Day-Lewis' Daniel Plainview, Jack Nicholson's McMurphy and Heath Ledger's own version of that iconic character in every single "All-Time Greatest Character Portrayals" list you can get your hands on. Arthur's character arc is absolutely not the only ace that this film has up its sleeve: the mesmerizing soundtrack by Hildur Guðnadóttir, the captivating visual storytelling achieved though Lawrence Sher's masterful cinematographic approach, the unexpected re-imagining of Thomas Wayne - there're so many more things to love and contemplate about after seeing that amazing masterpiece. Review Title: Rotten Tomatoes Doesn't Know What a Film Is
Review:
I'm going to be blunt: I initially only went to see this film because I had heard it was "problematic". Of course I am also a fan of DC comics, but due to their more recent film titles, I will admit I did not expect much.
That's when I was blown away.
The story is immaculate. The development of Arthur as a character through direction and script is one thing, and on that alone you could call it an incredible film. But the in-your-face vivid performance by Joaquin Phoenix proves that this is beyond "another comic book movie". Lighting and camerawork are masterful, giving the viewer a look into how dirty and evil Gotham is in a physical and metaphorical sense. Sickly green lighting lets the viewing audience see the decaying city through Arthur's eyes, and this makes every action taken by him not only extremely "real", but it makes even the most vile crime sympathetic.As far as film events go, it's an extremely plausible story. If I were to see a police report on the news tonight about a man with a mental condition dressed as a clown starting riots across NYC, I would absolutely believe it. This is NOT an "over the top comic movie". This is a film that yanks you into the very real, dangerous world of mental illness. Viewing the world through the eyes of Arthur, knowing what he has been through, understanding the psychology around his situation, he is a very easy character to sympathize with.In conclusion, this is likely the greatest, most impactful film I have seen in ten years. Of course, this is an R-rated film, so do not fool yourself with the subject matter; this movie is NOT for children. That said, this is a must see film. Don't let media-based reviews fool you, this movie is a masterpiece, and deserves to be seen by anybody with an appreciation for a good film.

I made an account just to review this film. I have been hyped since the first trailer dropped (which I must have watched several dozen times, and several more in the run up to the release), and had the pleasure of seeing it last night.This was hands down one of the greatest cinematic experiences I have had the pleasure of being part of. There's nothing I can say that hasn't been said already. The hype is honestly real and deserved.Everything from Joaquin Phoenix's performance to the music score, directing, and especially the writing, was flawless. This was such a beacon of hope in a time when big blockbuster CG films are all the rage. All that matters when you strip that away are characters. If you don't have great characters, no matter how pretty your film looks, it's not worth the time of day - and this film proves that. I hope more directors and writers learn a thing or two from this. And I don't mean to copy: I mean to write better characters and stories.I'll touch on the negative media reviews quickly by just saying: once in a blue moon, a masterful piece of art like this comes around, and of course the media try to create a moral panic around it. I won't deny that aspects and themes of the film are relevant to this day and age. After all, art is a reflection of the society it was created in. There's two levels to art: face value and what the piece itself represents at its core, and then its wider connections to the real world. It's up to us how we interpret it, and that's what art is supposed to do - to get people talking. This film has certainly done that, and it's a good thing. It's one of those films that will be studied and looked back on in a hundred years, for both its cinematic marvels as well as its relevance to today.tl;dr 9999999999999/10 would watch again

Review Title: One of the best movies I've watched in years
Review: Before you think about it, I was very much hyped for this maniacal affair of a film. I'm reluctantly waiting for that one good DC film that I could watch and really feel entertainment at its finest, and it's here. If you're expecting action, there is little to none. This is a character study of the Joker. This movie does not breastfeed you with information. But one thing that does take the limelight is Joaquin Phoenix. Not only because Joaquin Phoenix is definitely one of the best actors as thus far and in the latter half of the decade. I did walk into this film, wandering how to grasp how awful it would be, but that's not what happened. I personally enjoyed the film from the score, the acting, the gnawing tension present from the start of the film, and the camera angles. This is modern day Kubrik. It was as if A Clockwork Orange had taken a modern day approach to the naïve Alex Delarge. Shaky camera angles to add to the tension, unnerving shots, and a score to really keep you on your toes. I loved every single part about this film. But the message, although it's not inspiring to be a narcissistic psychopath, it's inspiring to the many people, including myself and others, ignored and are on the poor side of a self pursuing society. The Joker arises with his psychotic yet emotional dance, like a messiah that takes the stage. He is a Lenin to a Tsarist society, he may not be the right person to believe in, but he's that beacon of hope for the people. Although Joaquin voice might not put you to the famous titular Mark Hamill adaptation of the character, you get used to it. But his laugh, his laugh is haunting. A disability, something we shouldn't laugh at or make fun of, but we see happening. This ISN'T a batman film. We gain sympathy for the Joker, a character who wanted to do good but was met with reluctant hate. This movie, is going to be one of my most favourite movies released for several years, until Joaquin comes back of course. If you haven't seen the movie, you need to see it

Heath Ledger will probably always be my favorite rendition of The Joker, because of the charisma and intelligence he brought to the role.
With that said, I don't think anyone could have played this version of the Joker except for Joaquin Phoenix. He did things with the character, both through physicality of acting and through emotional depths, that both amazed and hurt me.
The movie is most definitely a drama and something of a personal journey of horror. It does not, as was my fear and the voiced concerns of many others, demonize everyone with a mental illness, or give justification for the incels and Red Pill Society members and MRA's to be terrible human beings. Neither does it say "Hey if you're alone and nobody likes you you can fix your problems with a little random violence." Instead, it shows us a plethora of factors, and a variety of nudges, that cause someone who's already struggling with who they are in life, and whether or not they actually even exist, to take a dark path. Joker shows us that those with mental illnesses, the 'clowns', the people considered broken or invisible or worthless by society as a whole, are being consistently let down by the system, at every turn. And Phoenix, and the writers, do an incredible job of showing us that The Joker is *human*. He's not some criminal mastermind, not at this point; he's very much figuring things out as he goes, and the film takes care to point out several times that the Joker is not making a political statement with his actions; he's not trying to enact sweeping change, or smash the Patriarchy, or fight The Man; he's just done with everyone's shit, and with how he feels the world is treating him. The movie doesn't have a lot of violence, but when it does it is brutal, harsh and quick; and it explores the ripple effects those violent acts cause.I found this to be an incredible film. I didn't come away from it feeling like it blamed those with mental issues or trauma; The Joker was very much responsible for his own actions, just as we all are. But it definitely helped remind me that underneath the makeup, there was still a human being in there, and it definitely made me analyze my feelings on the interactions between Batman and the Joker over the years.If you see this movie, expect to cry (I teared up several times) and to feel awkward; they do an excellent job of overextending an awkward situation until it becomes almost unbearable. Also, they somehow manage to be predictable without being boring; the predictability instead turns into a slow build of dread, because you can see where something is going a mile off, and then you're still along for the unavoidable end. And this movie is an R for a lot of language, and some fairly brutal violence.
It is not a movie that leaves you feeling good at the end, but it is one I am glad I went to see, and I hope that they tap Phoenix for the Joker in a future movie; he can clearly find that character's depths.

Review Title: Entirely new approach for a superhero genre, or birth of a villain fiction?
Review: I am not going to write in details. If you like Batman series, go watch it. If you don't like Batman series, also go watch it. I guarantee you will never regret the time and money spent for this film at a theater, where this film should be experienced.Directing, soundtracks, cinematography - all elements that you would normally expect from a great cinema are top-notch. But there are two things that definitely stand out for Joker. Acting and spectacular attempt to explore human nature, class division, and more importantly why the abandoned often behave in such an extraordinary manner. First, for acting, Joaquin Phoenix might surpass Heath Ledger in terms of the best Joker ever played. As we all know, Heath Ledger's Joker is regarded as one of the best villains in film history if not the best, and River Phoenix's little brother, with Joker, could have already achieved what the great Heath Ledger has achieved. His acting is that good and for his acting alone, this movie is more than worth watching. Secondly, the film beautifully portrays class division that is getting serious everyday and how it leads to lack of compassion and sympathy in our society. We often disregard people like a hard-core protester who self-immolates as someone with mere mental disorder. This film provides audience with a unique perspective (at least glimpse) of why such people have to behave in such an extraordinary manner.It might be a bit early to say but Joker seems to be already on track to become decade defining film series. I just can't wait for a sequel.

Review Title: Trying Too Hard // Cheesy At Times // Still A Superhero Movie
Review:
Alright, listen. It's a good movie. Some could consider it great, Look! I gave it a 7/10 that's a positive rating! But, it's not "Film of the year", it's not fantastic and it's not going to knock you out of your seat.Joaquin Phoenix is phenomenal, as usual. His acting is superb, so don't go in thinking he will ruin the film or in some way disgrace Heath Ledger's portrayal; it's a different Joker; get over it. However, because Phoenix is so good, it feels like every other actor wasn't; like they weren't pouring everything they had into their performances. And if Phoenix is going to, you'd better make some attempt to compete with him, even if you know you'll fail.The Cinematography is incredible, some of the best I've seen in past years. Lots of close-up spins around Phoenix as lights shine all over him - giving the film a kind of 'showbiz' look (which is,presumably what Todd Philips was going for). The editing is great and the song choices are perfect for the film (bar one, later in the film, which feels out of place).Now onto the negative stuff. The bad parts. The things that bring the film down from masterpiece status. "Trying Too Hard, Cheesy At Times, Still A Superhero Movie" is the title of this review and with good reason. Let's address them.Trying too hard: Todd Philips & Scott Silver must think themselves great writers and although they are good at writing early scenes in films, they begins to trip over themselves when writing later scenes. They don't know how to appropriately develop a character from a previous scene, and write how they will act in the next. Now it could just be that the Joker is a difficult character to write, and if so, It's a pity that they couldn't make him perfect. There are a lot of moments when you feel as though the Director is whispering into your ear "That was sad, wasn't it?" or "Look how insane the Joker is lol!"Cheesy At Times, Still A Superhero Movie: This could film could honestly stand on it's own, and by 'on it's own', I mean as not apart of the DC 'movie-verse'. Because it feels like a kind of 'Taxi Driver 2.0', it's not copying Taxi Driver, but the similarities are apparent. It's honestly a pity that the film is a 'Superhero Movie'; there are multiple scenes constructing the Joker's hatred (and justifying it) for Bruce Wayne's family & his father.
The reason I think the Joker is Cheesy (it can't be explained out-right, so I'll list some things) at times is because of the out-of-place flashbacks, edgy dialogue, funny justifications for things and the weird 'lol, that didn't really happen' scenes.To conclude, I think you should see this film and make your own decision on it; it sure is a puzzler. Is it as fantastical as people are saying, the best film ever? Hell no. It's decent and, I think, well worth your money.

Review Title: This is the kind of movie Heath Ledger's Joker would make just to watch the world burn
Review: This movie means nothing. They just went "what's big right now? Incels and antifa? Those are the same" and rolled it all into an existing character that could use politically and socially relevant anxieties as developing characteristics... but to make absolutely no "message." and no, films don't have to have a message, but it's so clear that this movie WANTS you to think it has one.It doesn't. Joker insists on telling you he's not political multiple times in the same way people tell you they're "sick of politics," only to ignore the influence of politics in literally everything that led to where he is- and you're never given a clear sense of what Phillips wants you to believe from that point on, because the chaos is so much more intriguing to him than anything of substance. Whatever.i generally like Todd Phillips movies and think they're fun, and despite this having a stellar performance from Joaquin Phoenix and generally enticing production design (whoda thunk a Taxi Driver-inspired film looks nice in 35mm!), this might be the kind of movie that upsets me the most, because it insists on masquerading as something smarter and more important than the "average flick."And no, i don't think Joker is an incel, and I don't think the movie is about antifa...I just think this movie uses the social and political contexts of two big modern "movements" (for lack of a better term) as a sort of set dressing for its story. I don't think Joker is an incel, but his "rise to madness" is set about by a provocation in the same way that incels very publicly enact violent acts against women. It's this idea that they've been pushed to violence because a sect of society ('society' in a post about Joker, finish your drink) has unjustly acted against them and this is their rebellion. Joker uses the same sort of justification and refusal to feel remorse for his violent actions as Elliot Rodger does, but without the misogyny.It also uses Antifa in the same way- the imagery of political violent unrest and masks, all literally and declaratively set in a large city and staged to be demonstrative against wealth and facism? Both his inspiration and the images he wants to conjure in your mind- yes, despite being set in 1981- is what he knows the audience will recognize to be closely associated with Antifa.The thing is, he uses these ideas and images and characterizations in a way that don't really...make any clear comment on the things themselves. Which feels weird. To make an extreme comparison, it's like writing a road trip buddy comedy that pulls heavily from the recognizable imagery and characterizations of slavery, but doesn't... seem to have any particular stance or opinion on slavery.

Review Title: It's art that will age well like fine wine!
Review: Joker, the movie grows organically on you. It's a deep take on society and how it treats people like our protagonist/antagonist Arthur Fleck who suffers from a peculiar mental condition. Am I crazy or are people around me crazy or is the world driving me crazy or is it all of it? At different points of the movie, answer to each of these questions unfolds. Arthur becomes our lens. His predicaments, sorrows, delights and delusions speak volumes. You feel for him, you feel his pain. But it's not just Arthur's take we get to see. The world around him has a voice of its own and through this lens, we see Arthur's condition deteriorate and that of the world around him. He is both a victim and perpetrator. Joker is a manifestation of the chaos around Arthur. And when chaos is embraced, Joker is born. Joker, in the end, embraces this chaotic world, and is ready for his act. And that's where it leaves you, mesmerised. Joaquin's take on Joker is fresh, original and something of his own. The writing, screenplay, directing, soundtrack and acting come together to create a piece of art that will age well like fine wine. I was not surprised when the audience erupted to give standing ovation in the end. This is different, dark, serious and yet enjoyable. I will watch this again and again.

Review Title: All it takes is one bad day to reduce the sanest man alive to lunacy
Review:
The film takes place in Gotham City in the 70's and 80's and follows the life of Arthur Fleck, an aspiring comedian and as he is known in the future, will become the Joker.
The direction and editing of the film is sensational, at no time do we see "unnecessary" scenes that are about to roll, he knows where he is going, where he wants to go and his end. However, we are surprised throughout the plot. The script is completely round with no unanswered questions.
The tense mood is all the time, even in the small moments of relaxation, when it soon breaks a tension that always shows itself. The soundtrack is fantastic and engaging.
Photography is beautiful and rewarding, always showing a city/society, given the filth, corruption and neglect of the richest to the poorest.
Joaquin Phoenix has a brilliant, Oscar-worthy performance. You can see all the nuances of his performance, from a look that shows total sadness and differs form a smile, even the way he speaks and gestures. Arthur's turning point and becoming Joker is wonderful, you notice a change/break in the way you're in this transformation. The other performances are very well done too.
The violence is as perfect as it should be, nothing that it doesn't have in Tarantino or Deadpool movie.
No moment puts Arthur as a victim, on the contrary, it shows an actual account of a person living with severe mental disorders and the consequences of society's negligence for her. It even contains criticism of the current and past lack of empathy in the movie, but all to the right extent.
Ledger or Phoenix? Without comparisons, there is no way. Both offer fantastic and different performances, Ledger is much more grounded in a comics, while Phoenix is really more palpable.
A masterpiece, worthy of being watched and Oscar.

Review Title: One of the best acting performances I've ever seen.
Review: Phoenix is absolutely unstoppable in this film. I read somewhere that Jared Leto was upset not be called for this movie, so what! Who cares? Phoenix is on par with Heath Ledgers Joker performance but in a new and different movie.People will always compare anyone who takes on the role of The Joker to Ledger, but I think with this performance that all changes (although Ledger is still the greatest in my opinion, but I prefer The Dark Knight as a movie). If my rating was for Phoenix alone, then it's easily a 10/10. The movie and performance really reminded me of Christian Bale in The Machinist, which is nicely apt considering we're talking about The Dark Knight himself. There are lots of moments in the film which really remind me of the Machinist, when you see it, you will know what I mean.As for the movie itself, if it were a standalone film about someone who suffers a psychological break, then it's a 10/10, but the fact it's a film about the Joker, I have to mark the writing down slightly. There are moments in the film, especially with references to the Waynes that irritated me, specifically the way they portray Thomas Wayne, it just doesn't fit unfortunately. What the movie did well though was show how someone could suffer such a psychological break in a real world situation, given what we know about psychological profiling etc.People have complained about the violence, and about the use of a Gary Glitter song (awkward), but for me this film strikes the right balance, and is well paced and exactly violent enough. I really loved this film, I just can't get past some of the artistic licence that was used with the character.Movie 9/10 for that reason, Phoenix 10/10 and should get an Academy Award.

Zazie Beetz's character, Sophie, is Arthur's love figure, having an unexpected plot twist. Of course, how could I forget Joaquin Phoenix. Review Title: Joker: A Deeply Unsettling Character Study About Social Isolation and Mental Illness
Review: Todd Phillip's Joker, a standalone film within the DC Universe, is a tragic and haunting cinematic masterpiece. A deeply unsettling film that belongs to the bygone era of the 70's and 80's. A type of film that Hollywood has since neglected in favour of producing big blockbuster franchises.Joker is not a film that everyone will enjoy and it was not produced for that purpose. Some will be put off by the dark bleak tone and the subject matter under discussion. While others will dislike the film for being extremely unconventional, especially for a character born within a superhero universe.Joker is a complex art house film that is essentially a psychologically driven character study of Arthur Fleck (also eventually known as Joker). It provides an insight into the brutal reality of social isolation, societal fragmentation and mental illness at a time when society lacks basic elements of empathy and humanity for its inhabitants.It is inspired and influenced by late 70's and early 80's art house films like Taxi Driver, King of Comedy, Mean Streets, Network and One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest.In order for it to be widely accessible it has been dressed up in the garb of a mainstream Hollywood film. Yet, make no mistake, Joker is a piece of cinematic art that we have been deprived of for decades. A type of film that has been missing for a generation due to Hollywood's obsession with maintaining the status quo.Without spoiling the film, Joaquin Phoenix plays the titular character Joker, who turns in one of the most astonishing performances ever captured on film. He presents us with a portrayal of a failed stand-up comedian named Arthur Fleck in Gotham City during the early 80's, who from the very first moment he is depicted on screen is shown struggling with mental illness. Over the next 2 hours, through no fault of his own, we are provided with a brutally powerful depiction of his apparent descent into madness.The film challenges and forces its audience to face themes they will find extremely uncomfortable. As a society we have made a habit of brushing our problems under the carpet. Joker not only lifts that rug, but it pulls it right from under our feet by showing us the brutal horror of what it means to be broken by society in every way imaginable.It is a film that is essentially about our ability to deal with trauma, our need for compassion and our capacity for destruction borne from the way we are treated by society. It is a story that should resonate with us on a personal level, about our position in society and how we deal with our own fragility and vulnerabilities. This includes our need to be accepted by others around us.The beauty of art house cinema is that it can be interpreted in a number of ways. However, several commentators have attempted to weaponise the film as a piece of political propaganda by interpreting it through the prism of the far right, Brexit, the Me-Too movement and Donald Trump. Sorry to disappoint those who choose to do so, but the film is not about any of those issues. This is something the protagonist makes very clear throughout the film.Rather, it points the camera inwards and presents us with a glimpse of our own insecurities. It highlights a personal and uncomfortable truth that no matter what we choose to identify as we are solitary human beings born on a planet which does not care whether we live or die, because the show must go on.Ever since we were children we have always been taught that if we live decent lives, are good to others then good will be done to us. But as adults, despite how uncomfortable it may be for many to admit, we have come to the painful realisation that in the societies we inhabit this is untrue.For many like Arthur, living in such an immoral and depraved world has led to perverse life changing experiences being inflicted upon them in their childhood that have carried on into adulthood through the manifestation of serious mental illnesses.Some social commentators have expressed how the film mocks mental health issues. It does nothing of the sort. Rather it shines a light on the burden placed on those who suffer from these serious conditions and the indifference in which they are treated by society. Arthur sums it up perfectly in the film when he says "the worst part about having a mental illness is people expect you to behave as if you don't".Despite what critics and some who want to use the film as a political tool have said about the visceral and raw violence depicted on screen, Joker is not a film about violence. Rather, it is about our need as a society to be empathetic. One act of kindness could be everything to someone suffering in isolation. The violence we see on screen is essentially a metaphorical response to the brutal feelings of isolation that exist when one is inflicted with serious mental illness. Being trapped by your own mind with no escape can lead many people suffering from mental illness to commit acts of violence on themselves, even in a non literal sense, especially in the way they perceive themselves.If anyone's take away from the film is to highlight the violence we briefly see on screen, then they have failed to understand that the film is screaming at us that violence is not the answer to our problems. In fact, more abuse and violence is inflicted upon Arthur than anyone else in the film and it is through this affliction that we begin to see the world around him for what it truly is.Ever since the film was lauded with the Golden Lion award for best film at the Venice Film Festival it has been met with controversy. Some have claimed that Joker leaves the viewer with a morally ambiguous message that will encourage incels, a trait recognised in Arthur, to commit murder.This is a predictable scaremongering media violence trope we have heard for decades about films by politicians and societal leaders to cover up their own failings that have led to the immoral and depraved society we inhabit today.Those reading this review may have been put off watching the Joker due to the subject matters under discussion, but this is why it is imperative that each and every one of us watches this film. By seeing the true depths of how our society can unintentionally or intentionally push ordinary people to the edge of insanity, maybe it will force us to reflect on our own expressions of compassion and empathy.

Review Title: A seminal work of our generation
Review: An incredible film, and in my opinion a seminal work of our generation. For those who'd like that statement justified with a deeper review, (but no spoilers) read please on for my ramblings.Beautifully shot with allot of low light and shallow depth of field cinematography, its classic intimate film making that you can't help but love. The Oscar worthy directing of Todd Phillips is phenomenal and although his back catalogue claims some of my favourite films you'd never guess that this was from the same director of Old School and The Hangover. The style of film making contradicts the current trend for bleached and over sanitised film making born from the generation Netflix. If you've seen and adored The Kings Speech or the newest series of Top Boy this is gonna tickle your filmic fancy.The performance by Joaquin Phoenixa is as intense as you'd expect it to be from him, and for an anyone that remembers Gladiator and has seen his mockumentary 'I'm Still Here' you'll recognise the character traits and the intensity of his delivery as essentially being part of his real-world personality. The music and scene construction is spellbinding almost to the point of being shocking, and for me as someone who struggles with the willing suspension of disbelief the level of submersion is as palpable as it is wonderful, you live in this film through the Jokers eyes.I'm not going to comment on the socio-political insights as their inclusion is subjective and I don't believe its meant to be a comment on the state of the world, although there's certainly allot to read in to. What is worth a thought is the affect that cutting public services can have on the most vulnerable people in our society, particularly those who've suffered abuse or poor mental health. Unlike the opinion of some American authorities i don't think it'll inspire violence or public disorder but you will love it and you will always remember watching it in the cinema.

Review Title: Intense, unsettling, very plausible and very, very good
Review:
If you were planning to study psychology, psychiatry or whatever is related to these, you will have to watch this film. I am neither a psychologist nor a psychiatrist, but I dare say that is irrevelant in this case.
What you watch when watching this film is a very plausible explanation why someone will do the things he ultimately does. Not because of one single reason, but for multiple reasons. The worst thing is, he feels he will become what everyone fears someone may become because of just one of those many reasons.
This is not a film for the faint hearted. Nor is it a film for young(er) people (ok, there is an R rating, but nonetheless). This is not a film one 'enjoys'. This film leaves a lot to be thought about. Society, the people that are neglected by it is possibly a better way of putting it.
I am not a professional as stated before, but those people who were afraid this film might lead to more aggression, they are wrong (have been wronged is probably better), so very wrong. This film will not incite aggression - it will prevent it.
Superhero or supervillain story? Not in the slightest way. This is a psychological thriller, it's a case study. An example of someone who tries to do his best not to become that person he knows he could become Maybe even fears he will become.
The film is good, but Phoenix is the X-factor. My God, his acting is so intense, he really transforms into his filmpersona. Of course the film is all about his character, but the way he performs, the way he portrays his character, I think all the rewards he has received prove that this is something one seldom sees.
If you haven't seen this film - please do. If you have seen it - you will undoubtedly agree with what I've written.

Review Title: One of the Best of the Year
Review: As a DC Comic Book film, it adds the appropriate character and story beats and delivers a thoughtful, compelling, insane origin of its most famous villain; however beneath the surface, the film dives into what society can do to someone and the discussion of nature versus nurture; what it means to be the average person in an otherwise average, uncaring, unjust society. Joaquin gives one of his best performances ever; He carries the character to an extreme where it would be an unworthy movie if any other person were to play this introspective take on Joker. The supporting cast, while not doing much, add to the story and thought process of Arthur himself. If there were one complaint, that would be that the way things play out in the film seem coincidental and some scenes are overwhelmingly obvious at points. However, those are just nitpicks. If you're looking for a new, innovative, creative, dark, faithful, introspective take on the clown prince of crime; then this film will easily make your top ten.

Review Title: Welcome to the Emancipation of Arthur Fleck
Review: #JokerCaution: The slow burning schizophrenic emancipation of Arthur Fleck will leave you deeply disturbed, mouth agape in some scenes of pure violence, shocking you to the core.Arthur's fall into insanity is like quicksand. It will pull you along with Arthur down the rabbit's hole. You could try and walk out of the theatre but I doubt you will be able to move.For comicbook fans, Arthur Fleck eventually became the Joker, the one man who could not be moved, the one man who saw the evil in everyone. The one man who knew how to push even the White Knights into darkness, while he danced with the Devil in the pale moonlight (!) laughing away in his own terrible pain, his own deep frustrations, his own madness...This movie is about the final leap he took. The leap into sheer madness. You will become mad along with him. So compelling is this portrayal of the Joker.You could blame the apathy of a dying society for the final push. You could blame his mother. You could blame his colleagues.But in the end, Arthur doesn't blame anyone. Not even the demons in his head.By the end of it all, he learns to dance with them...You can see him do that dance in the end, without saying a word. His deep mad eyes speak it out as if he's shouting it in your face.It will shake you up. It will make you cry.Because you and I, are a part of the Society that drove Arthur to become the Joker...I have never been so disturbed by a movie. I've seen some of the most horrific movies as part of my quest for understanding cinema.This movie is a first. It brings tears to my eyes to write this. You will feel sad for Arthur's madness, twist your heart with the pain he felt.But you will also feel the sheer murderous horror that Arthur becomes. Like an Antichrist rising from the fires of our collective apathy and the death of our tired souls.P. S. To sit through this movie took all of my love for cinema. I have never been so much in awe, ever.

"You wouldn't get it," has been the most important and iconic line from this year's most controversial film. Critics from around the world became scared with the release of Joker. They thought the film would inspire people to commit violent crimes. With Joker, director Todd Phillips takes a dark turn from his previous movies, such as The Hangover, and creates a gloomy cynical masterpiece exposing issues deeply rooted into the framework of society. Joker is the origin story of Batman's arch nemesis The Joker, starring Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur Fleck, also known as Joker. The film starts by giving the viewer a glimpse into the life of Arthur Fleck, a lower class, mentally ill, middle aged man who has a job as a clown to care for his mother, and also works on standup comedy in his free time. In the opening Arthur attends a therapy session with a government worker who prescribes him medicine for his mental illness. After the government cuts the funding for this program, Arthur is lost in a city that has forgotten him. From here, he begins to discover the dark flaws of society and his own past, all while he slips into insanity. Everything collapses when he is invited onto the Murray Franklin Show, Gotham City's premiere late night show, and surprises everyone.
The plot of this film is what made the film so controversial, but the main idea is to point out problems in society. Critics around the world were worried that this film would inspire people to commit senseless violence. People thought this film was unnecessarily dark and twisted just for the sake of evil. While the plot was extremely wicked, it only adds to the anarchy in which the Joker stands for. Joker carries on the tradition of Jack Nicholson's, and Heath Ledger's Joker, by having the Joker symbolize chaos and anarchy. The only difference is in this film chaos and anarchy are used to show how elitists create societal rules that leave the lower class forgotten. Joker's madness creates a domino effect that starts an uprising against the other class, showing how villians can be created if society leaves them behind. With heavy inspiration from Martin Scorsese films such as The King of Comedy and Taxi Driver, Joker exposes a mental health crisis in the world today and how important it is to tend to this issue. Ultimately Phillips creates a dark storyline, not just for the sake of evil, but to point out flaws in society and what those unresolved problems could mean.
Joaquin Phoenix's performance as Joker stands out immediately as immaculate. Phoenix is able to portray exactly who Arthur is intended to be through his slight facial expressions and movements. The film is relatively quiet without many lines by any character, but this does not diminish Phoenix's acting ability. Phoenix's is able to capture Arthur's slide into insanity through his dancing in the film. Arthur is often pictured dancing maniacally throughout the film, and Phoenix's slender build and slithering movements create a dark sense of fulfilment for the character. When Arthur does speak, Phoenix masterfully makes the audience uneasy with sinister smiles and a light voice. The way that Phoenix delivers lines such as "I always thought my life was a tragedy. But I now know its a comedy." makes hairs stand on end. Phoenix fortunately overshadows mediocre performances by Robert DeNiro and Zazie Beetz who play important supporting roles in the film. With Phoenix's soft delivery, sinister movements, and dark laugh, he is able to portray Arthur's descent into madness, and transition into joker, magnificently.
Finally the music in this film, while unconventional, amplified each and every scene of this film. There are two specific scenes in which the music drives the meaning. The first is when Joker is going down the stairs, dancing to the song "Rock and Roll Part II" by Gary Glitter. This scene symbolizes Arthur's complete transition into Joker. The upbeat song and dance moves signify how Arthur feels free for once and is no longer living in a tragedy. The choice of song brings an element of excitement to the viewer, as this song is usually used in sports arenas to hype up a crowd. Phillips wants the audience to share Joker's excitement. The second one is the final scene in the movie. It is a recreation of the first scene where Arthur is talking to his therapist. He tells his therapist "You wouldn't get it." after laughing at a joke he is thinking about. "That's Life" by Frank Sinatra starts playing and Arthur sings and dances to it. The song illustrates Arthur's lack of remorse for what he's done, because he simply believes that's how his life goes. This song is also from the time period in which the movie is set, adding to the realism of the setting.
In my eyes Joker is a work of art that will go unappreciated. Because of its dark message people will forever find the film disturbing, but it highlights real issues through a compelling plot, incredible acting, and unconventional choice in music. Joker has deservingly received nominations for multiple awards for the amazing cinematography. More importantly, Joker sends a message and makes the audience question society. So to the people that view Joker as a film created simply for the sake of darkness and violence, "You wouldn't get it." ***(Frank Sinatra's That's Life starts playing)

When first watching the trailers for this movie I was excited for a new DC based movie starring the Joker. It excites me that DC was returning to the dark, gloomy style of movies they do best like The Dark Knight and The Dark Knight Rises, so when I sat down to start watching I was already on the edge of my seat ready to watch the rise of the Joker.
Arthur Fleck who is mentally ill is struggling to fit in with society. Bullied and excluded, Arthur seeks comfort in humor. As we figure out, Arthur's sense of humor is unlike anyone else's. At first he was excited because he has always wanted to be a stand up comedian but is once again rejected by society. After this we watch Arthur slowly descend because of his mental illness and because of society being selfish and unwilling to help the people in need we see Arthur turn into Infamous Joker with the creepy laugh and the painted face.
My first thought after watching this movie was "wow". The acting is incredible. Joaquin Phoenix had an Oscar worthy performance, and that laugh, that creepy laugh gave me chills down my spine every time I heard it. The costume design was absolutely insane. With the make up to the dyed green hair they made Joaquin look like everyone's worst nightmare. Todd Phillips did an amazing job with the story line and the Joker's development as a character is amazing. He starts off as a poor citizen with a mental illness rejected by society and his city. As we watch we see his actions start to throw the city into chaos and eventually watch as he develops into the mastermind crime lord Joker we all know and love. Apart from all the good acting and storyline I was disappointed that he didn't face any obstacles or moments where I thought that he was in serious trouble. Everything went his way and he had no big setbacks, which is disappointing because in past DC movies there is always a big setback or obstacle to overcome. Even though he doesn't face any setbacks we feel like he is always struggling with the soundtrack that gives you goosebumps. The soundtrack reminded me of the show Chernobyl with all the slow, deep, rolling notes that keep you on the edge of your seat anxiously awaiting for something bad to happen.
I highly recommend watching this movie if you haven't yet. I have watched it multiple times already and every time I am stunned by what they were able to accomplish with this movie. Whether it was Joaquin Phoenix with his incredible acting, the make up design, the soundtrack that gives you chills every time the music starts playing or Todd Phillips brilliant and chilling story. Although they could improve on things like how the Joker doesn't face any major obstacles, this doesn't take away from how much I enjoyed watching this film.

Review Title: One of the best films of the decade, A unique film, A masterpiece
Review: For the first time in a long while, we have a movie based on a comic book character that is both interesting and different. I've long bemoaned the current fad for making superhero movies which try to delve into the imagined psyches and motivations of their central characters. For me, this usually doesn't work and completely misses the trick about why people go to see such movies. Joker is the exception. It is stunning. To be honest, this is probably due to their being more to play with in exploring what turns a man into an evil villain rather than a hero but the success of this film is largely due to a mesmerising performance by Joaquin Phoenix who portrays the downtrodden, mentally fragile Arthur Fleck, a put upon entertainer and clown, gradually turn from a social misfit into a psychopathic killer. Much of the transformation unfolds with simple meaningful gestures, glances and outbursts of maniacal and inopportune laughter from the character and Phoenix gives his all to the role. The backdrop of a greasy, dirty, crime-riddled Gotham city is perfectly realised as a thinly disguised New York of the late 70s/early 80s. It is a seedy, nasty city filled with grinding poverty and bleak prospects. Director Todd Phillips definitely raises the bar on what this kind of movie can be and has given us the best graphic novel/comic derived movie in several years. Let's hope this becomes the model for what is to bound come as the superhero genre is surely set to continue.
