**BACKSTORY**
If I had to describe this movie in one word, it would simply be "beautiful". From the cinematography, to the acting & improvising, to the outstanding score, Joker is by far my favorite film ever made.If you knew me before this review, you'd know that I used to always choke up when asked what my favorite film was. I could not answer, and any answer I gave was not sincere in the slightest. This one however, is.**IS IT A COMIC FILM?**
I will say this; it's not really a comic book film at all, it is *loosely* based off of the character "Joker", so you shouldn't go into this film expecting it to be 1:1 lore, but in my opinion that plays a key in making it so good. If this movie (in my opinion,) went with a more comic-like approach, I would not have enjoyed it as much as I do and I am certain about this. Take my advice, when you watch this movie, don't go in with the mindset that you're gonna see "Joker" the comic villain, go in knowing this is a film about a guy who just wants to make people laugh & smile, and is challenged by the harshness of the world he lives in. With this mindset, I can guarantee you will enjoy this film much more, just keep the DC lore to a minimal.I know what you're thinking, "Well then, why is it called Joker?"
Like I said, it's *loosely* based off of the villain, and just a creative take on his backstory. Other than that, I don't really have any great explanations for you other than I simply enjoyed the film better by looking at it from a real world stand-point.**REVIEW**
Joaquin's portrayal of Arthur Fleck was phenomenal! He reportedly lost ~52 pounds for the part, and it really shows during the film. The performance is INCREDIBLE. His uncontrollable laugh comes to mind, as in every scene it happens you can just feel the suffering Arthur is going through, there's a particular scene that I won't go into details about, but let's just say finally catches a break, and it's all ruined from his nervous laughter. These moments really show just how great Joaquin is as portraying emotion, you can feel every bit of the character's emotions through this film. Everything from his uncontrollable laughter, to his adorable kid-like nature, everything about this character seems real and genuine like he lost himself in the part.Joker would not be what it is without the collaboration of Joaquin Phoenix and Todd Phillips. Had Phillips not given Phoenix so much freedom, I don't believe this film would have been as successful and Todd know's this, he's acknowledged it in an interview with (I forgot who) by saying something along the lines of "You wouldn't be a great director if you had an actor like Joaquin Phoenix on and NOT allow him such freedom." Not word-for-word, but you get the drift.When you watch this film, pay attention the colors. The colors beautifully match the feeling of every scene, with the orange and cyan blue light's it really makes for a beautiful film, you can pretty much find a great still in every single scene that is filmed.**OVERALL**
I give this movie a 10/10 and I've never felt so sure about a rating in my life. I think it is perfect, and honestly I do *not* want a sequel, this film is perfect as a one-off and I HIGHLY recommend you see it in theatre's before it is too late, this is not a film you want to miss the experience of seeing on the big screen.

Review Title: Stands alone as a smart psychological thriller
Review: I saw this film last night, and believe me I could not wait to see it because it seemed like DC's last chance to redeem itself. I had high expectations based on the trailer, and for the most part they were met. I even postponed watching videos or reading reviews because I didn't want a single spoiler. But before I get into my actual review, let's briefly discuss the nonsense that has all the media's panties in a twist before the film even came out. There's so much BS about this potentially creating another Aurora shooter. What I think many failed to understand is that it was not superheroes or anything to do with Batman that created the Aurora shooter, he simply used that as a backdrop for something he already intended to do. When I came to the box office, there was a sign (and there were multiple signs like this around the theater) saying that no fake weapons (what about real weapons?), bags/backpacks, or makeup/masks were allowed in the theater, due the "heightened security" around the film. The only time I've ever seen that happen was when there was all that hype around Seth Rogen's The Interview, because of the fear of North Korea nuking us or something. If anything, the main message is that we should pay more attention to potential mass shooters and get them help before they go over the edge. It's not pro-mass shooter in any way. It's funny that it was initially the far right concerned about violent video games and movies, and then it was the far left, and now it's everyone on all sides of the aisle. I'll get off my soapbox and get into the movie.First of all, Joaquin Phoenix was excellent in this film (as he is in most of his roles)! He really added emotional and physical aspects to this character (especially with the dancing) and I think very few actors could have performed as well as he did. Everyone in supporting roles did well also, Robert DeNiro in particular (who of course starred in Taxi Driver, which this film probably drew inspiration from).One thing I did want to comment on was the weight loss gimmick. That and other components of this film remind me of The Machinist, which was probably best known for the weight loss and not much else, though I personally liked the film. Apparently Phoenix lost 52 pounds in several months! In other words, move over Christian Bale, Joaquin's coming for your record! (Funny that one of these actors portrayed Batman and another portrayed the Joker.) But from The Machinist onwards (and even before then with films like Raging Bull) actors losing or gaining tons of weight for a role has become commonplace, to the point where it doesn't really add to the character. Why is it that Arthur Fleck had to be so thin? What does that add to his character? If anything, it just makes it less believable that he had the strength to kill all those people. The whole point of actors losing or gaining weight for a role is it's supposed to make them more believable, because they look like the character they're playing. But neither The Machinist nor Joker provide an actual explanation as to why their protagonist looks the way he looks. My only theory is that it provides a physical analogue for how tormented their characters are. And I can personally vouch that people do tend to lose a lot of weight, sometimes to the point of becoming underweight, when they are depressed/stressed out or going through a more restrictive type of eating disorder like anorexia, ARFID, or forms of ED-NOS. So it's not entirely implausible that many people with severe mental illnesses can be underweight. (Then again, there are also plenty of overweight mentally ill people who stress eat and have a lot of cortisol in their system, but I guess portraying that doesn't get you dat sweet sweet Oscar buzz, does it?) So maybe I'm wrong.But while we're on the subject of other psychological thrillers this film resembles, let's just say this film has a very predictable twist that most psychological thrillers these days steal from a certain movie that actually is celebrating its 20th anniversary of its release today. (For those who might be in a different time zone or see this long after I post it, that would be October 15th, which is also close to my 20th birthday!) I would make an obvious reference to said film, but I don't want to give it away that easily. I predicted the twist in Joker from the first moment it came into play, and was like "oh here we go again" and sure enough, I was right. (This is probably only because I've seen a lot of psychological thrillers/horrors and so I was conditioned to pick up the signs.) That being said, the twist wasn't incredibly integral to the film or anything, so it wasn't that bothersome. There was another thing I thought was going to happen in the way of a literal Chekov's Gun, but it actually ended up playing out in a different way. So at least that subverted my expectations *insert RedLetterMedia meme here*. Funnily enough, I went to see this film with my dad (we are both big DC/Batman fans) and he predicted the second twist but not the first, and I was the other way around.I also liked how realistic this film was. Picking up from the Nolan Batman universe and moving the ball forward from a fantastical almost magical universe (as Burton and Shumacher envisioned) to a dark, gritty realistic universe quite like our own. The only unbelievable thing was that at one point Fleck gets full-on hit by a car and is apparently completely fine. (Hey, kind of like The Machinist!) Even the uncontrollable laughter is a real thing (when I was in a mental hospital, there was a woman with some form of catatonia, and one of the very few expressions she could make was uncontrollable laughter. It's apparently common in people with schizophrenia and related disorders, the proper term for it is "inappropriate affect").That said, there were some pacing issues with this film, particularly at the end. There was a moment where it would have been perfect for the film to end, and yet the film dragged on for another 10-15 minutes. Other than that and the predictable plot twist, I really didn't have much issue with this role.So you're probably wondering, do I think Joaquin Phoenix is the best Joker? I would say yes, but mostly because he gets so much screen time to develop his character. That and I like this particular portrayal of the Joker as a tormented and somewhat relatable soul. (However, the film did not glorify or excuse the violent actions of Arthur Fleck/The Joker in any way, unlike the likes of CNN would have you believe, it only provided a explanation for them.)The funniest thing that came out of all of this that Jared Leto is apparently really butthurt that he didn't get a whole Joker movie to himself. Stay mad, Jared. You don't hold a candle to anyone else who's taken the gauntlet of the Joker role.

Review Title: Now that The Hype Has Died, the Truth Can Be Exploited!
Review: On the 24 of July, the year 2008, Batman returned to the cinema with a new character in mind. A character so deep in meaning, that an ounce of BS from it would be enough to end the franchise of the dark knight. Months before the Dark knight debuted, hardcore fans of the D.C universe were in slight shock to hear that Heath Ledgers would take on the role as the infamous Joker in the upcoming movie titled the dark knight. The fans were puzzled assuring themselves that this will at least be a decent movie right? But it was no mystery to what was really going on. The D.C fandom were in fear that this could be a huge upset for the future of the D.C universe if the Joker is not played right. However, that turned out not to be the case. Matter in fact, Christopher Nolan as the Co-writer; executive producer, director and as Batman along with Heath Ledgers had delivered a real masterpiece. Hardcore fan or not, it appealed to everyone. The action; the emotion and the love for the characters had been the real gem that had fans leaving the cinema mind blown. But above all, people could not believe how much devotion Heath Ledgers had for his role as the Joker. Even first timers, were mind blown by the heart and devotion of the legend Heath Ledger. This movie broke records upon records settling for the fourth best movie in the history of film-making. To narrow the success, it is still to this day the greatest superhero action movie ever to be produced. Not so long after the debut of the dark knight, it was time to reveal the Oscar winners. The hosts took to the stage in a woof of excitement. As they steered their way through the long line of awards, the much awaited awards neared. Finally, the time had arrived to announce the winner for best supporting actor. A drum roll was given and a name was drawn. Heath Ledgers had won the Oscar award for his gratifying performance as the Joker in The Dark knight. But as much as it was a night to celebrate films success, it was also a night to remember the passing of Heath Ledger. A legend in the industry of film making best known for his performance as the Joker. It was clear to Warner Bros and the D.C fandom that it will be a long wait till the Joker makes a reappearance on the big screen. 8 years later, Warner Bros release a film known as Suicide Squad. Fans are in complete anticipation until they are awfully mistreated by Jared Letos poor and underwhelming performance as the Joker in Suicide Squad. This has fans up in anger demanding refunds for disrespecting Heath Ledger with a poor performance of the Joker. Articles pop up all over the world ranting on about how much of a mistake it was to let Jared Leto take up the role as the new joker. By then, Warner Bros are aware of their mistake and think not to go down that path again. 3 years later, Warner Bros are excited to announce that the new film Joker is in the works and is expected to hit cinemas later this year (2019). However, the announcement of the film Joker didn't grasp much attention. As all were occupied with the controversy behind the continuance of the marvel universe after the global sellout film Avengers endgame debuted. Followed by Spider Man. Nonetheless, the D.C fandom were still in shock of how much of a risk and upset this could be for the D.C universe. Enough to put an end to ever seeing the Joker appear on screen again. But they remained optimistic in the hope that it would be a surpassing surprise. On the 3rd of October, Warner Bros accompanied by Joaquin Phoenix snuck their way through the long line of critics an into the premiere of the Joker. Word is the Joker scraped up to 90 million dollars on the opening weekend. Tumbling over strong competitors like the film Venom and into the realms of Hollywood. Moments after its release, articles from all over the media are popping up with grasping captions like THE D.C FRANCHISE IS RESTORED or THE JOKER HAS HIT HOME ONCE AGAIN. What is the first thing I do? I tail on and watch it for myself. After 2 hours 2 minutes sitting stone cold in a bat cave, the lights flash on. As my eyes are still rendering the dimness of the lights I think to myself... It was good but not great?!?!? The Joker has always been about a genius of a person who is twisted by his psychopathic nature. Leading him to become the king of the underworld. In the Joker, It helps us to understand his rough upbringing and how it corresponded to the person he becomes. But it does not show us how twisted he is through his ingenious nature. More or less, it paints him as a sad miserable dude who is not so smart at all... JUST CRAZY! Now to dive into the logical side of the story. When I think of the Joker as a standalone film, I am thinking of a younger version of Heath ledgers. NOT HEATH LEDGER'S FREAKING GRANDDAD! In this portrayal of the Jokers upbringing, we are led to perceive the Joker for a forty year old man. Shouldn't the Joker be dawning his prime age? I mean for gosh sake, he was not even thirty by the time he started terrorizing Gotham with his contagious laughter an inhuman acts of tyrant. If you want a movie to be as touching as can be, then you must appeal to realistic factors like age for example. So, If there is a next time, I dearly hope you appeal to the audience with a more logical approach ;)

I thought Phoenix was fantastic in his other roles, but this one is jaw dropping and left me speechless, but wanting to discuss the intensity and emotions with anyone who would listen.This movie is not a nod to violence. It is a nudge to wake us up as a society with how people are truly affected by others, their past, the people they should be able to rely upon. While the Joker IS a villain, is it because he was conditioned by society to be so? Or was it forced, him being shoved into a dark place when he just wanted to make people laugh? The Joker is not a villain, but a punching bag for the world to take out their insecurities on.Go see this movie. Immediately. And then go be kind to someone. Phoenix deserves more than an Oscar.

Joker the most anticipated movie of 2019 following it's DC's competitor Marvels Avengers Endgame. "Joker," Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix), seated in front of a mirror, hooks a finger into each corner of his mouth, and pulls. Up, then down: a grin, a grimace. We are meant to think of the masks, comic and tragic, that were worn by the actors in ancient Greek drama. Over the next couple of hours, those two moods will be welded together, until we can't tell the light from the dark. Seating the movie theatres was extraordinary. While watching this movie every scene had me on the edge of the seat. Todd Phillips who co-wrote it with Scott Silver, and whose previous films, from "Road Trip" (2000) and "Old School" (2003) to the "Hangover" yet proved himself to many people by creating a movie with so much drama and suspense. I must say i had not faith in Todd because of his past in comedy movies but I was proven wrong. This version of the joker is the most authentic we have ever scene on screen. Joaquin's previous competitors included Heath ledger and Jack Nicholson and yes I will not include Jared Leto, let's forget he existed and I must say he really did prove himself, Joaquin effectively captured the trauma and anger and guilt a person with a meantl health disorder goes through and we had not seen that on screen before. The movie took it's time to show us how "Arthur" or Joker became the man we see in the comics and some may say it became a little boring at times and yes I do agree but in order to fully understand a character so exceptional patience is key. At times the pacing was a little too slow, I would say that there are some scenes that could have been cut short, however, these are just minor details that really don't matter. "Joker" descends upon us. The online discussion has mounted from the rampant to the manic, undeterred, or perhaps exacerbated, by the fact that nobody, apart from critics and festivalgoers, has actually seen the movie. (Emotions run high when people are low on facts.) In one corner are those who crave a masterpiece: a film that will unearth a new psychic intensity in the domain of the comic book, ideal for our distended times. In the opposite corner are those who fear that Phillips and Phoenix may give license to all the lonely people out there-in particular, to any messed-up white guys who feel wretchedly uncherished and would welcome a tutorial in the art of lashing out. The composer Hildur Guðnadóttir not only proved herself yet again after composing"Sicario" 2016. The music made my heartbeat exceed every time I heard it. For such heartless cruel evil and vile character, it made me feel sorrow and anguish for him and I applaud her for that. This film was everything I wanted it to be and more. DC should stop trying to do what Marvel has and capitalise on this realistic R-rated style and tone for their films. Not many people could pull off a convincing Joker for an entire film, and neither did Phoenix. This film is about Arthur's transformation, he doesn't fully become Joker until the very end of the film.
This is the story of a man's descent into madness done in the most realistic way possible, taking little inspiration from source material and focusing on what makes the character at his core so polarising.
Aside from the incredible acting, the cinematography, score and pacing of the film married perfectly with Phoenix's take. No screen time was wasted, everything that happened had a purpose or a meaning.
The inclusion of the Waynes in the story was a surprise but a welcome one.
Laying the groundwork for the upcoming Matt Reeves Batman film potentially.
I truly do hope we get to see Phoenix do Joker properly in a future film, but for now I hope this is the catalyst to start the DC Dark series with more films in this realistic R-rated style and tone made for adults and not kids.

It's been 12 hours since I saw Joker at my local cinema and my head is still spinning.
I didn't get much sleep and I'm still trying to process what happened.
It was nothing short of a feast for the senses and I just wanted more.Make no mistake - this is cinematic brilliance at its highest level.
A masterpiece.
Hauntingly beautiful, magnificent, mesmerizing.
Stunning.
Chilling.
I honestly don't think I blinked during the two hours in fear of missing something.The onscreen world immediately captures you and pulls you in to an 80's Gotham City.
The thunderous Dolby Atmos soundtrack is beautiful, chilling and at times downright terrifying.If you are expecting a non-stop gore fest then you will be bitterly disappointed.
There are a handful of shootings.
What you will experience is a classic film of unprecedented genius, both artistically and technically.I must admit I went into the theatre with a bias towards Joaquin Phoenix.
Everyone has read the stories of his whacky antics and frequent meltdowns.
I'd seen his on set rant on talk show Jimmy Kimmel a few weeks back and thought him to be just another pretentious actor.
All is forgiven.
His performance in this film is truly breathtaking.Joker is not just another DC superhero film, it's a journey into the mind of a twisted psychopath who needed help but didn't get it.
For some reason, actors who have previously played this character (Nicholson, Ledger, Leto, Romero, etc.) have all turned in both sterling and mesmerizing performances.
But it's Phoenix who now wears the crown as The Clown Prince Of Crime.
Here is my rather modest prediction come Oscar season.Best picture.
Best screenplay.
Best director.
Best cinematography.
Best actor in a leading role.
Best musical score.
Best sound editing.What I'm trying to say is this is undoubtably the best piece of modern cinema I have ever seen.P.S. For those uneasy about Gary Glitter coining in the royalties for his track in the film, his catalogue was bought out years ago by a UK based publishing company so he will not be receiving a dime for the tracks inclusion.

This film isn't just what we needed as DC fans but what DC and Warner needed to present to the fans. After the disappointment of Suicide Squad and Justice League and the mediocre Wonder Woman and Aquaman, DC needed to regain some faith in their comic book movies. In steps Hangover director Todd Phillips taking on the biggest challenge of his career. What we are seeing here is that less is so much more. With a budget of just 55 million dollars (peanuts compared to 300 million dollar budget for Justice League) we have a film filled with suspense, dread and pure horror from a man isolated from society and is just a couple of bad days away from madness. In steps Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur, a lonely man segregated both physically and mentally and we join him on a downward spiral of madness and his transformation into the prince of crime. And taking on such an iconic role it's fair to say he has rather big shoes to fill.
But what Phoenix and Phillip's have managed to create with this film is a Nolanesque masterpiece of gritty realism and horror of what goes on in a mans mind, who is, through no fault of his own, having a mental breakdown. From perfecting the spontaneous laughter and the 52lbs weight loss, Phoenix gives a career best performance as does Phillip's in the directors chair. From the gritty 1980s New York feel of Gotham City, to the subtle references of Martin Scorsese's classics Taxi Driver and The King Of Comedy and Hildur Gudnadottir's heart pounding score, this film perfectly shapes the world of a lonely man struggling to find his place in a divided world where the rich are rich and the poor are forgotten.
With a storyline that's gripping from start to finish and a particularly violent suspense which is unseen in most modern 'comic book film's' the whole event packs an enormous punch which leaves us with 1 emotion, astounded.
A worthy standalone that grips firmly on both modern day issues and somehow, a realistic comic character's origin story.

There exists a certain reputation in the field of film critique, of which we're all aware but never really speak of amongst ourselves. There exists a serious divide between the audience and the critics, on e which threatens to cripple or even destroy the industry entirely. There is a movie that I absolutely love, and I found myself ostracized within the community for it. I'm talking about Todd Phillips' Joker. This movie is an absolute masterpiece that left audiences crying out for more. It smashed the box office, becoming the highest grossing R-rated film in American history.And, of course, the critics hated it.Joker was called provocative, unpleasant, empty; the critics completely trashed this movie, and (as always), they were dead wrong.So why is it that the audience can never seem to agree with the critics? Why did they seem to hate Joker, and why is it so beloved by audiences today? It's a difficult question, but I think I might have an answer.Humans are storytellers. It's in our blood. We live by the things we pass down to our children, and to their children, as well. Stories are always behind something larger. Some folks call it a moral. Others call it a theme. But it honestly doesn't matter what you call it, because it will always be there. Critics are taught to worship the theme. They kowtow to the magnified and sanctified name of the moral, their G-d and savior. They meticulously overanalyze and study every shot, looking for layers upon layers of messages. Critics are taught to analyze, not appreciate. To most of them, quality is synonymous with complexity. And I think Joker confused them deeply, because there is no clear message in this movie. Of course, one could certainly draw political commentary from this story, but deep down, it's just a movie about a man and the broken world that failed him. It's meant to be appreciated, not analyzed. Phillips just wants you to listen to Arthur, because no one else will, and his is a story worth telling. But the critics don't understand that. Every story has to have a clear cut eat-your-broccoli-and-take-your-vitamins moral for it to be worthwhile. And that's why they'll never be in touch with the audience. Captain Marvel? The critics loved it. They raved on and on about the power in showcasing a female hero, and the commentary on anti-immigrant politics. But the story just wasn't that good, and the movie fell flat. Take another example, Ghostbusters. Not the original, mind you; I'm talking about the all-female remake. I can appreciate diversity in the film industry, but an all-female cast does not make a movie good. The story was garbage, the characters flat, the dialogue terrible; nobody liked this movie. Except the critics, of course. The fatal flaw with film critique lies not (as some have said) in a class divide, but in the nature of storytelling.This is the critical divide, and it's why I started AudienceOpinion in the first place. I love the art of film, and I hate the way it's treated by the critics (of course, this thing got quite a bit bigger than I expected, and now I am a critic). They're just so out of touch with the audience that I can't fathom a world in which popular film critics manage to perfectly capture the emotions of the audience.Joker is a fantastic movie. It's heartbreaking and terrifying and spectacularly disturbing all at the same time. It's easily the best comic-book movie I've ever seen, mainly because it's not really a Joker movie at all. Joaquin Phoenix isn't playing the same character as Jack Nicholson, Heath Ledger or Mark Hamill. This is a movie about Arthur Fleck and his life. And it's downright brilliant. From the haunting soundtrack to Phoenix's brilliant performance, everything about Joker is incredible. Every shot looks perfect, every frame a painting. The plot is complex, but not convoluted. The story is disturbing, but not unpleasant. The dialogue is rare but perfect, and the characters are totally believable. The attention to detail is spectacular. It's just really good.I will say, I have a bit of a soft spot for Joaquin Phoenix. I've always admired his work. But this movie is really damn good. It's good for a lot of reasons, but most of all, it's good because there's a solid story behind it, one I really do want to hear. And the critics might not understand that. But it doesn't matter, because the audience has proved them very, very wrong.I love Joker. I thought it was frighteningly good, one of the best movies I've seen in a long time. I just wish more people would understand why. I don't care about the political commentary. I don't care about the "moral," whatever it is. I like the story, and I've elected to grant it an 8/10.You don't need to fall victim to the critical divide. You don't need anyone telling you what it is and isn't okay to like. Because if everyone listened to the critics, then we wouldn't have this movie, and what a shame that would be. Think for yourself. Don't analyze the story -- appreciate it. And most of all, go watch this movie. I think you'll be pleasantly surprised.

Review Title: Todd Philips is more predictable than you may think.

Totally void of anything that defines the Joker the way he' been depicted in earlier stories.The reason we (at least some of us) love the Joker is because we know he's been hurt, but he's got too much pride and intelligence to ever let it shine through as something personal. Instead he takes out his anger on the hypocrisy of the world to punish those lucky enough that never had to deal with the hardships of the world. He's the existential antipol, the punisher of ignorance and therefor the antihero, just like everyone else who dares stand up to the so called civilized people of the world.That is NOT the same think as being a ******* goof, who runs around and dances by himself to pretend the world isn't what it is. The real Joker is a hustler, a master of manipulation who knows exactly what he does at all times. He's smart, charismatic and on a never ending mission to make the world more honest with the pathological means he possesses. Not this other moron.

Review Title: Everything I want in a movie
Review: This movie has everything I want - good character development, a beautiful look and music that effortlessly propels the story along, genuine emotion that makes it shockingly relatable, and real meaning. Arthur Fleck's backstory gives Joker a sense of humanity that I like seeing in villain characters. He's not just some crazy psychopath, he's an actual person with thoughts and pains. He's real. And that's something that's carried over into the rest of the movie, as well. They made the movie feel like it's something that can actually happen. It's not overdone, it's not artificial, it's not pushed, it's just the story of some guy who felt distressed and unintentionally affected society. He had no out-of-this-world plan, that's actually just absurd if you think about it, to make a story. And the movie didn't have a plan to say anything about society. It's not political. It uses principles that are found in society to tell a good story, but it gives no call to action. And that realness, the raw storytelling, shows what it actually feels like to be someone like Arthur. It's truly artful.

Review Title: When Social Justice Becomes Stereotyped Exploitation
Review: The most insulting thing about this movie is that the writers clearly think that they are "bringing awareness" to mental illness, when in fact they are not only exploiting it but providing a grossly inaccurate portrayal of mental illness, ironically even making fun of it despite its shallow criticism of people who make fun of the mentally ill. I don't know exactly what type of mental illness Joaquin Phoenix is trying to mimic here, but there is no existing illness that is remotely similar to this. His acting comes across as somebody who has heard rumors about mentally ill people but never had any exposure to anybody with any form of mental illness. This is a step backwards in Hollywood's effort to capitalize off of stereotypes of "crazy" people, an ignorant, distasteful mockery even exceeding that of Dirty Harry. The fact that this film has received such positive reviews only shows just how far society really is from understanding and accepting mental illness.

it has a lot of poorly supported choices by characters that are just lazy.

It has been written about already a multitude of times, but the lengthy exposition on each prominent character draws you into the movie in a unique way. In addition to the drawn out character development, the musical direction plays a prominent role in pushing the story in a unique way- the score goes beyond the use of eerie ominous drones, and instead incorporates some of the background tunes on the Telly and Radio to invoke a deeper understanding for what the protagonist is feeling.

This wasn't it.

You won't actually be putting on a happy face while watching Joker, what you'll be doing instead is witness the greatest film of the year and the Oscar-worthy performance of Joaquin Phoenix. His performance is extraordinary, every single time you hear him laugh, you know something is wrong and you start to feel uncomfortable, add all that to his facial expressions and acting skills and you've got yourself a perfect performance that will be talked about for years to come. What this movie does to its viewers is fantastic, you're on the edge of your seat through all of its runtime which is about 2 hours. Joker is full of shocking scenes and so many surprises and it utilizes its R-rating very well. As we know this movie talks about mental illness and what it does to people and how it affects them specially when those people get abused or be made fun of, and Joker portrays this so perfectly that you even tend to sympathize with the main character, not that he is a good guy, he's not, he's the Joker after all, but by the way of how they portrayed this, you will be able to relate to this character and understand what he's going through so that by the time his story comes full circle and you see his character evolve to the clown prince of crime we all love to hate and hate to love, you'll be very satisfied and upset at the same time by how he becomes the Joker and it's all in a good way. Joker has quite the Easter eggs and references to other movies like the King of Comedy and Taxi Driver as the director Todd Phillips said that those two movies inspired him to do Joker, so you'll definitely feel some elements of those movies in here too. Talking about this movie without spoiling it is so difficult, but all i'll say is this: Joker is a drama masterpiece and it's not like any other comic book movie that's been made before, this is an original story that is based on the character "Joker" from DC comics but with a new and a deep origin story that is basically a character study that'll leave you wondering and thinking about how devastating it is by the time the credits start rolling.Verdict: Joker is one of those movies that after viewing, you will need to sit down and try to take it all in because it dives deep into what mental illness is and how it can affect people and how society can be a part of that transformation.

Review Title: Joker echoes the echanting spark that films once had
Review:
From catching that first glance of Joaquin Phoenix as the Joker a year ago, I have been painfully anticipating this movie month to month counting towards 2019's October (while also avoiding as best I could any early reviews, and the second trailer).The day arrived and what a day it has been! - JOKER 2019 is nothing short of OUTSTANDING! - a truly beautiful dark twisted film focused on the life of a very confused and lonely protagonist ... ahem antagonist, encapsulated and thrown around within a terrifying but gorgeous 80's Gotham set behind him wherever he may roam. Films like this DO NOT and WILL NOT come around often, so see it on the big screen.Pros: As a someone who can confidently say I am at this point in my life a seasoned cinephile first, and a movie watcher second, I was growing tired of most recent superhero movies and the seemingly safe cookie cutter movie making format used over the last 5 years or so.I prayed, I made my bet and I was relieved to see my horse win -- Gone are the quick cuts and rapid quippy one liners between foes or friends, gone are the 'sheathed characters, cities and worlds with souls of rubber' that never quite seem to be affected by a characters cause and effect. Gone too are the politically correct actions and statements peddling to each member of the audience - the film perhaps asks you to be offended and torn, and to sit and process it, without escaping - Bold film-making indeed.Here is a hark back to the true pre-blockbuster cinema of the 70's; there's the long shots and long takes, the moving music, loose, fun and unsaturated colors, the design, the conscious thoughtful speech, and no speech but guided emotion - the writing and the heart all melds together dangerously in an industrial vat of chemicals, with a good dash of that old school daemon, acting genius (and now older) - Robert De Niro we all new was still hiding under those direct to blu-ray and B-comedies of late.Mr. Phoenix's performance as Joker is almost comedically haunting - 'Arthur' is a man fed up, ready for empathy and wanting to give it. He is gracefully rage filled with laughter of deep sadness, and impressively thought out.
Much like the performance of the late Heath Ledger - The Joker is hard NOT to root for, even when he invites you to the front row for his grimmest of deeds.Todd Phillips's departure from directing his mostly great original comedies into a movie like this is surely a welcome surprise and only goes to show how far he has come as a serious director, while seemingly holding a mirror up to his animalistic 1993 documentary about societal pariah 'GG Allin'.Cons: This is a rare movie that I wanted to be a half hour LONGER rather than shorter!, that's it.
Just as we glimpse into his mind and go beyond, and as the Joker and Gotham are finding their nail-biting footing, and the city screams and cries for change - we are back in that confused quiet waiting room of Arthur Fleck's mind, plotting and scheming, wondering what the scene will be, when the end comes for us all.BATMAN 2021, please Mr. Phillips, Mr. Silver and Mr. Phoenix?

Review Title: An amazing collaboration- Todd Phillips and Joaquin Phoenix have really done it!
Review:
This was the first DC movie that I actually paid attention to and paid money to see. I did go into the cinema with high expectations after watching the teaser for the film. Already, Joaquin Phoenix had astonished me with his talent. It was within the first 10 minutes of the movie that had captured me.It is clear that writer, producer and director Todd Phillips should be credited for this as he kept the audience hooked from the beginning till the end.The way in which Arthur Fleck's life was portrayed was truly amazing storytelling and really took the audience to new lengths in explaining his real life story. Interestingly, Todd Phillips uses the struggling society and city of Gotham to reflect the physical and mental state of Arthur. In doing so, he explained contemporary anxieties and how society's actions impact our lives in terms of behaviour and how it makes us who we really are.From a young age, we are taught that there are heroes and villains. We are always told that the hero needs to defeat the villain and shouldn't be questioned because it is for the "greater good". However, we never really stopped to think why it is we have heroes and why we have villains in this world. Instead, we're immediately taught that villains correspond to being evil- that a villain should be punished by a hero. However, after watching the life story of Arthur fleck, is it actually correct to call him a "villain"?Should someone who has been so badly treated by a toxic society be labelled as a villain? Isn't it true of nature for someone to cry when they are upset? To laugh when told a joke? Actions do have consequences. This is simply the same way it is for Arthur fleck to criticise his society for kicking him when he was down- for pushing him away when he wanted him- for refusing to put on a happy face when all he wanted to do was to be truly happy when society didn't let him.So yes, Arthur may have done some things that make him fall under the category of a "villain", but who is the true villain?- him or society?After continuously being beat down and trampled on by society, Arthur fleck began consultation where he would receive medication and "support" from a therapist. In this way, it could be said that the medication Arthur was given, may have made his condition worse eg: depression/ anxiety. Aside from this, Arthur had a therapist who would simply "read lines from a script" instead of listening and actually helping him. This is part of the major issue in society whereby the people who are vulnerable and needy are pushed away by those who have power, even if it is only a little bit. People like Arthur are neither seen, nor heard and the only time they will be - when they do something that goes against the "rules of society" because "putting on a happy face" doesn't work for everyone.As the film progresses, Arthur is taken off the very little support he will have been given and stripped from his job. With nothing left, Arthur began hallucinating and suffering from psychosis- believing that things were real when they actually weren't- developing negative thoughts. All he has is "negative thoughts".Moving onto the acting in this movie...Joaquin Phoenix as the lead role was a brilliant decision made by Todd Phillips and other casting directors. It is vital that that a role such as JOKER should be played correctly, without a single fault- especially after Heath ledger's Oscar winning performance. Joaquin was nothing short of excellent. Utter perfection. Not a single fault in his acting. From breaking out into laughter to playing an emotionally and mentally wrecked character- Phoenix mastered it all. An Oscar Win is essential and exactly what he deserves. Every moment, every word spoken and every frame that was shot was done to perfection.By Saniya Khan

Review Title: Can you combine a powerful story with a deep drama in a comic book movie?
Review:
Normally, it helps me more to put DC or Marvel movies under a different category from other movies to be fair when I rate them, but this one was really on another level. A great script that gave us a deep story, well-organized chapters, superb acting performance and yes it was based on comics!
Even though it's a slow-paced movie, I didn't feel like there's a slow buildup in any chapters, which is not easy to avoid in these kinds of dark drama movies. Joaquin took the movie to another level, and it's really fair enough to say it's 'Joaquin's movie'. He really made every scene counted on the screen. I can't remember any scene was there just to help the story, not his character. Everything in the movie should be about him, and that's what he did.
When I watched the movie in the cinema, there were mixed emotions between the audience for most of the scenes. You don't know if you should laugh? or feel sad. These stressful situations were greatly made with the help of Joaquin's performance. He was always in control of these kinds of situations and when things require outsourcing support, the soundtrack comes in the right moment. Hildur made a great job by giving the soundtrack theme a character that I felt personally it's a little bit inspired by Hans Zimmer's masterpiece the Dark Knight, but with a more slow pace and dark feel.
I liked how during each chapter there were these scenes that look like some encaustic or painting to recap the joker personality changes.
Some people are saying the story is not 100% loyal to the comic, but what's wrong with that? Make a nice movie and implement all film success factors then I'm more than satisfied.
The only thing that I felt is not 100% complete after watching the movie for the second time is the last 20 min. I think it was necessary for an extra 15 or a maximum of 20 min for the last Joker personality transformation. But maybe the writer wanted to focus on what things that made the Joker as he is instead of the Joker himself. So yeah it's fine.
I know there are obvious ideas that can be reflected in other ones in the Taxi Driver movie, but it's really been used brilliantly. If someone watched the two movies and focused on the last Joker chapter, he will understand why I'm saying that.
It's really hard - without considering the comics' loyalty thing - to not give this film a full mark. It's been years since I watched a deep movie like this one.
I had a big question after I finished the movie, what's wrong in having a good script that leaves the freedom for actors to give a stunning performance in superhero movies? What's wrong with a good deep story instead of just counting on CGI? A lot of people are really starving for a well-written drama superhero movie. I hope Joker can help in this direction.

I am a person who never watches trailers nor reads reviews before seeing a movie. I am not immune to hearing what people/news say though. I did hear that this was a violent, disturbing, etc. movie. It is and it is not.
First of all, it is a gem of acting, producing, directing, camera work, and last - but not least - story line. There are scenes that make you cringe, but they are part of the story. I walked in thinking this will be one of those super-hero level movies where a lot of is happening, difficult to follow what's what and why, etc. It is not.
It is a story of a man.
Unhappy man.
A victim of how he was brought up, but more importantly - a victim of Gotham society.
Then... Joker is born. Comes out of the deepest hole filled with garbage we call humanity, and becomes a complete opposite of Good. What I take my hat off to is, first, the story. Humanity had multiple chances to avoid it... and it failed that man. What seemed to be a broken (but pure) soul, stuck in routine unhappy daily life - by our measurements, and just like in parallel universe, that soul found all its happiness is in a complete opposite spectrum of what we call Good.
Second, I take my hat off to Joaquin Phoenix. BRAVO, sir! BRAVO!! I will not insult the actor with my unskilled evaluation of one's acting, but to me that is an Oscar winning acting, which I don't see how it would be easy for anyone to beat. BRAVO, sir!! Review Title: Cinematic Gold and a Breath of Fresh Air
Review: Joker received so much attention before it even released that it was hard not to want to see what all the hype was about, even though I've been a fan of the Batman series for as long as I can remember and both Joaquin and River Phoenix are two of my favorite actors of all time. When you talk about films today, you rate them based on your overall opinion and perhaps one or two performances that were convincing enough to impress, and when you go to a comic book movie you expect action and adventure, special effects, etc. Joker has NONE of this. This was a true piece of cinematic ART. This is the type of movie thst all film school students dream of making one day. The cinematic quality, camera shots, editing styles, color pallette and sheer grittiness of the picture combined with an outstanding score that almost tells the story by itself are absolutely glorius. The writing is excellent and the story keeps you locked in from the very beginning watching this character fall from forced mediocrity stemming from mental illness and amplified by public oppression into sheer insanity. Phoenix delivers a mesmerizing performance that is as beautiful and poetic as it is tragic and painful to witness. This is top grade filmmaking folks. This represents the type of movie we desperately need more of in today's fractured and divided society. If more people watched and understood more films like this one, we might actually have a chance to evolve as a species instead of warring with one another over superficial petty nonsense being spit in our faces by those who constantly complain and who undoubtedly represent the vocal majority of those who hated this film before even seeing it and bashed it further after seeing it over the concepts that Joker explores. Best film of the year by far and Phoenix deserves an Oscar for his amazing performance. If you have not seen it in a theater, please do yourself a favor and try to catch it in one while you still can. It is MORE than worth it! 10/10 A++ top notch movie.

Review Title: As a viewer, this movie was Perfect and Phoenix is a living legend for his role in this movie.
Review:
Audiences, as we know, can't get enough of a bad guy. It is a concept everyone loves in a movie. The worse he acts, the more we stare. Realistically, it is not something to admire, but in movies we tend to do so. The Joker, directed by Todd Phillips, does a great job exploiting this common misconception in present day movie theaters. Joaquin Phoenix follows along and plays the character of the "Joker" perfectly. Many experts compare this movie to the "Dark Knight" because both movies are centered around the topic of violence. As soon as the Joker was released into theaters, it was an instant hit. This was because it successfully tied together the idea of violence and a sense of humor, including a plotline that is spot on.
First of all, Joaquin Phoenix, who serves as the Joker, suffers from extreme schizophrenia. He tends to laugh at the worst times and makes each scene more intense than it should be. Due to this, he gets made fun of from coworkers and random people off the street. It's not something he likes, but he has to deal with it. At times, he takes his anger out on the people and it is not a pretty sight. By the end of the movie, the Joker had killed 10-15 people. Unfortunately, that is a big part of why the movie was so successful. People tend to admire the hateful acts in this movie because it is centered around the idea of violence. Joaquin Phoenix takes his anger out on many people, but the most noticeable one was his mother and his 2 friends from work. In most movies this would be talked about as "disgusting or "cruel", but in this one it made the movie even better. Each one of them played a significant role in his depression because they would not support him during his toughest times. This aspect of the movie is heartbreaking, but it does a fantastic job highlighting the importance of support from friends and family. Due to his mental illness, he laughs uncontrollably and tends to do it at the worst times. Todd Phillips does a great job incorporating this into the movie because without it, the movie would be very different. The plotline fits perfectly with each moment and reaches new audiences, even if they have not seen it. The perfect involvement of violence and sense of humor fits perfectly with each other and glorifies the plot even more. Right from the start, we are brought into the "Joker's" world. Immediately, people start to make fun of him and the viewer can clearly see his downfall unfolding. The plot line is unique in the way that it jumps from scene to scene, not focusing on one for very long. This aspect of the movie keeps the viewers involved because they need to know what happens in each scene to follow along. Because of the violent aspects of the movie, experts compare it to the "Dark Knight." They can be compared to each other because of the extremity of violence that is involved all throughout the movies. I'd say the Dark Knight is more suitable for children just because it involves Batman and they tend to forget about his flaws pretty easily. The joker is is more harsh and shows the bad signs of a "killer clown."
To conclude my essay, I believe the perfect blend of bad guys and good guys make it a perfect movie. Audiences love bad guys because it catches their eyes and keeps them interested. This is a common flaw in american movies that can be easily abused by directors. In the end, the Joker successfully integrates the plot with the inclusion of violence and a small sense of humor.

Todd Phillips's interpretation of the Joker and Gotham City is my favorite representation I have seen. While I thoroughly enjoyed this film there were some issues I had with it. I thought that the movie had too long of a build-up, I felt like most of the movie I was just waiting for something to happen, but the story was laid out in a way that only allowed for excitement at the end. I would recommend allowing more opportunity to captivate and catch the audience early. Phillips directed and helped produce Joker and he did a great job of it. Joker was a big shift for Phillips from his cheesy comedies like the Hangover series. Casting the famous Robert De Niro and the relatively unknown Joaquin Phoenix was crucial for this film. After his amazing show of acting skill in Joker, Phoenix demonstrated that he has earned his place in future major acting roles. While costume design is often a forgotten part of films, Mark Bridges proves that costume design is important with his detailed work in Joker.
Arthur Fleck or as he is known later in the film "Joker", is a mentally unstable man living in the slums of Gotham City. Arthur's day job is a clown for hire and by night he is at home taking care of his mother and watching Murray Franklin who is the Jimmy Fallon of their time. One day Arthur gets fired from his clown job for misconduct during a performance at a children's hospital. Getting fired from his job mixed with his mother having health issues sends Arthur into a downward spiral. Arthur goes off his medication for his mental illness and starts to lose his sanity, believing that his life is no longer a tragedy, but a comedy.
The main cause of Arthur's situation is the current conditions in Gotham City. There is a big divide between the rich and the poor. The poor are left to watch as their public services get slashed and there living conditions deteriorate quickly. The tension in the city is as high as ever and the poor are ready to riot at the drop of a pin. Three Wallstreet bankers are shot and killed on the subway by a mysterious clown. People believe that this is a purposeful statement, and start to dress like clowns and riot throughout the city.
Todd Phillips did a very good job directing this film. It was a big turn around from his previous films such as the hangover series. His expedition of directing and writing a phycological thriller was a huge success for him. I think this film established him as a serious director that has earned respect in the industry and demonstrated that he can direct award-winning movies. Also, he shot one of the most famous scenes in modern film on the stairs in New York City.
The acting in this movie is what really sets it apart from other Joker movies and captivates audiences. Joaquin Phoenix really demonstrated his acting abilities in Joker. From the start of the film, you could tell how much time Phoenix put into getting ready for this film. Arthur as a character really changed and developed throughout this film and I think that it was because of the way that Joaquin Phoenix represented him, making his emotion come to life. I think that this display of acting proves Joaquin Phoenix's skills and shows why he deserves an Oscar for his performance.
Costumes and makeup were a huge part of this film. The whole movie revolved around the clown face, it was the main theme of the movie that brought people together and gave Joker his identity. For these reasons, it was crucial that the film had a good makeup and costume department, and they very much succeeded in this. The art department was able to give Arthur (Joaquin Phoenix) so many different looks. It started him off as a sad-looking clown for hire that was down on himself, and throughout the movie transformed his look as Arthur transformed as a character, making his costume always match where he is in the movie. Also, there were so many clowns they had to differentiate Joker from all the other, which they did.
I went into Joker not expecting to enjoy the movie as much as people told me I would because creepy mind twisting movies arent what I like. That being said Joker turned out to be one of my favorite movies, the main thing that caused me to love it is the acting. Joaquin Phoenix's performance as Joker is one of the best displays of acting I have ever seen. Phoenix has such a convincing, emotional, and captivating that this movie could have been a documentary about a mentally unstable clown. I would highly recommend this movie to anyone, it is something that is so good it can be enjoyed by any type of moviegoer.

On a movieIt is commonly clear that screens are of the products designed for the mass market such as blockbusters or franchises, as well as non-standard films with a narrower focus. To somehow separate these two phenomena, many cultural figures often resort to the terms "commercial" and "author" cinema.The classification gradually transformed, was refracted by various film critics and cinematographers, which ultimately led to the formation of an ominous image of a commercial film - a film end-to-end designed for profit. As a rule, it has a universal scenario, accessible to everyone, unified visual form and entertaining emotions for the viewer who came to watch a commercial movie in the theater to spend the time with fun.If the concept of profit-oriented commercial cinema appears in the coordinate system, it is logical to assume that financial success turns into an important criterion when defining a film in one or another "camp". The situation seems simple when it comes to "Avengers" or "Fast and Furious": a one-chord plot combined with a simplified movie language and billions at the box office. It is precisely on such examples that the idea of classification into authors and businessmen rests.But what about examples that are not so clear? "Joker" by Todd Philips cost only $70 million and brought in a billion at the box office. The Joker's laugh is still hearable as an echo in manifold cinemas around the globe. However, the script is notable for its complex psychologism and references to Scorsese's "Taxi Driver", and directing demonstrates masterful work with the actor, a characteristic visual solution and a love for the New York streets typical of the director. It is no doubt that a huge part was brought here by people familiar with DC, Joker, Batman and superhero movies. I will not take into account this part and concentrate on the mass market's role.Does "Joker" belong to the commercial cinema by virtue of its huge profits or does it retain the status of an author's project thanks to the means of artistic expression? Does the engagement of the mass market basis only on the entertainment stamps and features of the commercial movies or it could be found from something different?On the movieWhat makes Joker laugh? With no doubt, it is fair to say its face and story. The acting method of the Joaquin Phoenix that performs the role of Arthur Fleck (the Joker) is radical - it not only transforms physically but surrenders to the hero completely and plunges into his life and feelings.What is this story? This story is a fantasy. Sick, dark and personal. The way its story presented on the screen is the way the character of Joaquin Phoenix, Arthur Fleck interprets it for himself. His vision of the world does not differ from reality. His world is a reality. That is what he claims and that is what a viewer sees when watching the movie for the first time. The cut of the film despite the usual cinematography methods does not highlight this at all to penetrate viewer to the world of Joker in both direct and indirect meaning. It can only be caught via inconspicuous elements such as color correction bringing the character's emotions or a music sound ambiance accompaniment. By the end of the movie the reality that was presented in it, dark, smoked & sick, fears with its hopelessness. And it makes you fear more when released this fantasy makes you astonished of how deep and dark can be the inner world of a sick person and instills a mysterious awareness of what happened in the real-life of Arthur. Of course, if Arthur is a man shown in the white rooms of the hospital.And here we come to the second motive that makes this smoky black and sour colorful smack of the movie which is hopelessness. Every time a viewer sees that it can not be more worth it, it is. The rise and fall of the hero in this film are moved through the painful theme of hopelessness. The heroine of a single mother performed by Zazie Beetz is a direct symbol of hope in the film and the hope of Arthur himself that the world can be good and kind. Kindness and hope are what Arthur needs. Her presence in difficult moments for him e.g. at the stand-up or in a hospital showed that the cure was a ray of light of one for whom he matters.The hero seems to be striving for her throughout the first part of the film, in particular, we understand this when finding out that she was only part of this fantasy. This gives us food for thought that it is possible when everything is over, he will burst in, as he wanted to give her a hot kiss as if rewarding her for living in his imagination all this time and giving him hope. And if through the veil of his illusions, this light appeared to him, which even makes his illness disappear for a moment it means that Arthur has still existed. However, this was not destined to happen - so we get into the world of the Joker, the black where hope exists not.Sum it upWhat makes Joker laugh? The division into commercial and author's cinema is rather untenable than vice versa. This classification is more suitable to confuse everyone. But if it is incorrect, what classification should be used? This is a big question. For any other classification is faced with its mass of contradictions. The combination of Joker's fantasy and centralized Joker's character performed by the brilliant acting play of Joaquin Phoenix defines the movie as a great balance between commercial and author's movies. There are commercial elements such as Batman character franchising and the potential of creation of the universe from the character of Zazi Bitz that apparently could be a perfect Harley Quinn in a real-world out of Joker's fantasy. There are author's features such as twisted, art-house vibes, smoky hopeless atmosphere and unusually created world. It is impossible to distribute everything smoothly into genre movies - exceptions will constantly appear.The reality of the creative process is much more complex and diverse than even the most sophisticated classification can offer. Maybe we should hang up labels less and pay more attention to practice?

Review Title: ONE OF THE BEST MOVIES I'VE SEEN THIS YEAR
Review: I'm a really big fan of Joker ever since I was a kid. Heck, I even rooted for him over Batman countless times. And the thing I love most about Joker is his personality. That certain characteristic we all condemn in real life but love in secret. His unrelenting perseverance in creating anarchy, chaos, and more problems for Batman. I myself wouldn't want Joker wreaking havoc happen in real life, but seeing him do it in comics and movies makes me feel somewhat relieved. It feels like all my pent-up anger and emotions are released with whatever mischief Joker brings about. That's how powerful Joker is. He brings to life all our emotions, feelings, and probably our worst and darkest imaginations. He epitomizes "freedom" in a certain way that's both horrible and wonderful, and we love him for it.This brings us Todd Phillips' Joker who is magnificently and superbly given life to by the one and only Joaquin Phoenix. The story revolves around Arthur Fleck, a downtrodden man who erupts into uncontrollable laughter at the most inappropriate moments. As the film progresses, the audience learns that his outbursts are the symptom of a brain injury. And while the script never names the Joker's disorder, it's based on a real-life medical condition called pseudobulbar affect.Pseudobulbar affect (PBA) is characterized by frequent, involuntary bouts of crying, laughter, or other emotional displays, which are exaggerated or disconnected from the individual's actual emotional state. It's most commonly caused by brain injuries or neurological disorders that impact how the brain processes emotion.Anyway, the story progresses and will lead you to one of the best character developments I've seen in movies so far. I won't elaborate any further as that would defeat the purpose of you guys watching the film. But I'd like to say that you would get mixed emotions while watching and as the story ends, THE HYPE GETS REAL. YOU WON'T REGRET IT.

Review Title: Dark, gripping, and compelling...a must-see film
Review: Joker is the first DC movie I have watched. This is an incredibly dark, disturbing, and even depressing film, yet it resonates with so much truth that it's truly heartbreaking. It was stunningly executed and brilliant. As much as it horrified and saddened me, it equally fascinated me and kept me intrigued and emotionally invested. It's plain to see why Joaquin Phoenix received an Oscar for his portrayal of Arthur Fleck in this film - he bloody well earned it.This film hits home on an astounding number of levels. Arthur Fleck tried, repeatedly, for so long to do the right thing, to be what society deems a decent person. Sadly, his efforts proved to be the definition of futility. He navigated obstacles, setbacks, and failures, each slowly degrading his spirit and robbing him of hope. It's like he was forced to endure death by a thousand cuts, but each of these defeats and losses served to erode his soul, his humanity, until there was nothing left.In many ways, this film is an incredible example of art imitating life. First, there is the stigma surrounding anything involving mental health and those who suffer with such afflictions. Society's herd mentality leads to those with mental health conditions to be shunned and ostracized, and for what? Because 'normal' individuals have been conditioned to fear and dismiss what they do not understand and to reject anyone who is incapable of conforming to societal standards and expectations.Arthur makes a comment about how everyone feels so sorry for the three individuals who were killed on the train, yet Arthur himself remains invisible. The same Gotham citizens who expressed outrage over the loss of those three lives would simply step over his dead body, were it lying on the sidewwalk. This feeling of invisibility is relatable to all individuals who have been marginalized by society. To me, it speaks toward social justic movements such as the BLM protests, and, dare I say, even the riots. (I do not condone rioting, but can understand the palbable frustration of following traditional avenues and appropriate channels, and yet your voice remains unheard and you remain invisible).Due to Arthur's mental health issues, it is difficult to discern whether certain events in the film are actually occurring or if they exist only in his mind. This aspect builds a suspense and uncertainty in a way that keeps the audience guessing and increases their emotional investment in both the film as a whole and Arthur as an individual. From dealing with the dumpster fire of events that daily life continued tossing his way and his absolute train wreck of a mother, it's little wonder that Arthur's already fragile psyche finally snapped.If, by the time you finish watching Joker and cannot find it in yourself to be empathetic and more understanding to the Arthurs of the world, then you are part of the problem.
One thing for sure, this movies's gonna stuck in me for very long time.

Review Title: A haunting masterpiece that makes you question the meaning of your life?
Review: My wife and I got to see a sneak preview of The Joker last night here in Thailand. All I can say is WOW! Hands down the greatest acting performance and perhaps movie I've ever seen. Do not listen to the "safe space" critics that think this movie is a giant dog whistle for Donald Trump. This movie is a masterpiece in the same league as Taxi Driver. The movie received a standing ovation here in Thailand. Considering that most of the audience was reading subtitles, that's pretty amazing.This Joker movie embodies the ethos of "cheerful nihilism" / "Clown World". Clown World is the idea that the world is becoming more and more like a grotesque freakshow, with degeneration on various fronts becoming worse (social, political, racial, etc.). Instead of bearing the emotional burden of what some believe is the multi-faceted downturn of society, "honk honk" "Put on your smiley face" "Why so serious?" represents the option of cheerful nihilism, where one acknowledges the world's absurdity but decides to laugh and make fun of it. "Why get riled up when none of it matters anyways?" "I thought my life was a tragedy, then I realized it was a comedy" says the Joker.This movie really makes you think about life and it's meaning. Whether or not Trump is the Joker is for you to decide. Definitely go into this movie with your thinking cap on. This isn't your typical mindless superhero flick designed for low IQ audiences.

Todd Phillips is clearly trying to pay tribute to the film legend that is Martin Scorsese. However, in doing so he has created a movie that only really functions as a mashed together mess. It takes from him (music, story, look), it isn't influenced by his work (like Todd Phillips was ranting about how he was influenced by classics like Taxi Driver and The King of Comedy). This isn't Logan which had very clear influences to Westerns but still held its own as a great film. This isn't The Dark Knight which clearly drew influences from Heat. This is a phoney director trying to mark somebody elses much better work as his own for a modern audience and honestly I find it completely despicable.
Joker is a good film, maybe a great one but the best of the decade? I'm not too sure if copying something that came out 30/40 years really means it deserves these acolades
The one thing I hope people will do after this movie is try, just try and watch some classics from Scorsese and DeNiro; Watch Taxi Driver then watch King of Comedy, please. I promise, as an anonymous internet user that watching these films will change your views completely on this film. The 2 of them have much more going for them and you'll see very clearly how Todd Phillips, the man behind some moderate but not ultimate successes such as The Hangover trilogy, Old School and War Dogs was able to create what some are calling 'the best film of the decade' (he cheated)

Review Title: Not your average comic book movie
Review:
I should preface this review by saying that I'm a comic book collector and comic book movie fan; so I was wary going into this film after the questionable choices made in Warner Bros. recent cinematic outings with Batman.
I had nothing to worry about; the movie was engaging and engrossing from start to finish.
Everyone talks about Joaquin Phoenix's performance and with good reason. His portrayal of a downtrodden, broken man on a self-destructive path is compelling, intense and yet beautifully nuanced.
There have been many comparisons to Taxi Driver, which I had heard before going into the cinema and the comparisons do hold up. The story, from the start to the end, has strong parallels to Taxi Driver and stands up well as a similarly bleak cautionary tale of a man driven past his limits.
The cinematography and music both work to elevate what is already a fantastic film to the level of high art. Hildur Guðnadóttir's score is dark and haunting, and in certain scenes (the dance in the dank public toilet, in particular) serves to reflect and amplify the emotions of Phoenix's Joker.
I don't often feel the urge to write a longwinded review that exceeds my abilities as a writer, but Joker is the kind of film that inspires that in me.

After the first 20 minutes, I was highly tempted to walk out. Yes, it was going deep in establishing character. I support that 100%. Too many movies these days forget to set up character. Character development must happen so we care and invest. So many new flicks go to CGI and action forgetting about character which makes those movies so boring.Not this movie! It went old skool.But this character was so sad, so objectionable, so dour, so real and not entertaining that it felt like I was in the middle of an old-style mental hospital. It's just not something I choose to do on my free time. But in deference to the hype, I stayed to find out if there was something more that I was missing. Was there?Joaquin Phoenix was brilliant as always. I love all of his work. In my view, his menacing disturbing portrayal of Commodus in GLADIATOR (2000) made the movie. His Johnny Cash in WALK THE LINE (2005)? Excellent! And my favorite; Joaquin as Abe Lucas in IRRATIONAL MAN (2015).His JOKER was gross, deathly skinny, leathery, sweaty, very sickly, sad and uncomfortable.The job of an actor is to make you feel they are the character. And he did that magnificently. The weight he had to lose to make this work had to be dangerous. He should win top awards; probably an OSCAR unless Leo DeCaprio or Rami Malik pop out some gems between now and December.JOKER was very 70s; perfectly staged reminding us that GOTHAM aka New York City was a gross, filthy, drug invested, tenement ladened place back in the day. Very Serpico! The colors were perfect. The cinematographer used a perfect filter to give it that proper look. The red JOKER costume and his daywear were made from perfect 70s material.So yeah, retro fans who wallow in nostalgia will love the settings and costumes. It will remind them of TAXI DRIVER (1976). But I was there back in the 70s, it was NOT pretty or cute. It was the Mean Streets back then. It was horrible; a perfect setting for JOKER and the madness that followed.I think the best part of the movie was the end. You knew it was going to get worse and it did. The scene when JOKER appears on the talk show with DeNiro was very disturbing.Frankly, it is so disturbing that I will NOT be surprised if some nut job takes a cue and does something terribly similar. Joker was made to be a society ANTI-HERO and that is very appealing to those who are lost in a supermarket.All in all, while the movie itself is a good film and Joaquin Phoenix is great, but I would have preferred to spend my buck on something more entertaining and less real; especially given the climate of mental illness and gun use in America. It just made me sick.So forgive me if I don't applaud this film as entertaining. It was not. It was a treatise into madness and anger giving context to why JOKER is so crazy in the latter times of Gotham. In fact, there are NO memorable lines that stuck with me except "I think it sucked"; which is what I said leaving the theatre.

Review Title: Not what you're expecting, but not in a good way
Review:
I've had this movie on my watchlist for a year and, as a fan of the comics, cartoons and movies, I couldn't wait to see it. But after seeing it, I was a bit disappointed.What did I like about the movie:
*Great acting. Joaquin's performance is so good, it's a bit worrying...
*The style of filming fits perfectly with the story and manages to give you that feeling of mystery, sadness, cringing and chaos as you would expect in a movie about the Joker.
*There have been movies that absolutely nailed it when it comes to use of music/audio. Movies where the sound just perfectly compliments the scene. I can't say that that was the case here throughout the movie, but there were certainly some moments that were made unforgettable due to the good use of audio.
*the movie has a very powerful ending. I won't spoil it, but as a fan, it definitely put a smile on my face.What I didn't like about the movie:
*there was one thing I really missed in this movie, and that was the truly dark side of the Joker. Although the movie has greatly managed to take a character of fiction and make him realistic, I believe it also took away the true villain. Throughout the movie I was on the edge of my seat, waiting for the moment that we would finally see the Joker become a truely dark and twisted man. No logic, just crazy evil and out of control. And for some brief moments, I think I caught a glimpse. But if only we got to see a bit more of that. The final transformation after which the connection with the character turns into something dark that no one could explain or relate to anymore. It was right there, but we didn't get to see it.*there doesn't seem to be much connection with the Batman stories or characters. If you're making a movie about the Joker, you (in essence) need to set out how a man turns from zero to a confident psychotic manipulative criminal mastermind that is aimed at killing Batman and creating chaos in Gotham, because in the end, that is who the Joker is. In this movie however, the Arthur Fleck is (even in the end) a sick, weak, old, unstable, insecure and sometimes just depressing person, who unwillingly managed to create some chaos and seems to have no motivation for anything. That is not the Joker at his finest.All in all, I would definitely recommend any fan to go see this movie. If you're not a fan, the movie might seem more like an intense, realistic and sad documentary of how a man goes mad... and you should only go see it if you're into that.
