Todd Phiillips' Joker is both an outstanding mentally-ill-disable-clown-turned-accidental-villain movie and a disastrous Joker movie.Arthur Flecks, lacks all the wit and geniality that's able to win over Batman from time to time, no evil mastermind in sight.Joaquin Phoenix is amazing given physicality to the character but falls short giving him an The kind of emotional backbone that was brought by Jack Nicholson's whimsicality or Heath Ledger's insightfulness.Todd Phillips makes his point as a drama director but misses all the marks when constructing Joker's motivation and evolutions, he takes the easy road of madness for the sake of madness to give ground to the story.Among the most annoying things on the film: Phillips try to simulate a period piece removing all technology elements (except costumes and cars) ala Gotham but at the end he moves the plot forward using an artifact only plausible on the digital age. The gratuitous insertion of the Wayne family inside Gotham's and Arthur narrative just a as fan servicing device.The movie's after taste is Phillips got so attached to his lead that he couldn't gather the courage to let Joker take him to the levels of evil he was supposed to reach.With all and all, if you forget this is related to Batman, this is a very enjoyable movie (we might have to use this advice again with Pattinson).

Forget about Marvel's summer blockbusters: Joker is not a superhero (or supervillain) flick.
It is a love letter to 1970s' and Martin Scorcese's cinema, and more especially The King of Comedy (1982), whose script Joker draws heavily upon. I strongly advise viewers to watch the two films one after the other to appreciate the influence Scorcese had on Phillips. You just have to consider these two films as twins, Joker being the deformed, nevrotic sibling of The King of Comedy.
Phillips' movie also presents an economic and social panorama of the end of 1970s America - although some might say this comment may still be true nowadays.
Phoenix is incredible: his performance is a real tour de force, an Oscar-winning one.
Of course, one could point out one or two flaws in the film, but overall Joker is the masterpiece everyone was waiting for.

Review Title: There is a hero in this movie, and his name is Joaquin Phoenix
Review: I came into this movie with high hopes. Reviews from critics at this point are mostly positive and fans seem to be in a craze over this film.This film really shines with Joaquin's stellar performance. His ability to convey Arthur's psychotic transition from a schizophrenic man who's life has been an entire to becoming the Joker was truly remarkable. For that alone, this movie is worth watching.Where this movie falls flat is in the first half. With Arthur's character properly cemented roughly 35-45 minutes into the movie, the writers keep the pre-transitioned character from making that leap that would change Gotham forever. Scenes become dragged along, Arthur seems to be stuck in this unnecessary loop of battling his demons and his fate, and ultimately, we see a lot more of Arthur rather than Joker in this movie... maybe a little too much.I'm convinced that if ANYONE else would've taken on this role, this movie would've been a huge lack of vision and execution from the writers.What separates Joaquin's acting from anyone's that I've ever seen take on a similar role's that he was able to be relatable in an odd manner. Feeling unheard, alone, lied to and forgotten by society's a battle that many face and we can all relate to Arthur's struggles in some way or another. You empathize with his battles but remain shocked by the switch that flips inside of him.I know that a lot of people would say that I'm perhaps crazy for only giving this a 7 out of 10, but aside from Joaquin's acting and some good cinematic scenes, this movie was 30+ minutes too long or 30+ minutes of irrelevancy. It wasn't perfect, but Joaquin truly was as close to perfection in terms of performance.Good cinematics, amazing acting, and decent writing.Go and enjoy this movie in theaters but it'll be equally as enjoyable at-home when it's released.

Review Title: Best Film I've Seen in Years
Review:
The people who didn't like this film are the people who expected it to be something it isn't.This isn't a Marvel film. There isn't much action, it is rarely humorous, and it's primary objective isn't to keep you entertained. I wouldn't call it a superhero (or villain) film at all, even though it's set in Gotham city, and we follow the man who becomes the Joker. This is the type of film that holds a mirror up to society and we are encouraged to take an uncomfortable look at ourselves.
Anyone who has worked with, or studied people with mental illness, will find that this film rings incredibly true. This isn't about one event that triggers Athur's fall. This is about how trauma, abuse, familial mental illness, poverty and social isolation can create an incredibly toxic environment which leads to mental illness and even violence. As Arthur wrote in his journal: "The worst part of having a mental illness is people expect you to behave as if you don't". Society rejects those who are strange. We isolate them, laugh at them, ostracize them. And then we take no responsibility when these people come to hate the society that surrounds them, or when they might take extreme measures to feel visible. It's not a comfortable conversation, no one wants to sympathise with monsters. But monsters aren't born, they're created. Joker demonstrates perfectly how social rejection and isolation can take mental instability from bad to dangerous, and how a more compassionate society, with better mental health services could lead to less violence.
Joker is one of the best films I've seen in years. It is beautifully made and Phoenix is incredible as Arthur/Joker. But more importantly, this film is trying to say something that really needs to be heard.

I have mixed feelings about Joker. From an acting perspective, Joaquin Phoenix did an amazing job by delivering the story in a way where the audience can be fully immersed.
However, this isn't a movie you can watch and feel good about it afterwards. The movie forces the audience to recognize a lot of the ugly parts of modern human society. It focuses on the mistreatment of people with mental health issues, the lack of support for these individuals, and the disparity between the rich and the poor. These are topics most people try to ignore in their everyday life because we lack the answers. This film brings forth the darkness in society that we try to ignore and that is why I feel uncomfortable watching it.
I also find the revolutionary message for the poor to fight against the rich coupled with the violence in this movie to be a dangerous theme. It immediately made me think about the current events in Hong Kong, where things are already very unstable. It truly only takes 1 mentally unstable individual to take on the role of "Joker" to turn the protests into a full blown violent revolution. It also made me think about the wealth inequality in the states. I fear that this film may be the catalyst that will push an individual, who is on the fence, into committing an act of terror. The lack of social support for the mentally ill, coupled with lax gun control laws in the states make this fear of mine very probable. Perhaps I am just overthinking it and I truly hope that I am, otherwise this film will have a lot of unintentional consequences.
In the end, I still recommend watching this film. If not for the thought provoking story line, go for Joaquin's stellar performance. Either way, don't expect walking away from this film feeling good like any other superhero movie.

Review Title: Joker may very well be the way back to good movies
Review: This movie may have hit me many times harder than the average person, mostly because I dealt with depression for over a decade. Some of Arthur's depressive statements hit me right into my core.For me, watching Joker was not easy. It was disturbing and reminiscent of some of the feelings and despair I was familiar with so I even experienced physical discomfort in the form of pain in my chest. When the movie was over, I told this to my friend, who has never experienced depression or any mental illness, and he said that he felt mental and physical perturbation, too.Having said all that, Joker is a gem of a movie. Right up there with my all-time favorites but I couldn't call it my #1 favorite for the simple reason that I don't see replay value in it since it's such a hard watch (unlike Wolf of Wallstreet or Heat which I've watched dozens of times).Joker is, in my opinion, technically and artistically perfect. This movie was a breath of fresh air just when I thought Hollywood was too woke to ever make good movies again. I really hope, and I think it will, make a precedent after audience response has been taken into consideration.What is most amazing about Joker is that it's absolutely non-pretentious or commercial; it feels as a pure art form, and art is not supposed to be necessarily beautiful, but to make you experience deep emotions.10/10

I absolutely loved Heath ledger's Joker in the Dark knight movie. I was fine with the concept of a psychopath doing crazy stuff because his focus was on the object of his obsession, Batman. But Joker however, disturbed me a little. The reason being that the movie is trying to justify glorifying the character. The movie and the evolution of Joker from a mild mannered Arthur Fleck combined with the incredible acting was simply amazing.I was certainly able to identify with some aspects of the movie and see how closely our current society resembles Gotham in the movie. For example, people being rude when Arthur was being respectful and people being dismissive because of his awkward and weird behavior. I was especially angry when bullies take advantage of his mild mannered personality on a regular basis. However, that is where my issues with the movie begin.I am more than ok when a person retaliates and fights bullies. But, I am not ok when some personal incidents are used as a valid reason to start attacking the society in general. Yes, society can be bad and cruel at times, but it does not justify killing everybody that fall into similar categories based on societal definitions. I am not ok with categorizing all rich people as bad and all poor people as the ones being taken advantage of. Because it can be translated to any situation we want and can be used as justification for racism, sexism, nationalism and literally any other scenario we want. It is like saying just because a couple of rabid dogs bit me, I will now categorize all dogs as rabid. I can appreciate the acting and the movie itself but I can't appreciate the concept.

This film is a emotional roller coaster, that's for sure, it's a horrifying psychological drama that has one of the best character development ever but it has this one flaw: it's based on the Joker from comic books. Don't get too worked up, I'll explain as following:Joaquin Phoenix once stated that this film is *loosely* based on the comics. And that is 100% accurate. He made me feel almost all the negative feelings that one person can feel except for one: hate.The Joker from the comics transpire hatred, he is pure evil, evil at is very essence. I couldn't feel this from Joaquin Phoenix's interpretation. I often felt sad, sorry and mainly pity from this Joker.If you can remove the references to DC Comics Universe like Gotham City and the Wayne Family, this film would have been perfect - you could keep the main character being called "The Joker" even. The only thing that kept it from being perfect it's because it's based on the comics and because it is loosely based on those.Just a piece of my mind now, for the Extended DCU in the movies, I'd much prefer Jared Leto's Joker. I fail to see with people disliked his performance. He couldn't even get a decent screen time. The very little we could see from him was perfect. I could feel that insane hatred pouring from him.All in all, if you can get passed this *based on comic books thingy* this movie is a master piece and Joaquin Phoenix gave a brilliant performance from a tragic, bizarre, grotesque and haunting delusional person.I just hope WB and DC don't get things mixed up.

Review Title: Extremely heavy and depressing, with no real storyline.
Review: 'Joker' was an absolutely mesmerising experience, there's no doubt about that. The cinematography was exceptional and allowed the viewer to perceive the gritty reality of society from joker's perspective as an outcast. On top of that, the acting on Joaquin's part really made you question whether or not the actor was genuinely taking inspiration from the character as the severely broken vigilante antagonist, as for moments at a time you completely forget that you're not watching a real life depiction of Arthur Fleck.Unfortunately that pretty much encapsulates the entire film. The storyline wasn't really present in my opinion, only a frame-by-frame journey of maybe a month passing in joker's life. No sense of revenge or justice is felt on joker's part by the end of the film, only feelings of sympathy and depression. Furthermore, for the entire two hours nothing lightens the mood as only a melancholy undertone with consecutive heart wrenching scenes defines the film.

Review Title: Ordinary Film backed by a Extraordinary Performance
Review: Think of what you always thought Joker's origin story was, I will give you a second to think, Exactly right that's the story of this film. All the layers of beautifully haunting cinematography and a score feels like a character in itself backed with a performance that is going to haunt me for the rest of my life doesn't excuse the fact that Todd Philips really pulls of a Joker here. He resorts to the most basic tools to justify the actions of one of the most complicated villian of all time.Todd mentioned in interviews most of the screenplay was re-written on the fly and you can feel that disjoint to a point that this film has 3 climaxes. Instead of crafting a story Arc which went from how Arthur became Joker it feels like ok so this Joker now let's work backwards and see how Arthur can be. Citing The King Of Comedy and Taxi Driver as an inspiration is one thing and pushing your story to go there is completely other and that's where Todd fails miserably on his rich but. He crafts a story that at the core of it is completely hollow, uninteresting, cliched and has nothing to say.I give it 5 stars all of which is cos of what Joaquin did, it's one thing emersing yourself in a role and it's a completely different thing just baring your soul and that's only wish the writers and director had that soul.Joker is like a big birthday present that you open and there's another box and then another and after you open all of them there's nothing inside and you make a fool of yourself and that's exactly how Joker made me feel.

Review Title: A sensitive, artistic movie, above all
Review: It has perfect cinematography, excellent music, great script, magnificent direction and superior performances of the actors (yes, Phoenix shines more than ever) makes this not only the best and most mature comic-book film ever, but one of the greatest films in cinema. I could never imagined that the director of some of the most forgettable -and shallow themed- movies ever had it in him to make a deep and emotional film like this one. Yes, it's a homage of Scorsese and the 70's movies, but I think that it takes those influences and makes them his own, in his own world, in his own mood. I think that the 1 star reviews that expected some other movie or wanted some comic-based movie are missing the point. This is A Joker, and this is HIS Story. Period. You don't review a movie for what's not, but for what it really IS. So: see it and enjoy it for what it is, a movie in its own universe.

Review Title: The best DC film since Green Lantern, you're welcome Canada.
Review: JOKER is dark, violent, astonishing, mind blowing and an absolutely riveting piece of art. 10 mins into the film and you know you are in for a magnificent treat. It's beautifully shot, crisply directed and amazingly scored. I personally never found it dull even for a second and it kept me on the edge of my seat throughout.As many would already know, JOKER takes a lot of inspiration from 2 Martin Scorsese directed films in particular, namely TAXI DRIVER and THE KING OF COMEDY. If you've seen both, you should be able to recognize the similar elements, patterns and themes shared by them.Joaquin Phoenix was at his literal best every single frame, as if it was a tailor made role for him. His expressions, his way of talking, laughing, walking, running, dancing, everything he did was purely ravishing. Ive always considered him one of the best actors of this generation, and he never fails to win over my heart. He is definitely the best performer of the year so far, at least for me.I walked into the theatre with high expectations, and walked out with goosebumps all around. The end was stunning and I couldn't ask for more. This is DC at its finest, this is DC at its darkest, this is exactly what DC fans have been waiting to cheer for, for a long long time. The best DC live action film of this decade. Todd Phillips and Co. have created a masterpiece which easily makes it to the league of the best CBMs' ever.10/10.

Review Title: The Joker of a real depressing World but not the Joker we all love and embrace.
Review: First ever review. Totally understood what the director was trying to get across in a realistic, working class gradual breakdown of a man with severe mental issues and issues with reality. The constant laughter (which he had down to a tee), as a symptom of his narcissistic delusions and psychological breakdown made perfect sense, and the fact he was told this was a problem, and he realised that he should embrace his dark side to move forward with savage consequences. This was what you would expect of the Joker, however that is where the similarities end.There was no signs of the genius, charisma and humour that the Joker emblazons in the antihero we adore, the ruthless serial killer, and demonic icon that we have all come to love and applaud. Phoenix was very good, but needed to show the devilish beast that the Joker is. I found myself feeling sorry for Arthur rather than wanting him to teach them a lesson in tormenting the wrong man. Of course the acting was very good as you would expect from Mr Phoenix. However i cannot see how he would go up against the genius of Batman/Bruce Wayne if there was to be a sequel....???I know it's not a Comic book film, but that is what enables the Joker to be what he should be.

Joker is a character study of troubled comedian Arthur Fleck, from his earlier attempts in establishing a career in comedy, to the rise of his inner dark persona.The bleak tone of the film is set since its very first sequence, using a slowly moving camera at times and hand held one at others, the long shots follow the seemingly uncalculated movements of Joaquin as he portrays one of the most fascinating characters to hit the big screen.When a movie as massive but mostly as praised as Joker comes out, it is not hard to fall in love with it, but it is easier to hate it on the grounds that it did not meet the high expectations. Joker is not only a reimagination of a loved villain, but also a reinvention of its genre. Breaking the classic storytelling process viewers are used to in comic-based productions. It is funny, chaotic and devastating, and the ideal way to experience would be expecting nothing and getting lost in its sombre universe.

It has no
connection to any of the DC films that have come before it.

six weeks. And the divide between the "haves" and the "havenots"

Review Title: Believe what you read - this movie is next level!
Review: I'm going to be honest. I didn't really have any expectations when entering this movie. I had known of Joaquin Phoenix, however hadn't seen any of his movies (although my friends commended his acting highly). Not only am I impressed with this movie, but I don't think I will ever truly be able to get over how good it is. This movie is dark, it's twisted and it shows the affects of deteriorating mental health on a human being, especially when thrust into certain unfortunate situations one after the other. As someone who has studied media for well over five years, I can confidently say that the cinematography, the score, the directorial and acting choices, the story line are all incredibly strong in this movie, and it deserves nothing but praise. All of these elements combined create such a poetry within the world of the film.Despite its criticisms, the choice to portray mental illness in such a way remains very authentic. (As someone who suffers from multiple illnesses described in this movie, I can vouch for this). It's often films will glamorize mental illness and portray it as cliche almost. I am incredibly happy that we finally have a film that accentuates the pure torture a mental illness has on a human being, and when being unable to access appropriate methods of mental aid, you begin to understand the Joker and his motivations.I encourage anyone who is a movie goer, PLEASE do yourself a favor and see this movie. It hits every single mark in every single aspect of its production.

Review Title: Joker - One Of the Best Dramas of the 2010's
Review: This masterpiece is one of the best movies I have seen in years. 'Joker' is beyond just an origin story for the iconic supervillian, far beyond actually. This is a bold movie with sustenance and more layers than can possibly be covered in a review.The acting is wonderful, and I'm not going to simply repeat what everyone else has said. Phoenix's performance was masterful and Oscar worthy. The directing as well as the writing of the screenplay was equally brilliant. The movie is unique in the best way and cannot easily be compared to anything else; the only film that I could remotely relate this to is "A Beautiful Mind". That being said, the comparison is because of the clever 'uncertainties' that both films use to get the viewers into the minds of the main characters.The film's main theme revolves about mental illness and how society's ignorance and neglect to people who suffer mentally can have grave consequences. It is an unapologetic display of the mind of a murderer while quietly educating the audience that compassion and understanding can go a long way. Critics calling the film 'irresponsible' and 'tasteless' clearly do not understand the film's true meaning: perhaps they are looking for another cranked out, uncreative, sterile superhero movie, or maybe the reason is much more complex. Being that 'Joker' is the top selling movie for October - ever... and the majority of America is in love with the film, I can't help but think these critics, writers, and magazines are simply out of touch with what the majority of America thinks, and maybe there is a reason for that.There are hundreds of articles published every day by second-tier, and sometimes even first-tier media outlets finding great horror in a semi off-color joke in a movie, or how books, tv shows, and movies should be banned in entirety. The popularity of web articles in general today are dependent on social media shares and promotions, the outlets themselves getting their revenue off of advertisements on their own sites. However, there has to be an incentive to 'click' on an article in the first place. Articles get 'noticed' and ranked higher on social media based on how many reactions there are be it comments, likes, shares... dislikes... arguments by multiple people... Unfortunately, an article that is literally meant to 'split the room' will do great because there is no reason to comment or share something that is universally agreed upon. Perhaps divisive, overly political, and easily offended writers are deliberately hired for this purpose.That being said, America loves 'Joker' and so do I. Here's to many more movies from the talented team and the studio that produced it. This will certainly go down as one of the most memorable films of this decade.

Review Title: Negative backlash makes you enjoy the film that much more
Review: I saw Joker today, and rather than just speak only on the film itself I want to talk about the negative criticism it is receiving. *skip to my last two paragraph's if you don't care about my thoughts on this to read my actual review.*First and foremost I walked out of the film thinking just "meh", but the actual negativity surrounding the film has done the opposite of what bad reviews are intended to do, and that is instead of swaying me to not see the film it actually makes me want to view the film again.If there was ever an example of film critics feeding into controversy, mainstream cinema, and the crappiness that is society this is the film. The film that is studied on college campuses in film school and journalism for those reasons. I mean it almost seems these film critics are going over the top with the negative superlatives just for the sake of it. Just don't listen to the negativity surrounding this film, but please read a few after seeing the film for yourself to understand what I am saying.At the same time I feel that director Todd Philips accomplished what he set out to do. He wasn't looking for that 100% score on Rotten tomatoes or 10 out of 10 on IMDB he wanted people to think, and that is better than any 100% review you can get. He also wanted to do something different with a fictional character that slowly descends into madness.The only difference being that this fictional character happens to be in the mainstream among society and has a coat of paint on them. I think if you took away the paint it might get a little more positive praise because the naysayers think that comic book characters inspire people so much.Joaquin Phoenix is brilliant in this film regardless if he is playing our favorite clown prince of crime or just another day average Joe. The trailers don't give you his performance away at all, and I like the fact they only tease not spoiling the film by not giving you really anything at all. The score goes wonderful with the tone and pacing of the film and the cinematography is fantastic.Go see it for yourself. Original score 3 1/2 stars but changed it to 4 because the haters made me actually enjoy the film that much more not because I wanted to boost the actual score.

Avoid anyone who gives this film a score lower than a four and take the reviews that say it is a perfect 10/10 with a grain of salt. This movie is about the psyche of a man by the name of Arthur Fleck (The Joker) who downtrodden by society to the greatest extent. Joker isn't the most intellectually stimulating movie but it gets close to being up there, it blurs the lines between what is actually happening and what is just one of the Joker's hallucinations.Joker explores themes behind how being a good person and thinking about how you treat others can have a greatly positive effect on the world (sounds childish but is executed very well) and what society can do to someone who doesn't fit in. If Arthur had someone to vent to and someone to talk too, just one friend, then this movie would be the opposite of what it is in its current state but he doesn't have that so it shows the implications in a raw and visceral fashion. All he has is the cruel, harsh world.I understand some people wouldn't like this movie just because of the premise of someone insane lashing out at society but it is still worth watching for the following reasons:Joaquin Phoenix was amazing, his performance was truly amazing.
The cinematography was great and the dialogue is good without falling into the trap of being overwritten.
The interactions the titular Arthur Fleck has with the world and other people are amazing.
The movie is spectacularly directed and the pace never feels either too slow or too fast for me. Some people complain that this movie feels like it goes on for three hours but only has a two hour running time, I did in fact feel the same way but only because so much was happening in such a short amount of time and actually made me enjoy the movie more.
This bleak depiction of Gotham truly brings out the best in the city, the trash piling up on the streets, the mugging, the cold streets. At one point The Joker says (I'm slightly paraphrasing as this is written from memory) that if he was found dead on the streets nobody would care and I have a feeling that this is probably true.
The film can get very emotionally gripping at times, Arthur Fleck's relationships to his mother and to his "girlfriend" are both very emotionally gripping.My complaints are simply that this movie feels like it is longer than it actually is because of how much happens and that might annoy some people.
A few of my friends think it is trying to hard to be smart that it comes of as pseudo-intellectual but I don't see it.Sorry for any bad grammar, English is my second language.

Review Title: Masterpiece in storytelling and character study that will leave you deeply unsettled
Review: Watched the premiere last night in local theatre and while I did go in with a lots of high expectations, I can honestly say that they were completely fulfilled, perhaps maybe in a different way from what I anticipated. This is a movie that the media pants as shocking and disturbing, but wouldn't necessarily say it like that. Perhaps it is to those who think our reality is very different from the one in Gotham City, or that there aren't many people like Arthur Fleck in this world.I would much rather paint this film as an deeply unsettling. It's not entirely possible for me to put in words how it felt while watching it; towards the end, more and more nervous, deeply anxious to the point where I didn't know if it was because of the movie or something more than that.There isn't much to say about Joakim Phoenix' performance that hasn't been said yet. Just wow. There aren't words that would do justice to his performance. At this point I don't even care if he gets an Oscar for this, because he transcended the credibility that award (still) has. I cannot even imagine the mental straight, self-consciousness, talent and hard work it takes to pull a role like this and make it so natural and organic. Portraying an already established characters, especially culturally iconic ones such as Joker, is already hard, but having the story centred around psychological development and transition from point A to point B, is just terrifically complex. I can only say bravo to Mr. Phoenix and hope he is aware he reached the highest of the hights.It shouldn't be fair not to mention Robert DeNiro, who also carried his supporting role amazing, making every second he was on screen count. All other actors gave strong performances as well, and because of them the story felt even more authentic and organic.Applause to Todd Philip's, to every single person involved, because they truly made something original and magnificent. The cinematography is impeccable, sound mixing, music, photography, directing, I mean, everything that is to a film, just perfect.Masterclass in storytelling. Magnificent psychological study of a character and interaction between individual and society. A must see.I kinda wish they continue the story just so I could watch more of Joakim as Joker and Gotham through eyes of Todd Phillips, but this move is so good that it does not deserve to be followed by anything more. It should stand in all its glory alone.(On a side note, how the heck does this movie has 62 score on Metacritic and Ad Astra, while very solid and beautiful movie, has a score of 80?)

So many different actors have been the joker. A role that everyone knows and is familiar with. How many times can we remake the story of a person, even if we try to to tell it from different perspectives or if we tell dissimilar stages of their life. It still is the same story. But in this case we can see how good it can actually work. The story about how Arthur Fleck became Joker - the story about the beginning. But it isn't really the same we have seen before.
The movie focusses on mental health - it tries to show us how brutal the world can be sometimes, how violent people can be without even recognizing it. We still not really know where insanity exactly comes from, but we do know that often social environment has a big impact on it just as home/origin. Joker is a metaphor for all that. Of course it is a violent story but the whole rumors about it before the film actually has started in the cinema are a big joke. It does not praise terrorism, not more than any other movie about a human who loses control or about an antihero. He could be a symbol for anything that goes wrong in our modern society. It could also just tell you to behave more careful and respectful. You can interpret so much in it, whatever you may feel. But I don't think that Joker is a role model for brutal behavior. Sure, if you wear a mask, if you change your outer appearance you can be whoever you want, but it's nothing new, nothing we did not know before. So hopefully the whole absurd "drama" about the film doesn't effect too much on how you see it. It doesn't even has to have a political statement or something. Overall it is worth any award and every watching - whether for the acting (Joaquin Phoenix did a incredible job every move, every facial expression and every posture is just perfect), for directing (Todd Phillips), the coloring (wow, every frame could be just a wallpaper), the soundtrack (makes you feel more nervous than the entire story), the camera (how we follow him while he runs) and the setting. I can't describe how delighted I am. Besides each turn in the plot (no spoiler, its too recent) is precious, on point and a great decision.

Review Title: It's dark, it's real... it's genius
Review: It's about time we concerned ourselves with this super-villain's origin, and I don't mean just for the sake of understanding the world of Batman... I argue that this film brings the audience closer to understanding our own nature as humans--aspects of our biology and social psychology that we try to dismiss. But, as I believe the film shows, ignorance is not bliss.The film is visceral. Step outside the shelter you thought the world was, and cross the tracks into the other side of Gotham City. You'll quickly find things don't always go the way you think they should. Of course, every movie is just a window into a world that you have no say in. But this one really makes you put your hands on the glass and tell yourself that if you were there, you would have made things different, you wouldn't have allowed these bad things to happen... But is that really true?In super hero movies, Batman for instance, you constantly imagine yourself as the hero. The struggles that Bruce Wayne goes through, you find parallels for in your own life. His triumphs you equate to a path you see for yourself. As you watch 'Joker', it may be uncomfortable to you that the rock-solid strength and morals of the hero are simply not there. Instead, the film looks to you for the answers. But without Batman's playbook to glance at, you might simply have none. All you can do is watch, and learn, quite frankly.Does this movie glorify the villain? No, it just doesn't ignore him. It reminds you that he is there, whether you know it or not, painting a bloody smile every day you fail to do something about it. It's humbling. By the end, you'll find yourself asking: who is the real villain? The Joker? The system that failed him? See for yourself, but in my opinion you wouldn't want to be on either side. There is nothing clear-cut about the problems this film presents you with, or the solutions you're likely to come up with. It's dark, it's real... it's genius.I'll leave you with this: If you believe that you, yes you, sitting there blissfully with your popcorn and soda, are not equal in nature to the man you see on the screen, then you're just another drop of makeup on the Joker's face. Spoiler alert: this story doesn't have a happy ending.Go see it!

Batman could never be one step ahead of the Joker because the Joker was random chaos, he doesn't have a motive or reason like the other villains. In the dark knight movie. Joker spends time robbing banks and later on in the movie he just lights the money on fire. He was robbing the banks for fun and to attract attention and create chaos, he didnt even care for the money. That's Joker's personality, completely mysterious and unpredictable and Batman could never understand his psychology.In this version, he has a full backstory and although he is crazy, you can kind of understand why he is crazy because of everything that happened to him, there is a reason to his craziness. His true identity also gets revealed when he shoots the host on national television. If he were to fight batman now, batman could immediately know Joker's life story from a simple Google search. Review Title: Truly Divisive, Law and Order or Not
Review: This movie brings out the division I've long noticed between the people who are close-minded law and order type and the open-minded crowd that sees the whole thing from a more abstract, higher-level perspective. My reactions are mixed for this movie. But what I found really frustrating is the 1-star reviewers who can't accept a moview portraying the perspective of the "villain" and then they purposefully give this movie the lowest score possible. Those people have to see a traditional villain-lose-the-game ending in order to go to sleep at night. This movie didn't offer them that. Rather, this movie challenged their deeply fixated social and moral codes. This is what I liked the most from this movie. It brought a new angle that made a lot of people uncomfortable - something that they never thought could be on stage. It doesn't have to have a right or wrong. And quite frankly the movie cleverly avoided talking much about right or wrong. The lack of clear distinction severely challenges the people who can only see black and white but nothing in between. They live in their close-minded world and fail to see the story from the other side's perspective as they have been bent on blindly accepting the authority's interpretation as the one and only "right" perspective and all others are wrong and evil. They are shocked that so many people gave this movie such a high score. They don't understand the enthusiasm and sentiment behind this. It makes them scared. The sentiment has always been there. They just simply refused to acknowledge it. "Let them eat cake," they say.Interesting enough, the ratings for this movie is also divided on age. Those <18 gave it a 9.4 average, while those 45 and older gave a 8.6. The reason behind that is all but confusing. The younger generation is indeed different, and the challenges they face in this world is unique as well. Perhaps it's not the violence that we should worry about. Perhaps too often we attach fixated labels to others foreign and different and refuse to even look into the other person's perspective and narrative. Way too often we think the worst of others, and the best of us. We are always right; they are always wrong.

Review Title: Delivers great acting with an overall plot that, glorifys the worst parts of humanity.
Review: The film in itself was something to be excited about. Who doesn't want a Gotham's Joker adaptation? I found myself very anticipated to watch this flick. When I saw the film I left feeling like I watched an amazing movie. The cinematography was excellent. Had a lot of thought provoking shots that excelled in creating very dramatic scenes that supplied constant emotion and the "edgy" feel if you will. The story made you sympathize with the Arthur and why he became the villain he is. We see a man ostracized from society for being quite different. He has mental health issues and he really doesn't know his place in the world. He is peculiar which draws negative attention and back lash from people in general. The story in itself delivered in giving an adaptation of the Joker. My only problem with the film, isn't in itself the movie was bad in a sense. My problem is that we as people find these type of stories to be good to watch. Nothing about this film is "good". There are dark films that make us learn something about who we are as people. In the Joker Gotham shows a society in which we shun the black sheep. We hate and ridicule the unfortunate to be hung in effigy for what is considered normal. If you do not act this way you are therefore different and should be mocked and laughed at. This is relevant especially in today's day in age where people on the internet satirize celebrities forgetting they are regular people. What is equally bad is we satirize regular people who are just like you and me. Who at there core are human beings who should be treated with respect and dignity; regardless of what you believe in. What saddens me is that even though the Joker is fiction there are people like Arthur Fleck who experience the same struggles everyday and are one day away from taking their anger out on the world. The kindness you extend to others, you extend to yourself. On the contrary, the evil you extend to the world, you extend to yourself. I think this film is a sad reminder on what the masses can do in helping create the villain that ironically we end up idolizing and put on display to sell tickets. I would like to think we are better than that as a human race, but even through my past and my actions: I am sad to say we might not be. You realize we as humans you, me, and everybody else are stupid and unknowingly we could be creating the next Arthur Fleck. We don't know half the time why we are laughing at something not knowing there is a deep suffering to some of the humor we use. Decide for yourself what is worth your enjoyment.This movie overall sucked looking back and I am sorry I brought my little brother to see this.

I'll show you a magic trick and start on the positive note:"Joker" is filmed well partially, and you can admire some good - though no memorable - shots here and there.There are 1-2 scenes that blend in quite well with the Batman canon, making the Batman and Joker fans hearts beat faster.
"Joker" lives most of the time on his main actor Joaquin Phoenix. Phoenix is doing really well; he has always been a special actor. But in the end his performance is just that: good, not phenomenal.Due to the script he cannot give the character of the joker a new facet or add something new to it.The Joker's personality remains superficial most of the time and the screenplay unfortunately causes him to stumble along increasingly redundant, predictable and stereotypical plot-points, as we have seen too often.Both the movie and the joker remain empty and superficial and are hardly ever substantively enriched. The transformation of the mentally disturbed clown is surprisingly harmless and the pathology of his psychic nature terribly trivial and flat. But that's also due to the other leading actor in the film: Gotham City.One hardly notices the mostly just indicated sinfulness. Like the rest of the movie, it stays on the surface, but does not even scratch it.This is a pity and wasted potential, the old rule "show, do not tell" should have been followed here. It is never tangible to the viewer, this allegedly abnormal city and its supposedly so disgusting people. The city is on fire and burning - completely unnoticed by the audience barely shown through some piles of garbage, that can be found on New York City's streets on every given workday. Yes, this Gotham can be uncomfortable, as well as some characters in the movie. However, the Joker's inner diabolical pain is never shown in them, they are simple templates without really testing the limits of social and cinematic cruelty and the resilience of tried-and-tested viewers.Constantly one wonders whether this Gotham is so brutal or is it the Joker who is mentally too unstable. Or is it just me who has seen too many movies? Ok, I confess. The latter was a joke. No joke: The film wants to be provocative without being provocative. But what does it really want?Even with the portrayal of graphic violence, the movie is holding back so much that you really must wonder if Warner Bros. even launched the media-hyped reports of people fleeing the cinemas out of sheer horror itself.It would be possible because compared to thematically similar or visually related films like "Fight Club", "Seven" or even "The Dark Knight" - "Joker" is not a journey into the heart of darkness, but a journey into unimaginativeness. He's not that beast, not a monster, not even - and the joker itself would love that - chaos.Maybe the creators wanted a superficial film about a superficial society. At least that would be kind of Meta after all. And in a way funny. Because one way or another one would have achieved the goal: The film "Joker" is a Joke. Unfortunately, an average one.Redundant, superficial, pretentious, despondent.Ta-dah!

Review Title: What do you get when you cross Joaquin Phoenix and Todd Phillips? You get what every Joker fan deserves.
Review: Review originally posted on https://geeklysian.wordpress.com/I have a bad tendency to preface. I'm not sure why, just always have. It's instinctual. Whether I'm commentating a video, telling a story in person, or even writing this article at the moment, I like to provide all the background information. In this case, I should note that the Joker is one of my favorite fictional characters. Not simply a favorite comic book character, no, I'm talking all of fiction of any medium. I've even gone as far as to memorialize the character on my right forearm as a tattoo (my others are Mass Effect & Avril Lavigne). So, it's safe to assume I'm probably bias in regards to Joker because I did go in fully wanting to love it. However, instead of "bias", you could consider it a PSA as well."Warning: Your experience with Joker will depend entirely on the perspective and expectations you set before even taking your seat."Now, sure, I'm aware that can be said for any movie, but it feels especially true in this situation considering the drummed up controversy that has surrounded the film. The beauty and genius of Joker is that the narrative is spun in such a manner that there isn't any one superior interpretation. If you've fallen to the media's scare tactics and expect Joker to be a glorified, violent romp, then you'll probably leave the theatre feeling those concerns were validated and quickly take to your own respective blogs to share in the outrage. If you were supporting this movie to show Warner Bros. there's still interest in dark, gritty adaptations of DC Comics' properties in the hope that the Snyder Cut would be released, you'll be sorely disappointed and should start considering seeking professional help to overcome your inability to move on. If you're a fan that understands the character, is able to distinguish between fiction and reality, and is admittedly somewhat of an edgelord, you're in for a treat that'll be sure to make you smile as only "Mistah J" can."Wait, did you say 'smile'? But I thought this was a dramatic thriller about someone suffering from mental illness that spirals towards madness?"You're right, it is (thanks for that "short and not-so-sweet" synopsis by the way), but it's also a comedy. And before you alert any intelligence or law enforcement agencies: 1) I'm sure I'm already on numerous lists, so you'd be wasting your time. 2) Remember that comedy is subjective, which is actually a major theme during the story.When I refer to Joker being a comedy, I don't mean the kinds that the genre are known for. It isn't like previous films directed by Todd Phillips either. There aren't any middle aged, white dudes wilding out as they go through a midlife crisis... oh, wait, I suppose that would be somewhat accurate actually. Anyway, Joaquin Phoenix won't be blazing it up with Zach Galifianakis (thanks spellcheck) and getting abandoned on a roof or escorting Iron Holmes across country in time to deliver his unborn child. No, no, no. The comedy in this film is of the darker variety and evolves or transforms over the course of the movie alongside Arthur (Joker's name pre-transformation - "Jack Napier" who?). This was a highlight for me that I haven't noticed being discussed as much, instead being overshadowed by either the "problematic" nature of the scenes or the abundance of praise for the brilliant acting (which is completely fair). I suppose that it's also possible that I'm in the minority that found some of the later scenes and "jokes" funny, but I know I'm not alone, at least. Others laughed in the theatre too, I swear! That also just exemplifies the affect the film's narrative had on me by easily luring me in and enabling me to enjoy the chaos and macabre humor of the Joker. As someone that indulges in guilty pleasures though, like playing through the Mass Effect series as a renegade and kicking mercenaries out of skyscrapers, it was never going to be challenging for Joker to sweep me off my feet. This all circles back to my opening PSA, of course. If you're a goody-two-shoes (pulling out the elementary insults, Doc) then you'll need to be able to at least appreciate Joker for its darkness if you're unable to revel in it yourself.As for the acting, I briefly touched upon this, but allow me to also give Joaquin Phoenix a golden shower of praise for the best performance of the Clown Prince yet!"Uh, that's not what 'golden shower' means and *le gasp* what about Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight?"Oh, it's not? Well, time to remix the ignition on this review. Eh? Get it? Whatever.... And yes, it may be a hot take or recency bias, but I'd say this version of the Joker is, at least, on the same tier as The Dark Knight. I do think, though, it wouldn't be right to directly compare them since they're such vastly different interpretations of the character that which one anyone prefers likely is more so a result of liking the interpretation than actual critique of the performances. But hey, as long as we all agree Jared Leto never happened, I'm satisfied with Heath & Joaquin sharing the title of best live-action Joker.Despite this being primarily an origin story, a recurring theme in the comics, The Dark Knight, and in Joker is that if he has to have an origin story, he'd rather it be multiple choice. The cinematography lends itself well to this element of the narrative. If you've read other reviews or have been discussing the movie yourself with friends (wow, look at the big shot with his companionship) then you'll notice there's many opinions on what actually happened in Joker. This is because there's so many strange scenes or clever tricks of the camera that will cause you doubting what's real and what's another delusion of Arthur's spiraling madness. There's also a similar sense of evolution or transformation as I described with the humor. In earlier scenes Arthur is miserable, the lighting is dark, colors are faded, and in general there's a feeling of bleakness. Once Arthur starts to become the Joker, however, it's as if the world flips on its head. He's more confident, it's brighter, the world is more vibrant, and over all everything seems better, at least for him. This all helps you with connecting and understanding the character as each scene, each camera angle acts as a window into his mind.Last, but certainly not least, we have the score. I'll be honest with you (more honest than the Joker, for what that's worth), I actually had to update this article to include this as I forgot. I'm the type that's always preferred music be uobtrusive (so as you can imagine I wasn't a big Guitar Hero fan), so I never developed a critical ear for it. I'm usually more focused on the acting, the story, the cinematography, etc. That said, the score and one song in particular had a big impact on the film and has been stuck in my head since. Just as Joker breathes new life into a classic character, so too does it rejuvenate a classic song. In fact, that the song is so woven into the narrative itself is likely the reason I didn't consider the score separately during the original writing because with Joker everything just comes together as one amazing package. And I can't think of a clincher sentence now which is unfortunate, but hey, That's Life.ConclusionWhat do you get when you cross Joaquin Phoenix and Todd Phillips? You get what every Joker fan deserves. An iteration of the character to finally rival The Dark Knight's and a film in which every element of production came together perfectly to create one of the best movies of our time.Final Rating - 5/5 Stars! (Translated to 10/10 for IMDb)

Review Title: Joaquin Phoenix gives a brilliant and dedicated performance
Review: My first review. Not only is Todd Phillip's 'Joker' an incredible character study with Phoenix's portrayal of Arthur Fleck, but there are so many filmmaking techniques involved to make this film special. The use of certain colors to portray a dark Gotham City (which is really NYC), brilliant cinematography, clever shot structure and great direction. If Joaquin Phoenix doesn't win his first Oscar for this performance, then nobody should. This is coming from someone who is not at all a fan of DC or Marvel, which should show you how very special this film really is. Nothing, in my opinion, will ever top Heath Ledger's performance in The Dark Knight, but Joaquin Phoenix is just as great here, as he really allows the audience to witness Arthur Fleck's descent into becoming the Joker. Go watch this film and enjoy Phoenix's remarkable portrayal of one of cinema's most villainous characters.

I went back to see this movie two nights ago in a lonely suburban Edwards at 11pm because I wanted to see this film again, not for praise but because it's so controversial and because I still think it's fun to have these discussions anywhere online now. So...
The biggest thing for me is how lofty the film feels, as though the creative team is fully aware of the edgy grandiose sort of following it could acquire, couple that with the fact that the films plot very heavily relies mostly upon the joker the and the study of that character makes the main performance seem somewhat contrived. And the more I'm seeing ads, videos, pictures, interviews, articles or whatnot about the movie that feeling only materializes.Joker, the character itself is already such a demanding and engrossing role to begin with, and undeniably whoever plays the character on screen has played, and will play, will always create some sort of buzz of stir up some sort of drama. Note that this is very common knowledge, everyone knows how big of a role the joker is. When you that role for a 2 hour film that focuses solely on the character and almost nothing more, sure environmental and societal reflections peak through here and there and set up the context for the character, regardless, it feels unnecessary. As stated before in the review, yes the world is cruel, yeah it can make someone crazy. And I'm not saying that this is what the film is trying to say and that I think it's irresponsible to promote the behavior illustrated, in just saying it feels unnecessary; like writing a book about a father who died and a boy who afterwards grieved. What I mean here is that this is a film about a somewhat typical human response, albeit slightly heightened as he is the joker and quite literally goes insane, regardless there's no bigger lesson, or takeaway. And so for that people say it's a character study, okay that's fine I'd love to see that movie except it's not. It's not a fight club where the figures represent some piece of his consciousness or ego, allowing the audience insight into an interesting character, and done in a way that both engages the audience and keeps them guessing. It builds and builds, author gets beaten and pushed to the point where he snaps. And I guess I can sympathize with that, but only to an extent. Secondly and more importantly -and this connects back to why I mentioned the grand allure and notion of the joker role - I almost hate the film because it knows it's good, the performance, and it rides oh so heavily on it. It's being shoved down my throat and I get it, it is good. It's hard to hone in on the feeling I get specifically for the film without completely dissecting it, but it just feels as if every single person that made the film knew the amazing performance Joaquin Phoenix was putting on the table, capitalized on it, and revolved the entire film around it. It works, but to am extent, like yes the film is perfect for what they could do with it. Overall though I thought it was alright, maybe a good film with outstanding parts. In personal taste, and this is PERSONAL TASTE, I enjoy those performances that standout and that show those silvers of humanity in a basic role or in a scenario that didn't really beg for it, because that's how life works, that's realistic. The film is absolutely beautiful and the art direction if anything should win an Oscar, but sadly the aesthetic as gorgeous as it is, and perhaps the one great thing I admire about the film, just adds to the pretension when wondering whether this was also used to engage audiences into an otherwise drab plot. Joker (2019), directed by Todd Phillips, discovers an unreachable citizen who is supposed to give us an action packed show. Instead, we get a gut wrenching feeling as Arthur Fleck (Phoenix) fails to enlighten an audience with awkwardness and off-kilter humor. Arthur becomes lost through his mental illness and is displayed as a creepy and psycho character. Arthurs failure to connect with others due to his mental illness involves struggling depression where all he can say at points is "I just don't want to feel so bad anymore". For many, laughter can be the best medicine for sadness, anger, or confusion. Although, this statement is far from true for Arthur Fleck (Phoenix). The specific perception of Arthur leaves him with no friends and an intense, extensive struggle to maintain his job as a clown. Arthur continuously gets made fun of and receives failure to be understood which fumes anger and vengeance inside of him.Much like Taxi Driver's Travis Bickle (Robert De Niro), Arthur was a lost soul because of the absent interactions in his life. They both enter a breaking point where the population pushes them too far mentally. For Arthur, this starts with picking various fights downtown. This becomes an uphill battle for Arthur because he was going unnoticed by almost everyone and all most all didn't care about welfare. As the plot lays out throughout the first part of the movie, the viewers create sympathy for Arthur because of his mental illness and how he is treated by others. The sympathy created is because of Phoenix's great acting and perception of his charter. He gives Arthur a caring, playful soul instead of a character full of self pity. Although, self pity is very apparent when Arthur starts lashing out. He goes after those who he feels have betrayed or gone against him which is why people say "well he got picked on and pushed to his limits, no wonder he acted out as such". Either way, Phoenix's acting and performance was next to none because of the facts that he lets the viewer decide the way they perceive the ill-humored Arthur Fleck.Accustomed to being bullied, Arthur enjoyed having the "last laugh" for once. As a viewer, this became the biggest thrill with the movie. The suspense of all his anger finally piercing through his skin was a thriller and an occurrence wanted from the audience. This act was brewing inside of Arthur in which he finally snapped. This was a big plot shift in the movie where people started to perceive Arthur more of a villain than before.Although this was a great acting experience by Phoenix, I felt that this movie lacked a theme along with absent sense of humor. Throughout the movie, although Arthur did evolve, there wasn't an evolving plot around him. Along with that, the humor displayed was taken differently from everyone around me when watching which I felt showed weakness. Overall, this was a great acting performance by Phoenix which many different types of people can connect to and follow along with easily.

Review Title: Best Movie About The Joker Yet
Review:
Since the Jokers first appeared in the comic book Batman in 1940, the Joker has been a famous super villain character portrayed in many films and comic books throughout the years as the archenemy of Batman. Recently in 2008, Christopher Nolan produced The Dark Night which showed the sinister and evil Joker. In the origin story Joker, The director Todd Phillips took a different route on how the Joker character was conveyed and I must say I was impressed. Phillips created a new film where the Joker became the protagonist of and altered the way fans, like myself, portrayed the Joker character. Philips introduced a fresh and creative perspective of the Joker that made the film both exciting and captivating. As a Batman vs. Joker fan, it was very exciting to see a film strictly focusing on the Joker and its profound message targeting society and mental illnesses. On top of bringing a new perspective, Philips also managed to integrate the perfect amount of nostalgia from previous films that gave a whole new excitement for upcoming movies.
Joker is a drama/thriller that tells the story of Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix), a failed mentaly ill stand up comedian that slowly falls into madness as society continues to treat him poorly. After the last straw, Arthur turns to violence stirring problems in Gotham City.
To be honest, hearing that a movie about the origin of the Joker was a little worrisome, but after watching Joaquin Phoenix's exceptional performance acting as the joker, it truly gave me the chills. In my opinion, I don't think anyone could have done it better than Joaquin Phoenix. Although it may seem Heath Ledger is hard to beat after starring in The Dark Knight, but I still think Phoenix deserves a much bigger applause. In Ledger's defense, The Dark Knight portrayed the Joker as a sinister psychopath that was just truly evil. On the other hand, Joker portrayed him as a mentally ill loner who was just lost. One particular aspect I thought Phoenix did that made the movie mover captivating was when he did the iconic Joker laugh. Throughout the movie, Phoenix's horrific and scary laugh really made it seem like Phoenix transformed himself into the Joker character and made the film much more enjoyable.
Another key strength of the film that I really enjoyed seeing develop throughout the film was how the mood and music transformed throughout the movie. For the first half of the film, the scenes displays darkness and depression through Arthurs constant beat downs. During this first half of the film, Philips protrayes Arthurs life as sort of a living hell in which he feels like he doesn't belong which is one major theme Philips shows. This dark mood sets up the rest of the film perfectly as it changes drastically as the film comes to an intense climax and truly had me sitting on the edge of my seat. After finally figuring out who he is, Arthurs mood changes and so does each scene which began to show the real Joker we know and love. To show this mood and scene shift, Phillips used Arthurs dancing scenes symbolizing the feeling of belonging. Early in the play after Arthur was badly beaten, Arthur danced slowly in a dark bathroom which showed his bad state of mind and severe depression. In contrast, later on in the film Arthur danced again but with a clear shift. This time Arthur was dancing with happiness and freedom because he finally knew who he wanted to be. The music also shifted from a slow sad song to an upbeat rock and roll song that clearly shifted the mood of the fílm and I thought was a major contribution to the success of the film.
In conclusion, I highly recommend Joker to anyone even if they are too much of a Batman fan. The film didn't have too much action like past films with the Joker, for example The Dark Knight and all those sinister nail biting scenes. It would've been nice seeing a little more violent scenes in the Joker but I think Phillips did a great job integrating more about Arthur's personal life and not about killing people. I felt like with the help of Phoenix's acting and Phillips directing, the film Joker was exhilarating and left me more than satisfied.

Review: Preface"The Joker" is far from a social film about the poor and the rich, and certainly not about the Joker, whom we know from comics. All this is a wrapper in which the viewer can easily lose the essence of this picture. Having all our ideas that the Joker should not be such an extremely dull and weak character, as shown in the film, we miss the important thing, that first of all this is an author's film under the wing of Todd Phillips. Yes, he is a little clumsy in storytelling, and the direction is sometimes both outstanding and pretentious, but all this does not exclude one fact... The film has a high significance in a world where comic book films must be simple, regardless of what kind of ton of performance they are: dark or funny. This shows that the audience (taking into account the box office) is ready even for such films, where their value for the most part lies in what the author wants to say, and not in what huge money the producers will grab."Is it me... or is the whole world going crazy ?"The protagonist of the story about a psychopathic killer is Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix), who, being under the yoke of the dangerous, his inhabitants of the city of Gotham, where everyone is ready to bite each other's throats for nothing, continues to remain optimistic, no matter what. He wants to become a stand-up comedian with his non-standard sense of humor to see his share of charm in the manifestation of violence. And in general, all this flows for the entire film. The main character is reconciled with the fact that his whole life, which seemed to him a tragedy, was actually a comedy, a joke, in which only he understands the punchline. But even here it's not so simple. The film is based on Arthur Fleck, and not on anyone else, which means that if you look at all this correctly through the eyes of the main character, then together with him you can catch the very joke that he does not tell.I would like to write separately about how the musical accompaniment and camerawork make this film truly a masterpiece. I could talk for hours about the scene in which Arthur is dancing in the toilet, based on these cinema tools that convey a strong visual and audio narrative. So I will limit myself to the fact that the cameraman (Lawrence Sher) skillfully emphasizes the spiritual world of Arthur, as at this time the composer (Hildur Gudnadouttir) gives out music that is unusually creep with a share of romanticism, conveying the importance of this world for the hero. As for directing, everything is much more complicated here.Todd Phillips understands what the film is about, but when watching it, it seems that the director does not skillfully observe the narrative of the story, and sometimes even greatly exaggerates, adding so much eventfulness to it that the viewer will start to have a headache after that. The director weighs too much of the madhouse on Arthur, which makes you wonder how you can not hang yourself right after that. Some moments can be cut out (a love line; a false father, etc.). After all, there are already plenty of topics in the film that should already be competently developed in the course of history, but instead, the director overloads the viewer with unnecessary subtexts in the second act of the film, making it monotonous to hell, and that's why it's tiring.ResultSo what is the Joker's joke? To understand it, I want you to pay attention to how the scene in which teenagers beat Arthur is filmed, and the scene where little Bruce Wayne loses his parents, and then think about it yourself. For me personally, the film is not a masterpiece, but I will not deny the fact that this film will be a masterpiece for you. For the most part, the only thing that pleases me is that such a heavy drama with a comic theme has collected a huge amount of money with a modest budget, which means that it is possible that films of this kind will continue in huge numbers. This film was not about the Joker, but rather about the fact that everyone can become a Joker, and it only takes one bad day for this.9 out of 10.

Review Title: A film for people who actually read comic books!

It's hard to escape the heavy nod that Todd Phillips tips to Scorcese's "King of Comedy" and a healthy homage to Wally Pfister's cinematography in Nolan's Trilogy. This is a fun way to handle this type of material. Reinvent rather than retread. It demonstrates a similar type of maturity that began filtering into comic books themselves during the silver age of comic storytelling... when the art form began to take bigger and bigger chances, introducing politics and philosophy as ways for the stories to shine lights on the ills and troubles plaguing society at their respective times. If all art is communication, then the development of art is an aim towards becoming commentary that breaks through - a discourse rising above expected platitudes and transcending pure aesthetics. Mr. Phillips, I won't say that you've gotten any better as a director, but you remain provocative and a bit depraved, and you know who your subjects are and what makes them interesting. You've come a long way since "Hated", but luckily not TOO far.

As the film went on, it felt like a character study rather a film. A documentary depicting the mind of Arthur. As the film danced on you slowly saw him unravel with each laugh, smile and frown. You saw each shift in mindset and depth.
His persona felt chillingly natural and on numerous occasions I felt my heart rate increase and my body clench. Simply caused by the on screen anarchy. It was extremely uncomfortable viewing. But this is the genius of the film. Visually it felt old and retro however tonality it felt present and possible.
Joaquin stole the show. He was unsettlingly brilliant. He deserves every award and nomination that falls his way. The obvious question is how does he compare to Ledger? Quite frankly who cares. They are equally brilliant in their own way. In many ways they are incomparable and the only thing they share is the name of their character.

Review Title: A defenitive masterpiece propelled by a once in a lifetime performance by Joaquin phoenix
Review:
The opening sequence shows a group of street children picking on a helpless Joaquin phoenix. They proclaim that he is weak and beat him up. That's is exactly what is wrong with society. Be it the society in today's times or earlier times, bullying and picking on the weaker sections are constantly persistent and not being spoken of many a times. Joker is ridiculed, constantly bullied and picked upon which brings about a Change in him. The society has never cared for people with mental illness and quite simply neglects them. The gritty portrayal of the society in its real way is a great job done by direction and writing.Lawrence sher gives a cinematography which engages you and at the same time makes you wary of every little detail. The movement of the camera to cover the dance sequences of Joaquin phoenix is poetry in motion. The long shots intensely zoomed in on the joker gives us time to channelise and compartmentalize the feelings of those on screen.Robert de Niro plays Franklin Murphy which is almost the continuation of his role from the ending sequences of The King of comedy (1982). He represents everything the materialistic society which is comfortable with doses of fun and not caring for the real problem existing in the outside world.The film is haunting and stays with you quite sometime. This is mainly due to the theme it tackles and also partly because of its heart pounding music. The writing of the film says That "Society makes the man " and not the opposite which is usually said.
This film will surely stand the test of time and emerge as one of the greatest character studies made on a comicbook character. Heath ledger would definitely be smiling from the heavens.

This movie left me speechless and has stayed with me for days now.Joaquin's performance undoubtedly deserves a best actor nomination and sits comfortably among the best Joker portrayals. I don't think it's useful to compare his to Heath Ledger's effort as they are both excellent in their own right, and each serve their respective stories perfectly. This story however, is a different, much more gritty tale that the excellent Dark Night movies. This is something else entirely and as long as you are not expecting an adrenaline fuelled action romp then I fail to see how anyone could find fault here. The acting and cinematography completely blew me away and I hope everyone involved gets the recognition they deserve.One valid criticism I've heard is that this Joker doesn't show the kind of criminal genius that we might expect from one of DC's greatest villains. While I agree with that to some extent, what has been created here is exceptionally good and I feel it excels largely for not trying to bend to a more cartoon-like narrative.The movie doesn't feature as much violence as I had expected, but what there was felt all the more real and powerful for it. This film is the darkest, most raw and disturbing that I can remember. I'm not even sure if I'll re-watch it. I don't need to. It will already stay with me as one of the most powerful movies I have ever seen.

Review Title: Joaquin Phoenix, thy name is Joker
Review: O. M. G. Joaquin Phoenix, thy name is Joker. The clothes, the make-up, the mannerisms, the mad dancing, the laughter. I never thought it possible to top Heath Ledger's brilliant portrayal of Joker, but Joaquin Phoenix did it. Perhaps it's not fair to make the comparison, but there it is. Joaquin in full bore Joker mode BECAME the Joker. And it was a brilliant touch to attribute his uncontrollable laughter to an actual disorder: the pseudobulbar affect.I won't belabor. The script, the supporting cast, the musical score, the this, the that, I don't even care. I'll leave that analysis to others. Suffice to say Joaquin Phoenix carried the day. He alone is worth the price of admission.In a perfect world, this would be done up as a nice, tidy little trilogy.

A dark reflection of a man's descent into the nightmare world of mental illness and it's repercussions on a society that offers him no empathy, understanding or contrition. Arthur is a desperately sad individual who is the victim of his own utterly dysfunctional upbringing, a mental condition that causes him to laugh inappropriately and his complete inability to engage with his colleagues or interact with society. Phoenix is phenomenal, an actor who must have studied and understood the illness he expertly portrays and the catastrophic results if it is left untreated.
Arthur is a clown and a failed comedian who, due to the collapse of social care has his treatment funding and his medication withdrawn. He's his mother's carer and obsessed with De Niro's TV character. That's all you need to know.
The violence is extreme, bloody but totally in context with the character and plot, however many will find one particular scene extremely disturbing. You've been warned.
A brilliant film, disturbing, harrowing and thoroughly gripping. Washington Post scored it 2/4 - ignore it and make up your own mind.

Review Title: JOKER is not the film we deserved but the film we needed.
Review: JOKER is definitely one of the best films I've ever seen. An amazing viewing experience from beginning to end. The cinematography is absolutely incredible, the shots, the camera angles and locations, were spectacular. The musical score is simply brilliant and provides an intense emotional thrill throughout the entire film. Joaquin Phoenix's performance is impeccable and is completely mesmerising throughout. The supporting cast including Robert de Niro were also amazing. The film is one of the most intense cinematic pieces of art in a long time. This is how you produce a origin story for one of the most notorious and popular comic-book villains of all time. The film completely serves the title of JOKER justice and ultimately respects him as a legend and an icon in the comic universe. The film has the most intense sequences in cinematic viewing, leaving me on the edge of my seat towards the end of the movie. This film may not be for the faint of heart, but this film needs to be experienced in a theatre, even if you're not into comic-book characters or movies. It has a superbly written storyline, that needs to be told, and needs to be seen. I have nothing bad to say about it. There wasn't a single scene throughout the entire film that was bad. It's a piece of cinematic art. JOKER IS A MASTERPIECE.
